title: Packers-Cowboys Matchups: Green Bay Has Only One Advantage (But It’s Huge)
full_text:
The Green Bay Packers are riding high after a 31-7 win over the Chicago Bears, and will now move to their second of four consecutive games against teams that hope to be in the NFC playoff picture by the end of the season.
The Dallas Cowboys are coming to Lambeau Field for a Sunday night matchup, and they’ll be on extended rest after losing to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Thursday night.
Can the Packers string together some success, improve to 4-2 and get their season fully on track after it looked destined to be headed off the rails through the first month of the season?
Here are the matchups that will determine whether they do or not.
Jonathan Gannon and Dak Prescott are familiar with each other. Gannon was the defensive coordinator for the Philadelphia Eagles in 2022 and faced Prescott once during that season. Prescott threw for 347 yards, three touchdowns and led the Cowboys to 40 points against an Eagles team that fell just short of a Super Bowl.
They faced off when Gannon was the head coach in Arizona in 2023. Prescott threw for 249 yards, one touchdown and one interception while only being able to muster 16 points. Last year, Gannon held the Cowboys’ offense down again, allowing just 17 points.
Of course, the personnel is drastically different. Green Bay’s defense was dominant against Tyson Bagent and Case Keenum on Sunday. Yes, those are backup quarterbacks, but the Packers have struggled against Tommy DeVito in the not-so-distant past.
This week is a much more difficult challenge. The Cowboys are loaded with talent on offense, especially at receiver. CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens are arguably the top receiver duo in the NFL. The Packers’ secondary has been a potential sore spot during the season, but they have not really been tested by a top-tier receiver since facing Justin Jefferson in Minnesota the first week of the season.
Can the pass rush, which had four sacks on Sunday, make Prescott uncomfortable without Micah Parsons on the field? Last year, the answer was no. The Packers sacked Prescott once as he put up 40 points on Green Bay’s defense.
This is the matchup that will decide the game on Sunday. One potential key to watch is Prescott’s propensity to make some mistakes. The Packers are coming off a game in which they had five takeaways, including three interceptions. In a game that could be a shootout, takeaways could decide the game.
Much like the passing defense is coming off its best game of the season, Green Bay’s run defense was excellent against Chicago. Some of that was due to game flow, with the Bears chasing a two-score deficit for most of the game. Some of that was also due to the absence of Kyle Monangai, who is Chicago’s most violent runner.
Still, they held D’Andre Swift to 43 yards on nine carries. They held the Bears to 81 rushing yards, which was more than 100 yards less than their season average and by far their lowest total of the season.
Dallas averages just 3.8 yards per carry. The question for the Packers is how much will the absence of Javon Hargrave affect their run defense. Hargrave’s injury likely bumps rookie Chris McClellan into an even bigger role. Plus, first-year player Anthony Campbell will have to rebound quickly after missing the last three games with an ankle injury. Are either ready?
They’ll face an offensive line that is big and got a boost last week with the return of Pro Bowl guard Tyler Smith. Perhaps that will kickstart a ground game led by Javonte Williams. Overall, the Packers are riding higher coming into the game, but the unknowns on both sides make this too tough to call.
Dallas made some significant changes after their defense was one of the worst in football in 2025. Christian Parker was named defensive coordinator, Caleb Downs was drafted in the first round, and they did some work on their defensive line, including trading for former Packers edge Rashan Gary.
Through five games, Gary has 15 pressures and one sack. That appears to be another trade with the Cowboys that the Packers won.
Dallas’ defense is putrid. It’s ranked 30th in passing yards allowed per play and are last with an opponent passer rating of 120.5. They have zero interceptions and are 29th in sack percentage.
Conversely, Jordan Love is coming off his best game of the season. His reconfigured offensive line has afforded him much better protection than the one that stood in front of him for the first three weeks.
Green Bay’s offense tore apart the Chicago defense. Love completed 25 of his 31 passes for 367 yards and two touchdowns. He had as many completions on passes thrown 20-plus yards downfield as total incompletions. Both of his top receivers went for over 120 yards and Tucker Kraft looked as good as he has all season.
“Obviously, we’re always trying to get our playmakers the ball and those two guys are our best playmakers in that room right now,” coach Matt LaFleur said of Christian Watson and Matthew Golden’s combined 266 receiving yards vs. Chicago.
Sunday could mark the debut for Kevin Zeitler at right guard, although Travis Glover has played well since earning the starting job for the last two games.
Either way, there appears to be some stability up front for the Packers. Love is comfortable in the pocket – and a comfortable Love is not a sight a lot of defenses want to see. A bad defense definitely does not want to see that.
The stoppable force meets the movable object.
That’s not a joke, these teams are both ranked last in the NFL in this phase of the game. The Cowboys gave up 241 rushing yards against Tampa Bay. With Kenny Clark in the middle of the defensive line, they are last with 168.4 rushing yards allowed per game – 12 yards worse than any other team – and 29th with 5.10 yards allowed per attempt.
The Packers’ run game is so bad that we’re calling a game in which MarShawn Lloyd ran for 31 yards on 10 carries a step in the right direction.
It’s true. Lloyd looked more comfortable as a runner than he has during his career. He found the end zone twice, including running over Jaylon Johnson en route to his first score of the game. Is this the week the Packers’ ground game finds some traction?
It’s hard to say, but if there were ever a team to find some room to rumble against, it’d be the Dallas Cowboys.
Dallas’ special teams has one of the top kickers in football with kicker Brandon Aubrey, who is in scoring position as soon as the ball crosses the 50-yard line. He has struggled more than he usually does this year, as he’s 9-of-12 on field goals.
Their return game is led by KaVontae Turpin, who has some juice and is able to take the ball the distance. He did struggle last week against the Buccaneers with a costly fumble that resulted in points for the Bucs.
Green Bay’s special teams have been solid if unspectacular. The emergence of Trey Smack as a weapon at kicker and Skyy Moore providing competence in the return game has given them a baseline of at least average play.
Moore did leave Sunday’s game with an ankle injury, and Matthew Golden replaced him as a punt returner. That’s a situation worth monitoring this week, though coach Matt LaFleur said there was short-term concern for Moore – meaning it’s more likely that not that he will miss this game. Golden did have a nice debut with a 17-yard return late in the first half, when he looked more comfortable returning punts than he did all of last season or in training camp this summer.
Smack missed two field goals and one extra point after having a total of two missed kicks (one extra point and one field goal that was blocked) the first four games. Smack’s accuracy is something to watch this weekend.
“We’ve got a ton of confidence in him, and I think he’s built the right way in terms of his mindset,” LaFleur said on Monday. “I think you’ll see a guy that’s pretty determined. I don’t think he’ll be shaken up by that at all.”

title: Playoffs? After Terrible Start, Here’s Where Packers Stand in NFC Playoff Race
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers looked like one of the worst teams in the NFL when they were booed off the field in their loss to the Atlanta Falcons two weeks ago. Their victory over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers didn’t exactly create more confidence in their playoff viability.
So, what a difference one game can make. The Packers blasted the Chicago Bears on Sunday. For all of the stupid penalties and sloppy play, they have a 3-2 record. If the season were to end today – with 12 games remaining, the season, obviously, is a lot closer to the starting line than the finish line – the Packers would be in a familiar place.
The Packers are in fifth place in the latest NFC playoff standings. That’s the No. 1 spot among the wild-card teams.
2. San Francisco 49ers: 5-0
11. Philadelphia Eagles: 2-3
13. Washington Commanders: 1-3-1
14. Tampa Bay Buccaneers: 1-4
15. New Orleans Saints: 1-4
16. Arizona Cardinals: 1-4
Again, there’s a lot of season to be played, so Green Bay’s win over Chicago is carrying most of the weight in the playoff standings. The Packers, Lions, Bears and Seahawks are in fifth through eighth place in the NFC, respectively, with 3-2 records.
Seattle has the worst conference record among those teams so is eighth. That leaves the NFC North teams jockeying for position. In the division-games tiebreaker, Green Bay, which is 1-1 against NFC North foes, has more wins than Detroit (0-0) and Chicago (0-2).
The point here is that the Packers, for everything they did wrong during the first quarter of the season, are right where they need to be. The key for this opening stretch of games has been to stay afloat until Micah Parsons returns on defense and Josh Jacobs (potentially) returns on offense.
So far, it’s mission accomplished. But one game can’t be just one game. It must be the starting point.
“Man, it’s stacking,” quarterback Jordan Love said after the game. “You’ve just got to keep stacking stuff. Great win today but it’s all about how we get back to the film room, continue to build on this performance, continue to build on the plays we did well, cleaning up some of the stuff we didn’t do as well, and just attacking it.
“It’s going to be a new opponent next week, a new defense, so we’ve got to keep building on this. It feels good when everybody’s clicking and making plays. It’s something that we’ve got to keep it rolling.”
Of the eight teams with winning records, the Packers are the only team with a negative scoring differential.
Going in the order of the playoff standings, the Vikings are plus-45, the 49ers are plus-61, the Giants are plus-3, the Panthers are plus-12, the Packers are minus-8, the Lions are plus-16, the Bears are plus-23 and the Seahawks are plus-29.
Green Bay’s three wins have come against teams with a combined six wins, giving it a strength of victory of.400. That doesn’t seem too good, but the Vikings’ five wins have come against teams with eight victories and Detroit’s three wins have come against teams with four victories.
“There was a whole lot on display out there today,” receiver Christian Watson said after a dominant performance. “The defense came out to play. They put us in the best possible position, getting the ball back for us, what, five times? We can’t ask for much more from the defense. Obviously, we were able to put some points out there on offense, make plays when our numbers are called. That was big-time.
“I think that we all knew what we were capable of. We’ve got to just find a way to consistently be that, consistently be even better than that to obviously achieve the goals we want to achieve. That’s the team that we are.”
Five games, obviously, is a small sample size. But it’s not so small that remaining strength of schedule is irrelevant.
According to Tankathon , the Packers’ final 12 opponents have a combined winning percentage of .492. That’s in a six-way tie for 18th.
The Vikings have the toughest remaining schedule in the NFL, with their remaining opponents having a .568 winning percentage. The Bears are seventh at .533 and the Lions are ninth at .525.
After a soft open to the schedule, the Packers scored a big win over Chicago in their first big test on Sunday. They will host the Dallas Cowboys (2-3) on Sunday night, play at the Lions (3-2) the following Sunday and then host the NFC South-leading Carolina Panthers (2-2) on Thursday night.
Then, it’s a trip to New England to face the Patriots (3-2) and a home game against the first-place Vikings (5-0) before the pseudo bye week preceding the Wednesday night game at the Los Angeles Rams (2-3).
“I think just keeping the main thing the main thing,” safety Xavier McKinney said after the game. “Obviously, every week we want to go in and be 1-0. I think that we did a great job throughout the whole week of keeping the main thing the main thing.
“Having that urgency, having that mindset of going in and not really worrying about really the opponent but worrying about what we’re doing internally and figuring out how we can go out there and execute the play as given to us. I think that’s what we did this week and it was able to show today.”

title: Packers Injury Updates, Including Micah Parsons and Perplexing Achilles Tears
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers don’t practice by a power substation, but they are in the general vicinity of paper plants and an animal-rendering facility.
Whatever the reason, the Packers continue to get hit by big injuries. The latest was defensive tackle Javon Hargrave suffering a torn Achilles toward the end of Sunday’s win over the Bears. That injury was especially deflating to coach Matt LaFleur after the game.
Deflated Matt LaFleur’s opening statement. pic.twitter.com/q649Vz6EoH
It was the second season-ending Achilles injury in as many weeks, with Hargrave’s coming on the heels of star linebacker Edgerrin Cooper’s last week.
“I think it’s a fluky deal,” LaFleur said on Monday, “but, once you go through this, you always are looking back at everything you do and trying to figure out why certain things happen.
“It was definitely unfortunate. I know it took a lot of wind out of my sails last night after the game when you have a devastating injury like to anybody, let alone to a guy that has come in here and done things the right way and been a real asset to our football team.”
According to data from a few years ago , there are an average of about 20 Achilles tears per season since the NFL moved to a 17-game schedule. That includes training camp, preseason and regular season.
The Packers have had two this season. Plus, tight end John FitzPatrick and defensive tackle Jordon Riley sustained Achilles injuries in Week 16 and Week 17 of last season, respectively. So, the Packers are clear outliers on the spectrum with a perplexing four Achilles tears in their last nine games.
“Unfortunate,” LaFleur said.
Asked if there’s time during the season to dive into the search for reasons or if that’s an offseason project for the medical staff, LaFleur said:
“I hope everybody’s diving in and, if people have solutions into how do you avoid that, we’ll listen. If we have to adjust things from a practice standpoint and whatnot or a training standpoint, we’ll definitely listen to that.”
Micah Parsons will not practice this week, meaning he will not get to play against his former team, the Cowboys, on Sunday night at Lambeau Field.
His brother, who knows as much about Parsons’ comeback as anyone, said his “best bet” would be the Week 10 home game against Minnesota or the Week 12 game at the Rams. (The Packers have a short Week 11 bye before facing the Rams on Thanksgiving Eve).
Your best bet would prolly be Minnesota or the rams
“As soon as they give us the green light, he’ll be out there,” LaFleur said. “That hasn’t happened yet, but I think we’re getting closer.”
After this week’s game against Dallas, the Packers will play at Detroit. LaFleur was asked if playing on Ford Field’s artificial surface would preclude him from returning for that game.
LaFleur said, no, it wouldn’t. Rather, the short timeframe between now and facing the Lions would be the predictable obstacle.
“First of all, you’ve got to get him back on the practice field,” he said. “There’s a lot of testing that goes on before he gets medically cleared to get out there, and then I’m sure we’re going to want to give him some time to get back to playing football. As you see with most guys that are coming off a major injury, it takes a little bit of time.”
At the end of training camp, general manager Brian Gutekunst said he thought Parsons might be close to returning after the four-week PUP window.
That, obviously, is not going to be the case. Did something change?
“I think we were all hopeful,” LaFleur said. “He’s a physical specimen, he’s a creature of nature for sure and, sometimes, you’ve got to make sure that your body is [fully ready]. You don’t want one leg to be that much stronger than the other leg.”
The Packers’ depth at defensive tackle has evaporated in a hurry.
Warren Brinson started the season on the sideline due to a calf injury. In his first practice a couple weeks ago, he suffered a groin injury and was placed on injured reserve. And now, Javon Hargrave will miss the rest of the season.
That leaves the Packers with five defensive tackles: starters Devonte Wyatt and Karl Brooks, nose tackle Jonathan Ford, rookie Chris McClellan and first-year player Anthony Campbell. Campbell suffered an ankle injury in his NFL debut against the Jets and has been inactive for the last three games.
“Well, hopefully, we’ll get Campbell rolling this week, but it truly is a next-man-up mentality and guys got to get ready to play,” LaFleur said. “That’s just the nature of the beast and I think that’s one of the luxuries of having a 70-man roster.
“We tell our players this all the time, whether you’re on the active or you’re on the P-squad, you got to get ready to play. For those that we anticipate playing in the game that are up on gameday, we’ll make sure that they get the adequate amount of reps.”
David Blay, an undrafted rookie, is the only defensive tackle on the practice squad. The aforementioned Jordon Riley is on PUP following last year’s torn Achilles. He’s “pretty close” to returning to practice but, like Parsons, he’s going to need practice time to get ready to play in a game.
Finally, the depth at receiver has eroded, as well. Jayden Reed suffered a season-ending neck injury against the Jets in Week 2 and his backup, Skyy Moore, suffered an ankle injury early against Chicago.
“I would say in the short term, there's a little bit of concern, but nothing like too long term,” LaFleur said.
Savion Williams, who opened the season on injured reserve, was designated for return last week and was limited participation at all three practices but was not added to the roster.
“He's definitely getting closer,” LaFleur said. “I'm hopeful that we can get him there, but we'll kind of work through the week and see where he's at.”
The Packers have three receivers on the practice squad, including Isaiah Neyor, who has been with the team since August 2025.

title: Packers Stock Report: Risers (Playoffs) and Fallers After Beating Bears
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Any stock report involving the Green Bay Packers has to start with, well, the Green Bay Packers.
After a dismal 1-2 start, they are 3-2 following Sunday’s blowout win over the Chicago Bears. Here is a more specific look at who’s up and who’s down.
From Week 1 through Week 4, Jordan Love was one of 30 quarterbacks who had thrown at least seven passes 20-plus yards downfield. Love was 4-of-18 on those attempts. He ranked 26th with a 22.2 completion percentage, 25th with 8.0 yards per attempt and 28th with a 37.3 passer rating.
Against the Bears, Love was 6-of-8 (75.0 percent) for 258 yards with two touchdowns and zero interceptions. He averaged 32.3 yards per attempt and finished with a near-perfect passer rating of 156.3.
With the Monday night game to be played, Love was one of 19 quarterbacks with at least three deep attempts in Week 5. He is first or tied for first in completions, completion percentage, yards, touchdowns and passer rating. He had more yards on deep passes than the next two quarterbacks combined. Heck, his deep-yardage count would rank 10th among all quarterbacks overall for the week.
“I felt like we were rolling, definitely, play after play, drive after drive, making big plays,” Love said after the game. “It’s definitely a good feeling when you’re having a lot of explosive plays (and) putting up a lot of points. Obviously, defense played a huge part in that, getting us the ball back with all those turnovers, keeping them out of the end zone.
“It’s one of those things we’ve talked about, it’s flow state – feels like you’re flowing out there – just play after play we’re making those. It felt good to be able to do that at home.”
Jordan Love couldn’t have made all those deep throws – including his third-and-a-mile touchdown to Christian Watson – without the big guys up front. On that play, Love had about 4.6 seconds from snap to throw.
Here's another view of the protection on Jordan Love's third-down TD pass to Christian Watson. pic.twitter.com/CPTDxt1Omd
Laken Tomlinson has solved the team’s problems at left guard, where Aaron Banks has played 22 snaps in five games. Travis Glover solidified the issues at right guard, where Jacob Monk won the job but wasn’t good enough to keep it. At right tackle, Anthony Belton hasn’t allowed a pressure the last two games, according to Pro Football Focus.
The Packers don’t need to have a top-10 offensive line to win games on offense. Just look at the Chicago game for proof. Love just needs the time – which he got on Sunday.
With continued growth the expectation for Belton, left tackle Jordan Morgan and center Sean Rhyan, and with Tomlinson and Kevin Zeitler going to be the starting guards at some point, the arrow is pointed up in such a way that it could be a real strength by the end of the season.
“I thought Glove again went in there and did a really good job,” coach Matt LaFleur said on Monday. “So, we felt like two weeks in a row, our O-line’s played winning football for us.”
In terms of yards allowed per carry, Chicago had one of the worst run defenses in the NFL. The Packers couldn’t take advantage, though.
After eliminating the kneel-downs by Tyrod Taylor, the Packers ran the ball 24 times for 72 yards. That’s exactly 3.0 yards per carry. They all count, obviously, but if you ignore Kaleb Johnson’s 23-yard run midway through the fourth quarter, the tally falls to 49 yards on 23 attempts, which is barely 2.0 yards per carry.
It’s not good enough. And any spin job to the contrary is nonsense. At some point, the Packers are going to have to run the football. Through five games, they’ve shown absolutely no ability to get that done. The blocking needs to get better, to be sure, but the running backs have to do a much better job of turning 1-yard runs into 3-yard gains.
Christian Watson caught six passes for 143 yards and two touchdowns and Matthew Golden caught six passes for 123 yards. That’s a combined 266 receiving yards, a preposterous number. Including Jordan Love, only seven quarterbacks had more total passing yards than Green Bay’s dynamic duo had on its own.
With Monday’s game to be played, Watson is fifth in the league with 474 receiving yards and Golden is eighth with 397.
Christian Watson is on pace for 1,612 yards and 20 touchdowns. Only two players have had 20 touchdown catches. Randy Moss (23 TDs, 1,493 yards in 2007) and Jerry Rice (22 TDs, 1,078 yards in the 12-game 1987 season).
“Obviously, we’re always trying to get our playmakers the ball, and those two guys are our best playmakers in that room right now,” LaFleur said. “So, if their number’s called and the coverage presents itself the way that it did, then they’re going to get opportunities.”
The 17-game projections are ridiculous. For Watson, it’s 1,612 yards and 20 touchdowns. For Golden, it’s 1,350 yards and seven touchdowns. Combined, they are approaching a 3,000-yard pace. That’s been done only four times in NFL history. Detroit’s Herman Moore and Brett Perriman combined for a record 3,174 yards in 1995, and Miami’s Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle were the most recent with 3,066 yards in 2022.
“It’s hard to stop two guys who can run all the routes and stretch the field like that,” Watson said. “If you try to, it’s going to give us other opportunities elsewhere. Obviously, we’ve got Tucker Kraft and we’ve got a lot of guys who can make plays. It’s just tough when you’ve got playmakers of the ability we have in our room and our offense, to stop it all.”
The Packers kept six receivers on their initial 53-man roster and placed Savion Williams on injured reserve with an ankle injury. What would the Packers do once Williams was healthy?
Well, slot receiver Jayden Reed is on injured reserve and his backup, Skyy Moore, missed most of Sunday’s game with an injured ankle and there is a “little bit” of “short-term” concern, LaFleur said. That means there is a role available for Williams, who returned to practice last week.
The Packers took the unusual step of keeping seven defensive tackles on their initial roster. Good thing. Warren Brinson is on injured reserve and now Javon Hargrave suffered a season-ending torn Achilles.
That means the Packers are down to five players: Devonte Wyatt, Karl Brooks, Jonathan Ford, Chris McClellan and Anthony Campbell, who has missed the last three games with an ankle injury sustained at the Jets.
Big defensive tackle Jordon Riley, who suffered a torn Achilles in the December game at Chicago, is “pretty close” to returning to practice, LaFleur said.
Everyone knew the strength of the team would be the triumvirate of safeties Xavier McKinney and Evan Williams and nickel Javon Bullard.
They were superb once again. Williams had 11 tackles and recovered a fumble, McKinney had the team’s first two-interception game since 2022 and Bullard’s deflection created McKinney’s first interception, which the offense turned into a 14-0 lead.
“I was kind of messing with him today,” LaFleur said. “He could have had a scoop and [score] on that fumble as well. He could have had three takeaways.”
Daniel Whelan did it again. His four punts averaged 55.3 yards. Two of them pinned the Bears at the 10 and 13. His lone touchback was a 75-yard bomb that stuck the Bears at the 10 because of a penalty on the return.
He’s up to 14 inside-the-20s this year – the most in the league – with two touchbacks. That’s a 7-to-1 ratio, much better than last year’s 2.25-to-1 ratio.
Trey Smack missed one extra point and two field goals, leaving seven points on the field. It would be a huge story had the Packers blown another game against Chicago.
Of the 32 kickers who have attempted a field goal this season, Smack ranks 31st with a 70.0 percent success rate on field goals. Smack is 7-of-10 on field goals and 9-of-11 on extra points. He and the 49ers’ Eddy Pineiro have missed a league-high five kicks; Pineiro is last in the league in field goals (5-of-8; 62.5 percent) and also has missed two point-after attempts.

title: Three Overreactions From Packers’ Win Over Bears: The Pack Is Back! (Or Is It?)
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers were blitzed out of Minneapolis. They were largely incompetent against the Jets. They were run out of Lambeau Field by the Falcons. They barely beat an undrafted rookie quarterback at Tampa Bay.
That motley crew from the first four games looked like a Super Bowl juggernaut on Sunday against the Chicago Bears. The final score was 31-7. It might as well have been 131-7. It was total domination by a team that hadn’t dominated any phase of the game other than penalties, fumbles and dropped passes.
All of which begs this season-defining question: Were the Packers who trounced the Bears the real Packers? Or was it a mirage fueled by revenge and circumstances?
Let’s dive into this week’s Overreactions.
Veteran right guard Kevin Zeitler was active, but it was Travis Glover who started and played every snap.
“Going back to last week and his performance in Tampa, I thought he’d kind of earned the right to continue to go out there,” coach Matt LaFleur said after the game, “and Zeitler, he just got here, so he’s only had really one true week of practice. The previous week, it was just individual, so he’s had one solid week of practice where he was getting some team reps. So, it’s always a tough decision, but that’s the decision we made.”
Credit to Glover for solidifying the position the past two games after Jacob Monk struggled in his three starts. But the time to make the change will be Sunday night’s game against the Dallas Cowboys.
Without question, Glover has added some muscle to the run game and been significantly better in protection. The Packers saved their season the last two weeks, and Glover is a big reason why.
“When you’re getting hit repeatedly, it’s hard to play quarterback,” LaFleur said.
It’s not just easier for Jordan Love. It’s easier for LaFleur.
“I think it’s been immense, an immense improvement in terms of it allows us to call our offense,” LaFleur added, “and it’s a hell of a lot easier calling plays when the guys are blocking for the quarterback up front.”
It’s unfair to point to one or two reps over the course of 61 snaps, but Glover was beaten badly on the third snap of the game, with Love avoiding a sack and scrambling for 6 yards. And this certainly is not a representation of Glover’s play overall, but he got Love obliterated on this play early in the fourth quarter.
There's a lot going on here. Glover gets smoked. Strong isn't of much help. Love gets absolutely obliterated. Love throws just a ridiculous deep ball. The ref looks like me on skates. And Golden is Golden. pic.twitter.com/FxuEoDVOui
With more time, Glover might become a quality starter, but the Packers signed Zeitler for a reason. He’s started 213 games and is coming off a solid season with the Titans. With the Packers moving in the right direction, now’s the time to make a change to build what they’ll hope to be the starting line for the duration of the season.
Zeitler, for his part, is handling the process like a veteran.
“Here’s the simple truth: Wins are what matter, right?” he said after the game.
Wins are what matter. So does getting to the playoffs and competing for a championship. Zeitler gives them their best chance.
“I’m trying to jam a whole training camp into a week or two,” he said. “So, it’s just a million little things. We’re just going to keep attacking, keep trying to get better and, when the time comes … I’m super-pumped with how the O line has been playing right now, which is just outstanding. It’s the best thing in the world right now.
“So, I’m just going to keep working on it. Whenever the time comes, the time will be right.”
The Packers’ defense took care of business against the Bears, limiting one of the more potent offenses in the NFL to 246 yards and seven points while forcing five turnovers. Obviously, that comes with the caveat of that production came against Tyson Bagent and Case Keenum rather than Caleb Williams.
However, Bagent frequently had a month of Sundays to stand in the pocket and go through his reads. Of the 30 quarterbacks who’ve had at least 30 dropbacks this week, Bagent faced the fourth-lowest pressure percentage at 23.1 percent.
Sure, the Packers ended the day with four sacks, but that wasn’t a true indication of the power of the pass rush.
It’s a known problem for the Packers, who are trying to muddle their way through the absence of Micah Parsons and now have to do it without Edgerrin Cooper. Adding injury to insult, veteran Javon Hargrave suffered a torn Achilles in the final moments against Chicago. Hargrave ranks third on the team in pass-rush win rate, according to Pro Football Focus.
The challenge is going to get infinitely harder. On Sunday night, they’ll host Dak Prescott and the Cowboys. The following week, the matchup will be against Jared Goff and the Lions. Both players are big-time passers with excellent receiver corps and strong offensive lines.
In terms of clean-pocket passer rating, Prescott is seventh, Goff is fourth and Carolina’s Bryce Young, who the Packers will host after facing Prescott and Goff, is third.
Somehow, defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon must find some pass rush without putting too much strain on his cornerbacks. That’s going to be a tall mountain. For all the reason to feel good about the Packers after Sunday, the lack of a pass rush remains the big barrier to lasting success.
So, ultimately, what do you make out of Sunday’s game? Green Bay’s passing game was unstoppable against a defense that entered the day ranked fourth in points allowed. Green Bay’s defense held the NFL’s top-ranked rushing attack to 81 yards and a 3.4-yard average.
On the other hand, you know the asterisks. The Bears didn’t have their rising-star quarterback and top running back. All the intangibles were pointing in Green Bay’s direction.
So, will Green Bay’s win wind up being a real, season-changing achievement? Or will it be, to channel the legendary Ron Wolf in the aftermath of losing Super Bowl XXXII, just a fart in the wind and nothing more than one of those random results that make the NFL so much fun?
I hit on that question after the game and believe, yes, this was a win that could be the start of something big.
The Bears played without their star quarterback and top rusher. Yes, they would have impacted the game, but there is absolutely no reason to put an asterisk on the win. Here are three reasons why it's truly OK to be excited about the Packers. ⬇️ https://t.co/8OEmtykdAa
It’s worth exploring a bit deeper on a couple fronts.
First, coach Matt LaFleur has lamented all the self-inflicted problems. The Packers entered the week ranked first (or worst) in the league in penalty yards, fumbles and drops. On Sunday, they were guilty of four penalties for 25 yards, fumbled once and dropped one pass.
To state the obvious, it’s a lot easier to beat an opponent when you’re not beating yourself, first. So, that was a huge step in the right direction.
The second is the play of the offensive line. General manager Brian Gutekunst and the coaching staff mismanaged that group to start the season, but credit to them for pivoting before it was too late. The signing of Laken Tomlinson and the insertion of Travis Glover into the guard slots has taken care of the two big issues. Why Glover never got even a sniff of the right guard competition during training camp speaks poorly of the coaches, but at least they eventually got it right.
“It’s something we’ve talked about throughout the course of the season so far, and I thought they did a great job,” quarterback Jordan Love said. “They gave me a lot of time on a lot of those plays. Especially the one to Christian [Watson on their second touchdown], I had all day back there.
About 4.6 seconds for Jordan Love on the third-and-22 touchdown bomb to Christian Watson. pic.twitter.com/2To4WNX5rk
“They did a great job. I thought our run game has been improving. We’ve got some big runs going and we’re playing complementary ball right there. That’s…

title: Snaps, Studs and Duds From Packers’ Statement Win Over Bears
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Chicago Bears’ team song is “Bear Down, Chicago Bears.” On Sunday, it was “Beat Down, the Chicago Bears.”
The Green Bay Packers delivered an emphatic wire-to-wire victory over their rivals. It was total domination and no asterisks were required .
Here’s our weekly look at the snaps along with six studs and two duds.
The Packers played 61 snaps on offense.
Quarterbacks: Jordan Love played the first 59 snaps before Tyrod Taylor took a knee to run out the clock. Love had played every snap this season. After two games of quality pass protection, he will be feeling good headed into Sunday night’s game against the Cowboys.
Love was 25-of-31 (80.6 percent) for 367 yards and two touchdowns, good for a career-high 137.5 passer rating. It was only the second occasion in franchise history of at least 350 passing yards, an 80 percent completion rate and two touchdowns in a game (Aaron Rodgers vs. Washington in 2019).
AIR JORDAN ✈️ Jordan Love joins Ben Roethlisberger as the only players with 5 completions of 30+ air yards in a single game since ESPN began tracking the stat in 2006. pic.twitter.com/x9rY4KOKNu
Running backs: After last week’s game against Tampa Bay, coach Matt LaFleur said the best teacher is the bench for running backs with a fumbling problem. So, with two fumbles to start the season, Kaleb Johnson found himself on the bench until the game was in hand.
MarShawn Lloyd led the unit with 27 snaps. Pierre Strong, making his Packers debut after spending all of last season and the start of this season on the practice squad, played 25 snaps. Johnson got nine snaps at the end.
Lloyd led the way with 10 rushes for 31 yards and two touchdowns. The Packers need more of his first touchdown run, when he ran over Jaylon Johnson to gain the final 2 yards, because he’s too often taken down sideways and doesn’t fall forward for an extra yard or two.
Receivers: The Packers are running out of receivers. Skyy Moore, who had replaced injured Jayden Reed in the slot, dropped out after 11 snaps with an ankle injury.
As always, Christian Watson and Matthew Golden led the way. Watson played 49 snaps and Golden played 47 (with three more as the punt returner). Bo Melton became the next man up to Moore, who had been the next man up, with 30 snaps. J. Michael Sturdivant played only eight.
Among all receivers who were targeted at least four times this week, Watson was first with 4.77 yards per route and Golden was second with 4.56.
Melton played 16 on special teams and Sturdivant played 11.
Tight ends: Tucker Kraft played 47 snaps, with his 77 percent playing time a bit less than usual due to the score. Mark Redman, who has been invaluable as a blocker, played 21 snaps. Jonnu Smith also played 21 and Josh Whyle got 11.
The only statistical contribution was Kraft’s five catches for 64 yards.
Offensive line: The No. 1 line of left tackle Jordan Morgan, left guard Laken Tomlinson, center Sean Rhyan, right guard Travis Glover and right tackle Anthony Belton went the distance. With Glover making his second consecutive start, Kevin Zeitler’s Packers debut was limited to six snaps on special teams.
According to PFF, Belton and Rhyan pitched shutouts in pass protection. Tomlinson allowed only one pressure. Glover wasn’t as good against Chicago as he was against Tampa Bay, but he’s still been an upgrade over Jacob Monk.
The Packers played 69 snaps on defense.
Defensive tackles: It was a vintage Jonathan Gannon rotation. Karl Brooks, who had one of the team’s eight tackles for losses, led the unit with 39 snaps, followed by Devonte Wyatt with 32, Javon Hargrave and Chris McClellan with 31 each, and Jonathan Ford getting 17.
Now what, though? Hargrave suffered a torn Achilles late in the game. Coach Matt LaFleur was crushed.
“That kind of takes the air out of the room a little bit, when you lose not only a great player but a great guy, a key piece to this team, and it kind of puts a little bit of a cloud on the day,” LaFleur said.
With Warren Brinson on injured reserve, it will be Anthony Campbell’s time after he missed the last three games with an ankle injury sustained in his NFL debut against the Jets.
Wyatt had his first two sacks of the season. The first was a cheap one, with Tyson Bagent slipping and falling. The second was a sack-fumble that was the cherry on top of the victory sundae.
Edges: It was a balanced snap count here, too. Lukas Van Ness played 40 snaps. After that, it was Brenton Cox with 35, Dani Dennis-Sutton with 32 and starter Barryn Sorrell with 31. The tenor of the game meant more snaps for Cox, who is one of the team’s better pass rushers. (More on that in a moment.) Sorrell, meanwhile, played 16 snaps on special teams, so that probably impacted his workload on defense.
Dennis-Sutton might wind up moving ahead of Sorrell on the depth chart at some point. While he’s routinely lost on bootlegs, you can’t deny his big-play production. He had one sack along with a tackle for loss when he read and destroyed a receiver screen.
Linebackers: How would the Packers replace premier starter Edgerrin Cooper? Zaire Franklin played the first 64 snaps before he was removed at the 2-minute warning. Ty’Ron Hopper played 39 snaps and Isaiah McDuffie played 34.
The rotation was the way to go because both players are key cogs on special teams. Hopper played 14 snaps on special teams, giving him a total of 53, and McDuffie played 16 snaps on special teams, giving him a total of 50.
Franklin had nine tackles, one tackle for loss and one forced fumble, McDuffie had five tackles and Hopper had an interception.
Nick Niemann and Kristian Welch didn’t play on defense but got 18 and 16 snaps, respectively, on special teams. Niemann had two solo tackles.
Cornerbacks: Brandon Cisse was one of two defensive players to play every snap. Keisean Nixon played 61; he sat out the eight-play final series. Carrington Valentine played nine snaps as the next corner and Kamal Hadden got seven snaps in the slot to end the game.
Benjamin St-Juste was limited to six snaps on special teams as he continues to be plagued by hamstring issues.
The corners were excellent given the limited challenge brought by the Bears. Cisse allowed only one catch and had one sack.
Safeties: Evan Williams was the other defensive player to play every snap. Xavier McKinney played 61, getting to watch the final eight from the bench as Kitan Oladapo took his place.
Williams continued his hot start to the season with 11 tackles and McKinney’s two interceptions gave him three for the season. It was the team’s first two-interception game since Rudy Ford in 2022.
QB Jordan Love: Is there a better deep-ball thrower than Love? It wasn’t as if his receivers had to make a bunch of circus catches. For the most part, the balls couldn’t have been placed any better had Love hit pause, run down the field, and put them directly into the receivers’ hands.
On passes of 20-plus air yards, Love was 6-of-8 for 258 yards and two touchdowns. He had as many deep completions as total incompletions in a ridiculous performance.
WRs Christian Watson and Matthew Golden: The numbers are absurd, with Watson and Golden combining for 12 receptions for 266 yards. It’s not as if the Bears have a bunch of stiffs at cornerback. Jaylon Johnson is a two-time Pro Bowler and Tyrique Stevenson is one of the best young corners in the game. Stevenson missed half the game with a hamstring injury, but the Bears are high on rookie Malik Muhammad, who was torched.
Ultimately, it didn’t matter. Watson and Golden are on pace to finish the season with about 3,000 receiving yards.
Edge Brenton Cox: Cox had only three tackles with zero sacks, quarterback hits or tackles for losses, but PFF credited him with six pressures. Really, he was the only player providing something resembling consistent pressure.

title: Packers Report Card: Three A’s But Two D’s From Beatdown of Bears
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The grades are in for the Green Bay Packers after they played their best game of the season in a 31-7 victory over the Chicago Bears.
Yes, they played against two backup quarterbacks and a backup running back, and they were at home. Those are some pretty decided advantages.
A big day from Jordan Love and his top two receivers combined with some suffocating pass defense led to a rout at Lambeau Field that had to feel extra sweet for an organizatio n that had been on the bad side of the rivalry for the first time in more than 30 years.
The grades, as you might imagine, reflect the dominance that took place at Lambeau Field.
Christian Watson said earlier in the week there were holes in the defense that Green Bay’s offense could exploit. Matthew Golden chuckled while referencing that quote after the game .
As it turns out, Watson was right. Jordan Love sliced and diced against a hapless Chicago secondary that, save for a brief sabbatical in the second quarter, did not have any answers from Love’s aerial assault on their defense.
Love threw for 367 yards, including two long touchdown passes to Watson. His reworked offensive line kept him clean for most of the game, as Love was only sacked twice, both of which came on the same possession at the end of the first half.
Apart from that, it was Love throwing bombs all over the field to Watson, Golden and Tucker Kraft, who combined for 330 yards. Watson and Golden became the first Packers tandem to top 120 yards in a game in a decade.
“It’s flow state – feels like you’re flowing out there – just play after play we’re making those. It felt good to be able to do that at home,” Love said.
Love joined former Steelers quarterback Ben Roethlisberger as the only players with five completions of 30 or more air yards in a single game since ESPN began tracking that stat in 2006.
“That’s just one of them feelings,” Watson said after the game. “That was a great display we had out there today. Big time game from the whole team. Honestly, I was excited for each and every person who was out there making plays. That was a big-time win.”
Kraft had his best game of the season with five catches for 64 yards, including a 46-yard completion in the third quarter that helped set up a field goal from Trey Smack.
If you only watch the highlight tape, you’d think the Packers were able to move the ball on the ground for most of the game. MarShawn Lloyd found the end zone twice, including an angry run when he ran over Chicago cornerback Jaylon Johnson en route to the end zone to give the Packers a 14-0 lead.
Lloyd’s second touchdown was the nail in the coffin that gave the Packers a 31-7 lead. Kaleb Johnson, who was kept on the bench until late in the game, popped an explosive run of 23 yards.
Despite the big plays, there was not much room for Green Bay’s putrid ground game, which remains anemic at this point in the season. Pierre Strong had five carries for 7 yards. Lloyd had 31 yards on 10 carries. Overall, the Packers ran for 70 yards with a 2.7-yard average.
They desperately need one of their running backs to find a way to give them some punch in the run game. Maybe Lloyd can use his touchdown runs as a potential springboard next week against a Dallas defense that is one of the worst in the league.
The Year 2024 returned and Xavier McKinney is back in the saddle. On a day when the Packers should have had some opportunities to make some plays on the ball facing mistake-prone backup quarterback Tyson Bagent, McKinney obliged.
His two interceptions helped him surpass his total from last season, as he now has three this season. He was not alone. Ty’Ron Hopper picked off Case Keenum at the goal line. Evan Williams and Dani Dennis-Sutton recovered fumbles.
As noted by Packers.com’s Wes Hodkiewicz, the Packers have equaled their interception total of seven in 2025 in just five games.
“I feel good,” McKinney said. “I try to stack the weeks, stack the days. Even when the result is not what I want it to be every time, but still keeping my same process. So, my main focus is just making sure that I’m the best version of me every day and guys around me get the best version of me every day, regardless of what the result may be. But as long as I keep my process the same, I know the results will come.”
The tests are going to get stiffer in the coming weeks. Dak Prescott is one of the league’s best and he’s coming to town next week. He’ll be followed by Detroit’s Jared Goff, Carolina’s rising Bryce Young and New England’s Drake Maye. There are a bunch of elite receivers on the agenda, too.
On this Sunday, however, the Packers were dominant. Bagent and Keenum were erratic. They combined for just more than 200 passing yards. Combine that with four sacks and three picks? It’s almost a perfect day against subpar quarterback play.
The biggest storyline of the game was how the Packers were going to stop the Chicago ground game that entered play this week as the best rushing attack in the NFL.
Some of the punch of Chicago’s run game was removed when Kyle Monangai was ruled out with a toe injury on Friday. D’Andre Swift, who topped 1,000 yards last year, was still active, but the dropoff from him to Roschon Johnson was significant.
With the Packers taking an early 14-0 lead, however, Chicago’s run game was held in check. Swift had just nine carries for 43 yards and a touchdown. The rest of Chicago’s run game was kept under wraps, with Tyson Bagent being the Bears’ second-leading rusher with 17 yards on three carries. Six horizontal runs to receivers gained 11 yards.
The assignment will be more difficult on Christmas when the Packers will likely face Monangai and Caleb Williams.
Sunday, however, the goal was to make Bagent beat them. The Packers were successful.
Chicago had 81 rushing yards on 24 carries, a 3.4-yard average. The Packers would take that every day and twice on Sundays.
Matthew Golden looked explosive on a 17-yard punt return that helped set up the Packers’ offense for the second of two failed two-minute drills at the end of the first half. Outside of that, it was a pretty rough day at the office for Cam Achord’s group.
The kickoff-coverage team had some nice moments, with Kamal Hadden running through Chicago’s returners, but it also allowed an explosive return immediately after taking a 31-7 lead. That ultimately did not end up mattering because Chicago’s offense was as bad as it was, but that will matter next week against Cowboys returner Kavontae Turpin and prolific quarterback Dak Prescott.
Trey Smack had his first rookie moments as a kicker. He missed an extra-point attempt early, and followed it up with two missed field goals in the fourth quarter. Again, it didn’t matter because the Packers led by 24 points, but it will matter when they start facing real quarterbacks next week.
Smack has been good for most of the year, so next week against Dallas will be a chance for him to bounce back. Sunday? It was one of the few black eyes on an otherwise spectacular day for the home team.
Daniel Whelan outdid himself with a 75-yard punt that was ruled a touchback. Hadden was in on three tackles.
The first half likely embodies what the 2026 Packers are, but also what Matt LaFleur is at this point as a head coach.
There are flashes of brilliance. LaFleur was able to scheme up 14 quick points on offense to start the game. Everything he called worked.
Then the second quarter hit, and nothing worked. The Packers’ final three possessions of the half lasted nine plays and resulted in zero points.
Furthermore, LaFleur kept two timeouts in his pocket after a first-down sack and fumble was recovered by Jordan Love with the Packers threatening to get into field-goal range. As a result, the Packers were penalized for an illegal substitution. Love was sacked on the next play, and a drive that should have ended in at least a field-goal attempt ended with the Packers getting booed off the field while having a lead.
When the second half began,…

title: Jalen Pitre Injury Update: Texans DB Could Have Caught a Big Break
full_text:
We now know a bit more about the injury that Houston Texans defensive back Jalen Pitre suffered in Week 5's road trip against the Tennessee Titans.
And it seems like, while there is a chance that Pitre misses some time, the Texans avoided any worst-case scenario surrounding the health of their star defender.
According to NFL insider Tom Pelissero of The Ringer , Pitre has suffered an AC joint sprain in his shoulder that leaves his status as week-to-week.
Texans DB Jalen Pitre suffered an AC joint sprain Sunday and is considered week-to-week, per source. Good news overall for one of Houston's standouts, who avoided a major injury.
Pitre first went down with the shoulder injury during the second half of action in the Texans' Week 5 matchup against the Titans. Pitre would inevitably end up not returning to the action, and head coach DeMeco Ryans had noted that the team was still evaluating his status moving forward.
And now, with a bit more clarity on the severity of Pitre's shoulder issue, it does seem to hint towards a possible absence for him in their upcoming Week 6 game against the Jacksonville Jaguars .
However, without any expectation of a lengthy recovery, or any signs of short-term injured reserve being in play, it's great news for the Texans to hear.
Pitre has long been an integral piece of the Texans' defense as a versatile nickel/safety. He's been on the field for over 90% of Houston's defensive snaps this season as a fifth defensive back to play alongside Houston's strong corner and safety unit.
In the five games that Pitre has played this season, he's put together 24 combined tackles, one tackle for loss, five passes defended, and a forced fumble; really making an impact all over the defensive side as he has since emerging as a full-time starter in his rookie season back in 2022.
The Texans may have to do without his services for a game or two this season––which they had to also navigate in 2025 when Pitre missed three games with a concussion––but a week-to-week status might be the best-case scenario, considering the uncertainty that was surrounding his health after Week 5.
While the length of Pitre's injury absence is far from confirmed, there's a good chance that the Texans end up being without him for just two weeks, simply because of the placement of their bye in Week 8.
Houston could take their trip overseas against the Jaguars in Week 6 , then travel home to face the New York Giants in Week 7 without Pitre, then allow their star defender an extra week of rest before they're back in action in Week 9 against the LA Chargers.
For however long that Pitre does remain out, it feels like a safe bet that fifth-round rookie Kamari Ramsey will be the one called up to take his reps as a similarly versatile contributor at nickel and safety.
Ramsey is one of the few names on the Texans' roster with experience playing both at safety and nickel during his time in college at USC, and already managed to get snaps his way in place of Pitre when he went out in Week 5 against the Titans.
So far this season, Ramsey has played in 40 defensive snaps for the Texans, where he's recorded six tackles and one tackle for loss. If Houston's coaching staff trusts their rookie to claim Pitre's snaps for the time that he's out, Week 6 can be a massive opportunity to see those numbers jump across the board.
The Texans will have a couple of practices at their disposal before traveling to London this week to plan out their defensive plans more in depth without Pitre for Week 6. However, knowing that their star defender won't be sidelined for an extremely long period of time is great news for all involved in Houston.

title: Texans Week 6 Consensus Power Rankings: How Win No. 1 Changes Things
full_text:
The Houston Texans finally got their long-awaited first win of the 2026 season down in the books following their dominant 26-3 victory over their division rival, the Tennessee Titans, in Week 5 .
And because of that win, the general consensus surrounding the Texans seems to have taken a slight boost compared to where things stood this time last week. Back then, Houston was still at a winless 0-4, both sides of the ball had some glaring issues, and led to many selling their stock on this group .
Now, the Texans certainly might not have those same issues fixed by now––even after their recent trade to acquire Marvin Harrison Jr.––but they are in a bit of a better spot than they were previously now that they have what hopes to be their first win of many.
With that in mind, let's sort through a new batch of consensus power rankings to see just where the Texans stack up as they roll into Week 6 against the Jacksonville Jaguars in London .
Sports Illustrated's Conor Orr has the Texans at their highest spot in these consensus rankings by far. Spoiler alert: everyone else we have listed has Houston outside of their top 20 teams, while Orr is able to find them a spot in the top 15.
"Of the teams whose seasons are theoretically dead in the water, Houston provides the faintest glimmer of hope. Braden Smith, Tank Dell and Kayden McDonald are on the way, the Titans are up next on the schedule and 1–4 looks far better (with three examples of playoff teams in the last 25 years, by the way)."
Nick Shook went against the grain last week when he decided to shift the Texans up two spots from their previous ranking to land at 23, even after a loss. This time around, it's the exact opposite: Houston finally won a game, and Shook drops them back down to 25.
"Houston did what everyone expected it to do: take care of business against the worst team in the NFL. C.J. Stroud added another fruitful week to what is quickly becoming a very strong rebound season, the Texans finally got a little bit more out of their ground game (despite losing David Montgomery to injury), and the superior AFC South team walked away with an easy win. It’s a start, and we'll see what becomes of the Marvin Harrison Jr. trade, but it’s going to be a long climb out of 0-4."
ESPN 's writers were polled this week on their power rankings, where the Texans saw themselves right outside of the top 20. When D.J. Bien-Aime was tasked to point out Houston's biggest weakness on defense, that would be "health at all three levels."
"The Texans have dealt with injuries to key players. Pro Bowl linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair sat out time because of a groin injury. Nickelback Jalen Pitre just sustained a shoulder injury against the Titans, defensive tackle Kayden McDonald was on IR because of a quad injuryto start the season, and linebacker Henry To'oTo'o landed on IR after Week 1 because of a shoulder injury. That has factored into their defense giving up 234 passing yards per game (23rd). Overall, Houston is tied for 15th in scoring defense (22.4 per game) after ranking second last season (17.4)."
Josh Kendall and Chad Graff continue the trend of placing Houston right outside of the top 20, but give them a welcomed boost of three spots compared to where they were this time last week.
"Finally, some positive vibes in Houston! Beating the Titans is hardly much to celebrate these days, but at long last, the Texans are in the win column, and reinforcements are on the way. After trading for Kayshon Boutte just before the season, the Texans added another wide receiver this weekend in 2024 No. 4 pick Marvin Harrison Jr."
Pete Prisco made sure to have some praise for Texans quarterback C.J. Stroud for the strong start to the season he's had, which is more than justified. Even at a 1-4 record, Houston's signal-caller is averaging a career-high in passing yards (280.4 yards per game), is completing over 64% of his passes, and hasn't thrown an interception in five games.
"The offense with C.J. Stroud has been playing good football. The change to DeMeco Ryans calling plays seemed to work as they ready to play a big game this week with Jacksonville."
Ralph Vacchiano gives the Texans a nice boost of three spots, yet wants to see this roster keep up their momentum in Week 6 as they travel to London and face a much more difficult test in the Jaguars, compared to what the Titans just allowed.
"It says a lot about parity in the NFL that the Texans think they’re still in the race enough to trade a second-round pick for WR Marvin Harrison Jr...  Blowing out the Titans on Sunday isn’t enough to convince anyone that they can. This week’s game against the Jaguars in London will be a much bigger test. The sooner DeMeco Ryans and QB C.J. Stroud figure out how to tap Harrison’s old potential, the better."

title: Why Texans' DeMeco Ryans Is Fired Up About Marvin Harrison Jr. Trade
full_text:
The Houston Texans are the latest team in the NFL to make a major splash trade after the events of their Week 5 win over the Tennessee Titans–– ultimately trading a 2027 second and seventh-round pick for wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. and a sixth-round pick from the Arizona Cardinals .
It's a move from the Texans that has many excited for what's ahead, not only for fans outside of the building eager to see Houston have another weapon offensively, but also for several inside the facility ready to work with a top-five draft pick from just two summers ago.
And perhaps one of the most pumped up about the Texans' recent move is their head coach, DeMeco Ryans, who was the one that first announced the move during his post-game presser from Week 5 , and has since gone a bit more in depth about why he's so ready for Harrison Jr. to enter the mix.
Ryans recently appeared on Texans Radio after Houston's win over the Titans to unpack the move for Harrison Jr. trade among other topics.
And for Ryans, he's not only excited for what Harrison Jr. can add to the Texans offense, but also for the purpose of the 2023 No. 4 pick getting a fresh start in a new home.
“I’m fired up, man. Also, it is exciting to break news. It's fun, now I see why everybody's fishing for information," Ryans said with a smile. "To add a guy of Marvin‘s caliber, it’s a huge get for us. Huge get for the Texans. I’m fired up for Marvin."
"When you’re in a situation and it may not be going great, to get a breath of fresh air, go to a new place. I know Houston’s gonna be great for Marvin."
Harrison Jr.'s 2026 season hasn't gone exactly as expected, having logged just five receptions for 85 yards and a touchdown. But situationally, it seemingly wasn't the best fit by any means.
The Cardinals have been under .500 ever since he arrived in 2023. Harrison Jr. was gradually phased him out of the offensive game plan year over year, and quarterback-wise, things have never been the most seamless for him either.
Yet, in Houston? There's a good chance all three of those factors can turn around for the better, and thus, give the Texans reason to believe they can get the most out of the 24-year-old wideout.
Another aspect that Ryans sees as a major benefit for Harrison Jr. in his new situation–– as many have pointed out–– is the fact that he'll be paired up with his college quarterback, C.J. Stroud ; someone he has strong, prior chemistry catching passes from, and will now have an opportunity to build onto that connection once again.
"Having that prior relationship with C.J., I think it’s gonna go great for him," Ryans continued. "I’m excited to add him. I know he’s been a big-time playmaker in college; his first season in the NFL, he took off."
"Just go be yourself. Bring a great attitude. Everyone speaks about how hard a worker Marvin is; I’m excited to work with him. I talked to him on the phone, and he was elated. I can’t wait to meet him. I just know he’s gonna bring great energy to our building.”
Based on the Texans' strong investment of a second-round pick in Harrison Jr.'s services, it's a clear message that their lead decision-makers are confident in what their newest wide receiver can bring to the table.
And in Ryans' mind, if Harrison Jr. is able to be the hard-worker and high-end talent that he's been advertised as upon his arrival, the move could be an overwhelming success for the Texans in due time.

title: Texans Could Exploit Jaguars' New Offensive Line Injury in Week 6
full_text:
The Houston Texans have a date with another AFC South opponent on the horizon for Week 6 coming fresh off of their encouraging 26-3 win over the Tennessee Titans this past weekend.
And in the days ahead of the Texans' Week 6 trip to face the Jagaurs in London , we now know that Jacksonville will be down a key piece of their offensive line for this week, and for the next several games.
According to NFL Network's Ian Rapoport, Jaguars starting left tackle Anton Harrison is expected to undergo arthroscopic knee surgery when he returns from London.
#Jaguars starting LT Anton Harrison, starter since 2023, is expected to undergo arthroscopic knee surgery when he returns from London, per me and @JFowlerESPN . During the surgery, the doctor will determine how long Trevor Lawrence’s blindside protector is out — weeks or months. pic.twitter.com/euMcFlKvBa
It's a major loss for the Jaguars' offensive line, as Harrison has remained a steady starting piece of this offensive line for the last four seasons.
Ever since he was a first-rounder back in 2023, Harrison has started over 50 regular-season games in Jacksonville, yet might now be trending towards a placement on Injured Reserve.
So how does such a big loss for the Jaguars' offensive front impact the Texans' chances this week? Well, it certainly bodes well for their pass rush, which has been a unit that's gradually come alive over their past few games.
With the Jaguars now down their starter on Trevor Lawrence's blindside, Jacksonville will now likely turn to backup tackle Walker Little to hold down the fort for whatever stretch he's going to be sidelined.
And of anyone on the Texans' defense to benefit from that swap on the Jaguars' offensive front, it's going to be veteran defensive end Danielle Hunter; someone who primarily lines up against the opposing left tackle on a weekly basis, and now has an easier assignment on his hands with an experienced, yet not quite as consistent contributor in Little.
Looking back to the last time these two teams faced off against each other––which came back in Week 10 of the 2025 season–– it was a game to remember for Hunter .
The star defensive end put up one of his most impressive performances since joining the Texans , and perhaps just as a pro altogether: seven tackles, 3.5 sacks, and a forced fumble that eventually led to their 36-29 win, sparking what would be an eventual eight-game win streak to end the year
And who was the Jaguars' left tackle in that Week 10 matchup? It wasn't Anton Harrison––who lined up on the right side for most of the day––it was Walker Little; who presented a clear array of problems in pass protection, and might be put in a position for some similar struggles this weekend in London.
So far this season, Little has yet to start for the Jaguars, though he has been active for 39 games since being selected in the second round of the 2021 NFL Draft, and has 19 games of starting experience throughout his career.
Against this dominant Texans pass rush, though, that's remained one of the best in the NFL for the past couple of seasons, it could lead to Lawrence being forced under a bit more duress than he has been this season, as he's been sacked just 10 times through five games.
As for the Texans' defense, they've recorded 18 total sacks through that same stretch. Last week against the Tennessee Titans, it was Will Anderson who stepped up to the occasion for 3.0 sacks on Cam Ward , managing to tie his career-high in the process.
If the Texans' elite edge duo can keep pressure consistent on the Jaguars' passing game and make them feel the loss of Harrison on their blindside, then the road to a second-straight win might become a little easier on the road in London.
Therefore, expect Houston and their coaching staff to make that pass rush a primary emphasis in practice before Week 6 gets underway.

title: Texans Week 5 Snap Counts vs. Titans: 3 Things That Stood Out
full_text:
The snap counts from the Houston Texans' Week 5 matchup against the Tennessee Titans have officially been revealed.
And within those numbers, we're able to get a clear determination of exactly who was on the field for the Texans throughout this weekend's action, and see just how big a piece each player was to their game plan en route to a dominant 26-3 victory .
Let's take a look at how the action unfolded in Nashville for the Texans' snap counts, and break down three things from those numbers that have looked just a little different from last weekend's sample size:
While David Montgomery's limited day with only nine snaps was because of the groin injury he sustained in the first half, it was clear that the Texans had no problem giving second-year runner Woody Marks a ton of opportunities while he was ruled out. Marks was on the field for all but 10 offensive snaps for the day, and turned that into his best performance of the season thus far, recording 19 total touches for a combined 85 yards from scrimmage. If Montgomery is forced to miss any time, which, based on DeMeco Ryans' claim from Monday that the veteran runner's status is now "week-to-week", you can expect to see Marks continue to be a heavy piece of the Texans' offensive game plan .
Along with an injury to David Montgomery on the offensive side, the Texans also saw their versatile nickel/safety, Jalen Pitre, leave the same in the second half with a shoulder injury , which has also left him week-to-week heading into Week 6 against the Jacksonville Jaguars. And in the time that Jalen Pitre was out, who did the Texans decide to slot into his place? It was fifth-round rookie safety, Kamari Ramsey, who hasn't been much of a factor on the defensive side of the ball for the first four weeks of the season, yet could slot into a key role on the depth chart for a short period, depending on how long Pitre is sidelined. And the decision makes sense from the Texans' perspective too. Ramsey has previous experience playing the nickel along with safety during his time in college at USC, so maybe the first-year talent will be able to hold his own in that role.
After finally recovering from the ankle injury that left him on injured reserve for the first four weeks of the season, second-round rookie Kayden McDonald was finally able to get his feet wet in an in-game setting for the first time of his NFL career. And based on the limited chunk of reps that McDonald got, it seems as if the Texans wanted to ease their second-round rookie into the game plan, rather than immediately slotting him into a big role. Sure, 11 snaps isn't much for McDonald to work with. But as he gets more games and experience under his belt, those opportunities will only continue to grow, to the point where he could be starting next to Sheldon Rankins by the time we get to the end of the regular season. For now, though, he'll have to remain patient.

title: How Texans' Marvin Harrison Jr. Trade Reshapes Their Future at WR
full_text:
The Houston Texans' wide receiver room got a noteworthy addition after their Week 5 win over the Tennessee Titans when the announcement was made that a trade would be made to acquire Arizona Cardinals wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr .
Harrison Jr., the 24-year-old former top five pick, was brought in with the vision of being a young, talented fixture in the wide receiver room for the foreseeable future, as the Texans would wind up giving up a 2027 second and sixth-round pick for his services.
But now with Harrison Jr. in the mix for what's already an interesting (and pretty deep) Texans wide receiver room, how does his presence change the outlook of the position group moving forward ?
Let's break down some of the key takeaways surrounding the Texans' wide receiver room for both this season and onwards with Harrison Jr. now a part of the future.
There has been some lingering chatter around the Texans' acquisition of Harrison Jr. having some impact of Nico Collins' future–– who is set to see his current contract expire after the end of the 2027 season, and will be due for a major pay day once the time comes.
So could the Harrison Jr. addition be the Texans' form of preparing to move off of Collins once that contract is due? Definitely not.
Unless Harrison Jr. simply develops so well that Houston can't afford to keep both receivers on the books for long-term deals, the idea will be for both guys to work in tandem with one another, and help take this offense to the next level.
It's been a while since the Texans have had two reliable outside receivers to rely upon each and every week. If Harrison can offer that one-two punch as a secondary target next to Collins, this move can ultimately be a success even for the high cost of a second-round pick.
The Texans' pursuit of another dynamic playmaker at wide receiver seems to hint that they'll be moving towards the mindset of running a spread offense more than they anticipated entering the season.
That's because of the talent Houston can roll out all at once at the receiver position when adding Harrison Jr. next to guys like Jaylin Noel and, when healthy, Tank Dell .
Getting all of them involved on gameday seems like the best way for this offense to play to their strengths, while also helping C.J. Stroud build onto the momentum that he's collected throughout an impressive 2026 campaign.
So for Nick Caley's game plan on the offensive end, you can expect a little less emphasis on the run game and heavy tight end usage, while they instead double down on the talent and depth they have at wideout.
With the move to land Harrison Jr., his addition tends to immediately put two names in the Texans' receiver room on notice because of their contract situation: Kayshon Boutte and Xavier Hutchinson.
Both of those guys are in a contract year this season, set to hit free agency in the 2027 offseason. (Yes, Tank Dell has an expiring contract as well, but his status on the roster feels a little more secure.) And knowing the depth Houston can now roll out at wide receiver, spending any noteworthy amount to keep them around on a new deal might not be the best use of resources.
So keep a close eye on how the Texans utilize each in the weeks ahead. Depending on how involved they are in the offensive game plan, it might be a hint as to what their future in Houston looks like beyond this season.
The biggest question mark of them all as it relates to the Texans' wide receiver room after this weekend's trade: what does the future hold for Jayden Higgins?
On one hand, Higgins was a productive rising talent throughout the course of his rookie season in 2025. He was expected to claim a major role in the Texans' offense this year before ultimately suffering a season-ending ACL injury in training camp , and will now have to wait until 2027 to re-join the lineup.
However, the presence of Harrison Jr. certainly complicates his fit a little more; someone who also is viewed as a complementary outside weapon opposite of Nico Collins. Add that onto the depth Houston has with guys like Noel and Dell, and the role Higgins is going to have when he's back healthy is really a mystery.
In reality, it's a good problem for the Texans to have: they have more depth at receiver than they've had in some time. But realistically, it's tough to imagine Higgins and all of the aforementioned targets having a considerable role in the offense once everyone's at 100%.
