title: 3 Observations on Jaguars' Post-Eagles Roster Moves: Anton Harrison and Kaevon Merriweather Impacts
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars made a couple of roster moves Tuesday, each of which could have a profound impact on the next few weeks of the season.
Along with the signing of long snapper Jacob Bobenmoyer to the practice squad, the Jaguars also signed safety Kaevon Merriweather to the active roster of the practice squad, as well as placed left tackle Anton Harrison on injured reserve.
So, what do we make of each move and what it means moving forward, especially in the wake of the latest Anton Harrison update ? We break it down below.
Between this move and last week's usage at the safety position, the Jaguars are making it fairly clear where they stand on the safety pecking order. Until it changes during a game, it certainly appears the Jaguars' answer during Eric Murray's time out is for Rayuan Lane and Merriweather to be the No. 2 and No. 3 safeties behind Antonio Johnson, leaving third-round rookie Jalen Huskey on the sidelines. This was how the Jaguars approached Week 5, with Huskey logging zero snaps on defense as a result.
"But it'd be great to get Eric [S Eric Murray] back, hopefully, but if not, have a lot of confidence. I thought Kaevon [Merriweather] had a great week of practice, and did some nice things in the game," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said Monday. "I thought Ray [S Rayuan Lane III] did some nice things in the game. There's communication that's always going to exist when you have to play with some other guys. They stepped up, helped us win the game.”
We have a smaller sample size with Merriweather than with Lane, but this will be a situation to watch moving forward if Murray continues to miss time. But as things stand today, it is clear how the dust has settled.
The Jaguars' injured reserve list sure is growing longer. The Jaguars have now placed two key players on injured reserve in back-to-back weeks with Harrison and second-year safety Caleb Ransaw a week ago, with second-year defensive end BJ Green II also being placed on injured reserve after Week 1. This follows the Jaguars placing offensive lineman Patrick Mekari and defensive end Zach Durfee on injured reserve ahead of the start of the season.
Outside of Durfee, these are all critical players the Jaguars were set to lean on in some fashion this year, whether it be as starters or top depth options. The Jaguars have been mostly healthy, but the injuries have piled up over the last few weeks, and now so is the injured reserve list as a result of them.
With Harrison out for the next four games at least, the earliest he could return is in Week 11 against the New York Giants (if he is able to return at all). It is pretty clear that the Jaguars are set to place Walekr Little back in the left tackle spot that he once occupied, with Little playing quite well against the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 5 during the second-half. But what about the swing tackle spot that Little used to hold?
Second-year offensive lineman Wyatt Milum is set to likely to step into the swing tackle role for the next couple of weeks. The Jaguars could also start having offensive lineman Daniel Faalele active and could turn to him as a swing option, while Mekari gives them another option once he comes of the injured reserve.

title: Jaguars Report Card: Grades From Eagles Win Vary From Concerning to Gold Stars
full_text:
In the NFL, all that really matters at the end of the day is the result, and the Jaguars got the one they were looking for in their 19-17 win over the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 5.
But which Jaguars position groups shined during the last-second win, and which position groups played a big role in the game being so close to begin with? We break it down with this week's report cards.
Trevor Lawrence was certainly fired up at points during Sunday's game, and it is not hard to see why. For the second week in a row, penalties set Lawrence and the Jaguars up with far too many 2nd- and 3rd-and-longs, which made the offense feel very stop-and-go at times. They did move the ball well largely thanks to Lawrence, though, and he was once again made a handful of throws that it feels like only he is completing. The interception was a bad throw while under pressure, and Lawrence did hold onto the ball a bit too long a few times, but overall this felt like a productive outing from the Jaguars' franchise quarterback.
Despite not getting a lot of efficient production from the running game on Sunday, it still felt like a strong outing from Bhayshul Tuten. He broke a lot of tackles to turn big losses into, at least, neutral plays. It feels like had the Jaguars trust him a bit more in the red-zone, he could have made a difference when it came to converting those trips into touchdowns. Chris Rodriguez Jr. did not do much with his limited touches, though, and it felt like the worst rushing performance of the year as a whole for the team.
Parjer Washington continued to do big, big things for the wide receiver room. Washington was one of the most important pieces of the Jaguars' win over the Eagles thanks to both his touchdowns, while the Jaguars were able to get production out of Jakobi Meyers and Josh Cameron when giving them targets. The only real negative plays were the few targets that Brian Thomas Jr. was not able to come down with.
It was a very productive day from the tight end room, with the Jaguars' duo of Brenton Strange and Nate Boerkircher combining for nine catches for 88 yards on 10 targets. There were a few small miscues, such as a few missed blocks from Boerkircher, a drop from Strange, and Strange leaving his feet near the goal-line. But overall, the Jaguars have gotten much more out of the tight end group as a whole than they did at this same time last season.
The Jaguars did see Walker Little step up i n a big way against the Eagles, pitching a shutout as a pass-blocker in the second-half. Little has often been far underrated amongst circles that discuss the Jaguars, and they will need him now with Anton Harrison injured. Jalen Carter did Jalen Carter things to the Jaguars, but penalties and the lack of production in the run game are what ultimately pull this score down. Carter is an elite player, but eventually the Jaguars' offensive line needs to prove that they can slow down those types of talents.
The Jaguars' defensive line had its best game of the season on Sunday, hands down. Not only did the Jaguars limit the Eagles in the running game completely, but they also sent their pass-rush at Jalen Hurts in waves. The Jaguars disrupted the Eagles' passing game and got Hurts to rush throws or make passes off-platform, with Josh Hines-Allen and Travon Walker making especially big impacts as pass-rushers. It took a team effort, too, with a number of depth players and blitzers at defensive back and linebacker chipping in, but the defensive line led the way.
I thought the #Jaguars dominated the Eagles OL up front, and that's what all the evidence says. 23 pressures (2nd-most in Week 5) and 54.8% pressure rate (2nd-most.) Both season highs despite Jalen Hurts having the second-quickest time to throw this week pic.twitter.com/OYkc4Pk2jk
Ventrell Miller is genuinely getting better each week. Miller had another stellar performance on Sunday, making several impressive stops both downhill against the run and in the flats as a tackler in space in coverage. Dennis Gardeck and Foyesade Oluokun also made impacts against the run and in the pass-rush, and this is a position group that is simply playing good football right now. Miller looks like a truly ascending player in Anthony Campanile's defense, and this was one of his best games yet.
There were some good things from the cornerback room; Jarrian Jones had a very effective outing, Jourdan Lewis and Antonio Johnson produced against the run and on blitzes, and as a whole the Jaguars tackled well in the back-end. But a 3rd-and-long pass-interference on Travis Hunter that eventually led to a touchdown dings them, as does some of the miscues such as the explosive 62-yard touchdown allowed to Darius Cooper in the first-half.
The only thing that keeps this from being an A+ is the fact that the Jaguars did miss an extra point and did allow a bit too much yardage on returns. But at the same time ... come on. Heath Farwell's unit returned a kick for a touchdown before a flag nullified it, then Ameer Abdullah set up Cam Little for his game-winning 57-yard field goal. The Jaguars had the better special teams unit on Sunday, and it is a big reason they won.
This felt like one of the oddest Jaguars games from a management and game-plan standpoint in some time. I do not blame Liam Coen for going for it on fourth downs due to the snap issues with Davon Hamilton and high snaps, but Coen also allowed an extra point attempt that looked like it was missed largely due to the snap. Why not be consistent? Coen also said Monday he took responsibility for a delay of game in the red-zone. Throwing the ball on second down on the four-minute drive was also an odd choice. As for the defense, I thought Anthony Campanile made great adjustments in second-half, but the first-half plan of man-blitzes was always a bad idea against Jalen Hurts, and he made them pay for it.

title: Jack Kiser Has Officially Become the New Jaguars Regime's First Draft Bust
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars' new era officially has their first draft miss.
The Jaguars saw former linebacker Jack Kiser get claimed on waivers on Monday by the Cincinnati Bengals, reuniting the former Jaguars fourth-rounder with his former Notre Dame defensive coordinator Al Golden. And as a result, the Jaguars have their first draft bust of the Liam Coen/James Gladstone/Tony Boselli era.
The Jaguars drafted Kiser with the No. 107th pick in the fourth-round of the 2025 NFL Draft, tacking Kiser just a few picks after they took running back Bhayshul Tuten at No. 104 overall. But while Tuten has turned into a key piece of what the Jaguars do a year later, Kiser never quite was able to get the same footing during his short time with the Jaguars.
Kiser was a reserve for the Jaguars as a rookie, with the former Notre Dame linebacker appear in 14 games as a backup last season. He recorded 14 tackles as a rookie, playing 43 snaps on defense and 193 snaps (53%) on special teams. But Kiser was dealt a tough blow at the start of training camp in his sophmore season, going down with a knee injury during team drills on the first day of practice.
Kiser never practiced for the Jaguars again during camp, and the Jaguars ended up waiving him after camp before signing him to the practice squad. Kiser was eventually elevated from the practice squad and signed back to the active roster earlier this season, but he never ended up appearing in a game for the Jaguars this season.
The Jaguars then waived him for a second time this weekend as they made a slew of roster moves before their Week 5 game against the Philadelphia Eagles, with the Jaguars instead signing fellow 2025 draftee Jalen McLeod from the practice squad to the active roster.
No matter what Kiser ends up doing for the Bengals, this can now be classified as the new Jaguars regime's first miss. He is the first of 19 draft picks over the last two seasons to play for a new team, and the Jaguars essentially picked McLeod over him this weekend. The Jaguars also picked veteran backup linebacker Jahlani Tavai over Kiser at the end of training camp, and that stance clearly hasn't changed.
Kiser was dealt a tough hand with injuries, but the fact the Jaguars never seemed to entertain the idea of him battling for a starting spot with Ventrell Miller and Branson Combs after the departure of Devin Lloyd in free agency indicated that this was a pick they felt comfortable moving on from after a season. It is better to pull the plug on a pick too early as opposed to too late, but this was an even tougher miss considering stud Buffalo Bills defensive tackle Deone Walker was taken just a few picks later.
The Jaguars do not seem to have any other 2025 picks in danger of falling into the same category as Kiser anytime soon. McLeod was in the same boat as Kiser just a few weeks ago, but he has impressed in a big way on special teams and has seemed to at least carved out a role there for now. The returns on third-rounders Caleb Ransaw and Wyatt Milum has yet to be there, but they are not close to being off the roster outright like Kiser.
He will not be the last draft pick the Jaguars miss on, but for the new regime he is officially their first.

title: Anton Harrison Injury Update: Latest On Jaguars' Blindside Protector
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are facing their biggest injury concern of their 2026 season.
The Jaguars saw left tackle Anton Harrison get carted off the field during the third-quarter of Week 5's win over the Philadelphia Eagle s, and the latest status update has provided a best -- and a worst -- case scenario.
NFL Network's Ian Rapoport reported Tuesday morning that Harrison will undergo arthroscopic knee surgery, during which a doctor will determine exactly how long the talented and valuable offensive tackle will be out. According to Rapoport, "Depending on what the surgeon sees during the procedure, Anton Harrison is either out 3-5 weeks (likely IR) or 3-4 months (out for the regular season).
"
#Jaguars starting LT Anton Harrison, starter since 2023, is expected to undergo arthroscopic knee surgery when he returns from London, per me and @JFowlerESPN . During the surgery, the doctor will determine how long Trevor Lawrence’s blindside protector is out — weeks or months. pic.twitter.com/euMcFlKvBa
It is hard to call this either good news or bad news, it really just depends on what the medical team determines when it comes to the severity of his knee injury. There are other examples of players sustaining the injury, such as Myles Garrett earlier this season. Garrett is on injured-reserve but is expected to return for the Los Angeles Rams at some point this season. But until there is a final determination on his status, it is tough to say how one should feel.
The fact that Harrison at least has a chance to potentially return is at least some solace. The Jaguars play a tough Houston Texans team this week before a Week 7 bye. Harrison will clearly miss this week, and if he is placed on injured reserve this week the soonest he would be able to return would be Week 11 against the New York Giants on the road.
Not having Harrison on hand against the Texans is clearly not ideal, though the Jaguars did see backup left tackle Walker Little step up along with the rest of the offensive line against the Eagles when Harrison was injured.
"Walker [OL Walker Little] stepping in, obviously, those guys fighting through. Just playing hard. It's hard in there, and they're playing a good group. And I felt like they just stuck with it. I thought protection-wise, for the most part of the day, I didn't think it was too bad," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said Monday.
"We held on on the ball a little bit long on a few when we did get the strip sacks and I thought we just settled down a little bit more in the second half as a group, and they played hard. They played their tails off. That's a damn good front. It's one of the bigger fronts that we'll see.  Obviously, will have a huge challenge again this week with another good front."
If the Jaguars can get Harrison back within the next month and a half or so, they could have him back on the field for a critical second-half stretch to secure the AFC South over the Texans. But if he is out for the season, then the Jaguars have the depth to sustain the hit, but will still clearly feel the loss of their talented left tackle.

title: 3 Takeaways on Jaguars Signing Long Snapper Jacob Bobenmoyer and What it Means
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are reportedly set to make a big addition before Week 6.
According to NFL Network's Ian Rapoport, the Jaguars are set to sign veteran long snapper Jacob Bobenmoyer ahead of their next battle in London against the Houston Texans. This, of course, comes after the Jaguars had to deploy nose tackle Davon Hamilton at long snapper due to an injury to Ross Matiscik in Week 5.
So, what does the Bobenmoyer signing mean for the Jaguars after their big 19-17 win over the Philadelphia Eagles? We break it down below.
Long snapper news: The #Jaguars are signing NFL veteran LS Jacob Bobenmoyer as their new long snapper, which means DT DaVon Hamilton can return to his day job. He’s already flown to London. Hamilton filled in admirably for injured Ross Matiscik, which won’t be placed on IR. pic.twitter.com/kFLoTpFqkf
The good news for the Jaguars when it comes to this report is that Matiscik is not expected to be placed on injured reserve. That makes sense considering the Jaguars bye week is next week, which means could sit this week and get two games of rest before the Jaguars start the second-half of the season. If the Jaguars had placed him on injured reserve today, he would miss Sunday, which is already expected, along with the first three games of the bye week since the bye week does not count as one of his four weeks missed on injured reserve.
By playing this form of roster gymnastics, the Jaguars have given themselves some flexibility with the long snapper spot. Matiscik is a legit weapon for the Jaguars at the long snapper spot thanks both to his consistency as a smaller and his tackling ability on coverage teams. The less time the Jaguars are without him, the better for Heath Farwell’s unit. He is a big piece of what they do, so you can certainly count this as positive news for the Jaguars and their special teams moving forward.
There is obviously not a lot of room to breakdown long-snapper tape, but we can go off numbers. Bobenmoyer has been an active long snapper on coverage teams just based off how many tackles he has record. He has recorded at least three tackles in every season, recording 22 tackles in 97 games over the last six years. By comparison, Matiscik also had 22 tackles in six season before entering the 2026 season.
In short, he will likely not be Matiscik on coverage teams because, well, nobody is. But he should at least give the Jaguars something on coverage teams, which makes sense consider the Jaguars likely wanted to target a long-snapper who could give them similar things to Matiscik. Nobody is going to ask him to be a star tackler like the Jaguars' All-Pro long snapper, but he can help them.
Is there anything more we can say about Davon Hamilton? Not only has he been one of the best defensive tackles in football this season, but he stepped up for the Jaguars at a moment's notice and held down the fort at the long snapper position in a key one-score game. Hamilton was at his best when the moment demanded it against the Eagles, and he is a key reason the Jaguars won the game.
While the Jaguars won't need Hamilton to step up again this week, he got them through a touchy situation. He deserves all the credit he is getting for his performance against the Eagles, but it was also smart of the Jaguars to move quickly to secure a full-time long-snapper ahead of a key game against the Houston Texans on Sunday.

title: 3 Options the Jaguars Must Consider if Anton Harrison Misses Significant Time
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars might have a serious injury question facing them.
The Jaguars left Week 5 with a much-needed last-second victory over the Philadelphia Eagles , but it didn't come without its costs. Left tackle Anton Harrisonwas carted off the field in the third-quarter and did not return, and now his status is up in the air.
“Yeah, I mean, we'll have to see. He just got an MRI, just now, so we don't have the results back yet. We're kind of at the mercy of that and to see what that looks like and how he feels. He's a little stiff," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said Monday.
"I have a lot of belief in [Jeff Ferguson, Vice President of Player Health and Performance] and our group downstairs to be able to…If anybody's going to get him ready to play, it'll be them, and we'll have to be patient with, obviously, if he's not able to, you know, practice what that looks like and go from there. But, you know, it was a weird play. He was trying to block on the turnback, and it just tweaked on him a little bit. We'll have to see what the MRI looks like. We're at the mercy of it right now.”
So if the Jaguars are set to be without Harrison for an extended period of time, what are their options moving forward? We break it down below.
This is the most obvious, and most likely, scenario. Walker Little is a legit starting offensive tackle talent in the NFL, and there are not a ton of teams who he would have opened 2025 as a backup for. That is why the Jaguars have valued their offensive line depth the way they have over the years, and they have the rare luxury of having another starting offensive tackle ready to play if the scenario ever came up where they needed one.
Little played well for the Jaguars during his half of football against the Eagles, and there is plenty of reason to think he can hold his own moving forward. In this scenario, the Jaguars would likely have Wyatt Milum as their swing tackle option, with Daniel Faalele also joining the mix. Eventually, the Jaguars will be set to get Patrick Mekari back from injured reserve as well, giving the Jaguars another potential depth option for offensive tackle.
Little has started a lot of games at left tackle before, and the Jaguars are in a better spot than many teams would be if their starting tackle was injured. This is what makes the most sense for the Jaguars and their offensive line moving forward.
Another option could be to do some musical chairs at the offensive tackle position. Cole Van Lanen did some great things at left tackle last season when he earned his big-time contract extension, and Little has experience at right tackle as well. Daniel Faalele and Wyatt Milum are also better depth options as right tackles as opposed to at left tackle, which could make this the best way for the Jaguars to get their best five on the field.
That is not to say this option would be without its faults, of course. Van Lanen has spent every single snap of this season at right tackle, and the Jaguars even noted before Week 1 that Van Lanen's most comfortable spot is at the right tackle spot. He played great at left tackle a year ago, but he is still just five games into his season after a serious knee injury in January. Putting a position switch on top of that could be asking quite a lot.
This feels like the least likely option, but it is worth considering. There are not many teams that would be willing to part with starting-caliber offensive tackles, but I think James Gladstone is the general manager who could find a deal if there was one to be made. The Jaguars have a decent amount of draft picks to work with as well, which means Gladstone could get aggressive if it appears the Jaguars will be without Harrison for the long-term.
Again, the lack of options would be an issue, which is what makes this more of an extreme option than anything else. But the Jaguars have quickly put together trades to fill holes on the roster in the past, and it would not make much sense to count out Gladstone and the Jaguars from doing it again if the situation demands it.

title: Jaguars Week 5 Snap Count Analysis: Liam Coen's Staff Must Make One Big Shift
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- With the Jacksonville Jaguars facing their fair of injuries both before and during Sunday's Week 5 win, this week's snap count report looks quite a bit different.
The Jaguars had several players play their largest roles of the season in Week 5's win over the Philadelphia Eagles, but what do this week's snaps really tell us about how the Jaguars approached their latest win? We break it down below.
The Jaguars had rookie safety Jalen Huskey active for the first time in his rookie season on Sunday, but it did not result in him seeing the field very much. Huskey ended up playing zero offensive snaps and just three special teams snaps, making it clear that the Jaguars see him way down the pecking order at safety. While that even may be a fair argument for them to make since they know him best and see him practice every day, it is hard to imagine the Jaguars should let him continue to watch at safety if Eric Murray misses any more time.
The Jaguars had Rayuan Lane play 100% of the snaps and practice squad safety Kaevon Merriweather serve as the No. 3 safety with 34% of the defensive snaps. The Jaguars did not get great production out of the safety room outside of Antonio Johnson, however, and the Jaguars should consider a shift to Huskey as at least the No. 3 safety if Murray continues to miss time. Lane fills his depth role well, but he just looked a bit out of his element as a starter on Sunday.
If the Jaguars had not already made it clear, there is a lead back in Duval: Bhayshul Tuten, who had one of his highest rates of usage in his career. Tuten played a career high in snaps with 49 (68.1%), while his 22 carries were also an easy career high. When the Jaguars needed an important play on the ground, it was Tuten who they leaned into. The Tuten usage has never been higher, but that does mean it has to go backward for someone else.
That player is clearly Chris Rodriguez Jr., who has seen his role diminish significantly since even Week 1. Rodriguez played a season-low snaps with nine (12.5%) and only had two carries, making it clear that he is, above all else, Tuten's backup. He did get red-zone short-yardage work, but he is clearly just a role player right now, as opposed to Tuten being the Jaguars' clear No. 1 running back by really every single definition.
Tuten has seen his role take a massive leap, first compared to a year ago and now compared to Week 1. It feels like by the end of the season we will start to see Tuten get 20+ carries almost weekly considering how balanced the Jaguars' offense is.
The Jaguars' pair of rookie skill players combined for five catches on six targets for 63 yards (12.6 yards per catch). Josh Cameron caught three passes for 43 yards and Nate Boerkircher caught two passes for 20 yards, while playing nearly 50% of the snaps in a 12-personnel happy game plan against the Eagles. As a whole, the duo combined for 63 yards on 29 routes, which comes out to 2.17 yards per route run. For context, that would rank top-25 amongst all NFL wide recievers in yards per route run.
Boerkircher got plenty of run with 35 snaps (49%), while Cameron played 22 snaps (31%), with each player having a significant impact despite not playing full-time snaps. The Jaguars are getting instant production from each non-first round draft pick, which is an ideal outcome for any team like the Jaguars coming off a playoff season. The Jaguars' offensive rookies have already become true hits.

title: Jaguars Stock Report: 3 Players Rising, Falling After Eagles Win ... Starting With Walker Little
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. --  The Jacksonville Jaguars' roster has taken some significant strides over the last two seasons, and those strides helped the Jaguars improve to 4-1 in Week 5.
It took a full team effort, of course, for the Jaguars to get past the Philadelpia Eagles on Sunday. but in the NFL, a win is a win. Thanks to the performances from the roster in the 19-17 win, several Jaguars saw their stocks rise -- while a few others saw theirs slip. We break it all down in this week's Jaguars Stock Report.
At times like these, it makes it clear why the Jaguars have put such an emphasis on their offensive line depth. The Jaguars faced a serious injury question in the third-quarter with Anton Harrison getting carted off the field with a knee injury. The Jaguars have one of the best backup offensive linemen in all of the NFL with former starting left tackle Walker Little, and he quickly proved his worth against a tough Eagles front.
Little allowed zero pressures on 18 pass blocking snaps according to Pro Football Focus, making it clear that the Jaguars' plans for the offensive line and preparing for the worst-case scenarios have paid off. Little has played good football before for the Jaguars, and they are lucky to have him in the event Harrison now misses time, starting with Week 6 against the Houston Texans and the Will Anderson/Danielle Hunter duo.
It just continues to feel like this season is slipping away for Brian Thomas Jr., who now ranks fourth in catches (9) and fith in yards (105) this season. He has fewer yards (105) than sixth-round rookie Josh Cameron (117). The connection just has not been there for him and Trevor Lawrence, with Thomas having the lowest catch rate of any of the Jaguars' primary skill players. Right now, he is on pace for 30 catches and 357 yards.
I still think this has much less to do with Thomas and his talent than it does with his role in the style of Coen's offense. Thomas did have Quinyon Mitchell beat on a deep route that Lawrence underthrew after being hit on the throw, but it just hasn't worked out in the offense. On Sunday, he was out-paced in the passing game by Nate Boerkircher, Travis Hunter, and Chris Rodriguez Jr. I do not know where they go from here.
Brenton Strange was once again a significant factor for the Jaguars' offense on Sunday. Over the last three weeks, Strange ranks sixth amongst all tight ends in catches and third in yards, as well as ranking only behind Brock Bowers in yards per route run. Strange has had some miscues, such as a drop on Sunday, but he has elevated his role in the passing game in a big way over the last several weeks.
Part of this could be due to matchups, with the Jaguars playing three teams in a row who struggle against tight ends in coverage. But there are more teams who struggle to slow down tight ends than there are teams who struggle to slow down receivers, and Strange could be an X-Factor of the offense moving forward.
It felt like some of the Jaguars' failed red-zone trips on Sunday featured Chris Rodriguez Jr. for one way or another. The sequence where he had a near fumble (after Jalen Carter wrecked the play) and then missed the block on Zack Baun on the failed fourth-down sweep to Bhayshul Tuten was a tough one, and it just felt too often like the thought of "why isn't Bhayshul Tuten in the game here?" crept up over the course of the game.
Overall, Rodriguez only got two carries for the Jaguars as they leaned on Bhayshul Tuten more and more. Part of this might have to do with the fact that the Jaguars knew they would need a running back to create before the line of scrimmage, but Rodriguez's role has just yet to be overly significant in any game.
It feels like Antonio Johnson has been all over the place for the Jaguars over the last few weeks. He continued this on Sunday with some quality reps both against the run and in coverage, while also splitting a sack with Travon Walker. This was the first game in Johnson's career where he was the sole veteran voice at safety, and he certainly played his role well against the Eagles.
Antonio Johnson with a lot of big plays for the #Jaguars last few weeks: pic.twitter.com/vA5r8JO5VI
Johnson has stepped up for the Jaguars, and his game has improved even from his breakout season a year ago. Johnson is a key cog of this unit every week, but he is even more important now that the Jaguars are facing some injuries and having to play some backups at the safety spot next to him over the next few weeks.
Sunday marked the first start of Rayuan Lane's career, and he did do some good things. He was an effective blitzer and made some nice run fits playing downhill, but he did have some issues when the Eagles were able to isolate him in space. Lane plays hard and competes on every snap, but Sunday made it hard to see him having much success as a full-time starter at safety. Maybe more and more reps help, but this did not feel like a great step in the right direction.

title: 3 Things We Learned About the Jaguars vs. the Eagles: Trevor Lawrence's Fire
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars had to pull out all of the stops for their fourth win of the season, but they made it happen in Week 5.
The Jaguars survived an upset attempt from the Philadelphia Eagles thanks to Cam Little hitting a walkoff 57-yard field goal in a 19-17 win. But what did we learn from the Jaguars' narrow win, and what could it all mean moving forward?
Trevor Lawrence did a lot of good things on Sunday sans his second-half interception. He was faced with plenty of unfavorable 2nd- and 3rd-and-long situations due to the penalties for the second week in a row, but he made so many plays in and out of structure that helped the Jaguars move the ball. Had the Jaguars figured things out in the red-zone, the score would have more so reflected the performance that Lawrence had. But among all other things, Lawrence also showed some of the maturation as the general of the offense when he, well, was irate after yet another red-zone penalty.
Trevor Lawrence CRASHED OUT on his center 😭 pic.twitter.com/bUC2oV1z3Y
It was a sign of Lawrence's fire that, frankly, needed to be shown considering the situation. I have covered every single game of Lawrence's NFL career, and I never once saw him quite so frustrated and then let the rest of the offense know about it. Lawrence is a cool, calm and collected type of leader, and this isn't something he would have done a few years ago at least not in my eyes. Call it the Liam Coen impact, call it the natural growth of a franchise quarterback, but Lawrence showed the fire that many thought he was missing entering the NFL.
"I do like seeing him have that fire and that, you know, competitive edge. You know, he wants it to be good. He wants the operation to be clean. I think there was a lot of frustrations throughout that game that probably built up to be more emotional in that moment," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said on Monday
I thought Parker Washington had the best game of any Jaguars skill player, which is easy to say with two touchdowns and over 120 receiving yards. Washington is far and away the clear Jaguars' No. 1 receiver, even with his one-catch game in Week 4 in the rear view window. But after Washington, I think we are starting to see a second player establish himself on the Jaguars' pecking order in the passing game: Brenton Strange.
Over the last three weeks, Strange leads the Jaguars with 21 targets, 17 receptions and 195 yards despite ranking third on the team in routes in that span with 75. Strange has been effective for the Jaguars aside from a few uncharacteristic drops in that span. His increase in volumn does not seem like an accident, though, especially considering most teams are better at defending passes out wide than they are in the middle of the field.
Washington is the clear No. 1. Brian Thomas Jr. clearly is a small part of the offense. Jakobi Meyers has, so far, felt more like an auxilary option other than in Week 3. I think Strange is the No. 2 pass-catcher in the offense right now.
The Jaguars simply have to sort out their penalty issues. Some flags have certainly been silly calls by the officials, but some have been purely the Jaguars' fault. It is not the fault of the officials if the Jaguars are getting false starts and delay of games, which has happened far too often over the last two weeks especially. "The penalties are concerning when you start the season off in the first three weeks as the second-least penalized team in the NFL, and now over the last two weeks, we're arguably one of the most penalized teams in the NFL," Coen said.
The Jaguars have won each of their last 2 games despite 26 total penalties. They are the first team since the Seahawks in Weeks 10 and 11 of the 2011 season to win consecutive games with 13+ penalties in each game. Penalties are the major reason why the last two wins have had to come in one-score games, and the Jaguars simply have to figure out how to play cleaner football in all three phases. Penalties alone have wiped out three touchdowns and an interception for the Jaguars in the last two weeks. What happens when this happens against a good team and not just the Bengals or Eagles?

title: Chiefs On SI Mailbag: Will Cyrus Allen Step Up After Tyquan Thornton's Injury?
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs' bye week is over. Now, focus turns to the Los Angeles Chargers. With the Chiefs undefeated and the Chargers still winless, there's a bizarre undertone to this AFC West showdown. Meanwhile, the Chiefs still have uncertainty at left tackle and wide receiver.
Those are the topics we'll begin with on this edition of the Chiefs On SI mailbag .
What happens first? Cyrus Allen reception or Justin Watson reception? -@ReidsNuggies
I'm completely fine with the Chiefs' decision to reunite with Justin Watson on a practice squad basis, but for the season-long health of the receiver room, Cyrus Allen has to start seeing the field more. While Allen has played just 10 offensive snaps, resulting in two targets and zero catches through his first four weeks of NFL action, I do expect him to see an increased workload on Sunday against the Chargers, and I sure hope that includes his first NFL catch.
I could see Watson's role landing in any number of places. It wouldn't surprise me if Watson doesn't see the field for another week or two as he reacclimates to the offense, and it wouldn't surprise me if he took a decent handful of snaps on Sunday as a de facto decoy to keep LA's safeties honest as a theoretical deep threat.
My expectations for Allen's timeline have always been measured—rookie receivers have a learning curve in Andy Reid's offense—but a well-timed bye should help him add a few responsibilities to his plate.
The obvious part about Allen's potential involvement is that the Chiefs simply need one of their receivers to take more reps in Tyquan Thornton's absence. The exciting part is that Allen has the potential to provide much more than a handful of adequate snaps.
Is it Cyrus Allen time in KC? ⏰👀 pic.twitter.com/edTcQOI7Nn
On 3rd and long, what 11 defenders do you want on the field to get the stop? -@youjustreadmym1
This is a great question to cut through some of the challenges of picking favorites (and least-favorites) in a defensive rotation. Some of these picks are easy, some are toss-ups.
George Karlaftis and Chris Jones have to be on the defensive line. I'll leave Jones in the interior, with R Mason Thomas on the other edge. I'm still very bullish on Peter Woods, but right now... Felix Anudike-Uzomah as an interior pass rusher has been one of the more interesting developments of the season! Throw Anudike-Uzomah inside, next to Jones.
I'd be tempted to roll with only one linebacker, but having both Nick Bolton and Drue Tranquill seems almost mandatory, even though Tranquill may be playing better than Bolton so far this year .
That leaves me with five defensive backs: Mansoor Delane, Nohl Williams, Chamarri Conner, Alohi Gilman , and... whoever gives you the best chance in the slot. While L'Jarius Sneed has taken most of those snaps so far this year, I'd be inclined to give Chris Roland-Wallace my final spot against a smaller slot receiver, while Sneed gets the nod in a more physical matchup.
If Josh Simmons doesn’t return anytime soon, what is KC’s plan, and how do they avoid a repeat of the 2024 season? -@jacklerner.bsky.social
I think it's interesting to view the Chiefs' current left tackle situation through the lens of 2024, when the issues on Patrick Mahomes' blindside significantly impacted the offense all the way to the Super Bowl.
In 2026, the Chiefs have really had their share of issues from both tackle positions, but if Josh Simmons does return soon, KC can pick their choice of Kahlil Benson or Jaylon Moore at right tackle while sending the other to the swing tackle role. Without Simmons, of course, that gets murky.
I'm not surprised that we haven't seen him through the first four weeks, but undrafted rookie Diego Pounds, who the Chiefs acquired from the Baltimore Ravens just before roster cuts , had some very intruiging film from Baltimore's preseason. He's been a pure left tackle, so the idea of putting Pounds on the left side and Benson back at his natural right side does excite me... at least until I remember that would require Mahomes to be protected by a duo of undrafted rookies. That's not ideal, but it is an answer.
I can't see the Chiefs making a significant pre-deadline move to acquire a left tackle unless they have lost all confidence in Simmons in 2026 and beyond, and a tackle as good as Simmons almost certainly won't hit the market anyway. The best version of the Chiefs' offense depends on having Simmons back as soon as possible.
Do you think the Chiefs will be judicious with Kenneth Walker going forward? Will they be wary of keeping him fresh for the playoffs? -@toptrevor.bsky.social | Do you think we will mix Emmett Johnson in more post-bye, and should we? -@oscarbobo.bsky.social
Before the Chiefs' game against the Miami Dolphins, I wrote that it could be Emmett Johnson's time to shine . (He went on to have six carries for 17 yards.) Last week, I wrote that Johnson should be a bigger part of the mix after the bye week —this time, for sure! Ultimately, I understand why it's easier said than done.
The Chiefs have a one-man offensive easy button with Kenneth Walker in the backfield; if the passing game stalls this Sunday against the Chargers, my desire to see Walker's workload lessened will be overtaken by my desire for the Chiefs to, you know, win the game.
I stand by the idea that Johnson has proven enough to show that he can be a worthwhile No. 2 back behind Walker, and the team ideally would take a few hits off Walker's shoulders during the middle act of the season, but they'll need to have more offensive confidence in other areas before that can be put into practice.

title: The Jury Is Still Out on Chiefs' Safety Room Following Bye Week
full_text:
Change was the theme of the offseason for the Kansas City Chiefs' defense, especially in the secondary. It wasn't just the cornerback position that underwent a shakeup, either, as safety Bryan Cook departed for the Cincinnati Bengals and was replaced by Alohi Gilman in free agency.
The acquisition of Gilman, paired with Chamarri Conner returning to his more natural spot in Steve Spagnuolo's lineup, seemed to set the tone for a productive and disruptive pairing. For multiple reasons, however, that hasn't been the case through four games.
Lumping in a roller coaster of a campaign for Jaden Hicks and a limited workload for Chris Roland-Wallace does nothing but further complicate things. The bad news is that things must improve coming out of the bye week, although the good news is there's ample reason to believe that'll happen.
Starting with Gilman, the former Los Angeles Chargers and Baltimore Ravens standout isn't exactly lacking statistically compared to his last couple of seasons. Across Pro Football Reference , Pro Football Focus and NFL Pro 's data, his coverage data averages out to 10 targets and six completions, 8.3 yards per target and a 120.6 passer rating.
He's being tried more often down the field (13.9-yard average depth of target) and performing at his recent — albeit underwhelming — standard, but it's the lack of ball production that's really hurting. One of Gilman's main draws is his ability to make splash plays, evidenced by his 28 career pass breakups, six fumble recoveries, five forced fumbles and five interceptions. Four games in, he's been quiet, which is a concern.
Hicks is hands-down the most frustratingly inconsistent player in this group. In some instances, he flies around the field and looks like a heat-seeking missile who's oozing confidence. In others, though, he's lost in the shuffle, slow to react and ends up totally out of place. He leads the safety collective with eight "stops" on the year, yet it's coming with a unit-worst mark in yards per reception.
The low-key player to keep an eye on is Roland-Wallace, who played 190 defensive snaps in 2025, good for 30% of those available in his 11 games played. This year, that number is 55 (20%), and it's hard to see that share going up too much with Conner back. Roland-Wallace has some corner-safety versatility, so perhaps he occupies some slot snaps (he has 12 right now) in due time.
Conner stands out as quite easily the biggest X-factor here. The fourth-year man is in a contract season but started it on the shelf due to a knee injury that lingered for a while. While he was far from perfect in his regular-season debut in Week 4 versus the Las Vegas Raiders, the former fourth-round pick finished with six tackles and made multiple plays that showcased his quick trigger when running downhill.
There wasn't much of a runway for Conner to ramp up, as he played 63 snaps down in Paradise against the Raiders (75%). If he's back to being an unquestioned starter at safety, he'll form a heavy-involvement duo with Gilman and send someone like Hicks down a rung on the ladder. That may assist the latter man in finding the optimal role for his skill set.
Progress isn't linear, which might be the best way to sum up a group that's flashed some good and bad in the first month of the 2026-27 campaign.

title: Here’s Why Chiefs Rookie Cyrus Allen Could Finally Be Featured in Kansas City’s Offense
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs' bleak wide receiver circumstances worsened before the bye when Rashee Rice and Tyquan Thornton went down in the same game. While Rice's hamstring issue is minor and shouldn't keep him out long, Thornton will miss most, if not all , of the regular season with a dislocated ankle. Between rumors about a reunion with Tyreek Hill and bringing another proven wideout on board before the trade deadline, KC fans are starved for help in the receiving corps. However, a viable option may be waiting in the wings of the Chiefs' offensive unit.
Remember Cyrus Allen, who quickly transformed into a fan favorite with his strong training camp? There was a time when he looked like he'd be facing an uphill battle for playing time, but a scenario where he assumes a significant role in this offense looks a lot more realistic with the current injury situation.
Allen was selected No. 176 overall in the 2026 NFL Draft and brings plenty of versatility, as he's capable of lining up in the slot or on the outside. He led the Big 12 with 13 touchdowns as a senior, which helped his draft stock skyrocket. A shin bruise during camp slowed Allen's progress and has been cited as a reason why the coaching staff has been hesitant to use him. Before that, though, reporters viewed Allen as perhaps the team's best pass catcher not named Rice or Xavier Worthy.
During the Chiefs' Week 4 win over the Raiders, when the two aforementioned receivers got hurt, Allen only saw the field for five snaps and recorded his first NFL target. That could change now that the coaching staff has a week of preparation to get him more involved.
What Kansas City is truly missing in the receiver room is a playmaker who can make things happen with the ball in his hands. Rice is great in the intermediate game, but he isn't necessarily someone defenses are going to key in on to open things up downfield. And despite Worthy's tremendous straight-line speed, he's been largely ineffective in all areas of the offense in 2026.
Allen generated a lot of buzz in limited preseason action, with the biggest highlight coming on an impressive snag in the exhibition opener. Insiders and other observers have made it clear that he has as much burst and is shiftier than anyone in the short passing game.
When speaking to the media on Monday , head coach Andy Reid mentioned the possibility of Allen seeing increased snaps with Thornton heading to the IR. Those opportunities would only grow if Rice is unable to suit up this week versus the Chargers. "Yeah, I think he would probably work into the mix there a little bit more," Reid said. "He's a good football player, and even though he's young, he's got good ability."
Andy Reid on if rookie WR Cyrus Allen will receive more playing time moving forward: “Yeah, I think he would probably work into the mix there a little bit more. He's a good football player, and even though he's young, he's got good ability.” pic.twitter.com/mMeGf7WVX1
Those words don't necessarily mean Allen is going to see a dozen targets on Sunday, so his biggest supporters should take Reid's comments with a grain of salt. Reid tends to have a level of comfort with the players he trusts to catch passes from Patrick Mahomes, which helps explain why the front office brought two-time Chiefs Super Bowl winner Justin Watson back to the practice squad during the bye.
Depending on Rice's injury status before the upcoming matchup, this could be Allen's biggest chance to earn a consistent role in Eric Bieniemy's offense. If he makes the most of his snaps, even in a limited role, he could earn a bigger place in the game plan moving forward.

title: The Chiefs' Highest-Paid Linebacker Hasn't Been Their Best, and That's Alright
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs rolled into the year with plenty of questions on the defensive side of the ball, especially after an offseason filled with change. That applied to the linebacker position as well, with Leo Chenal departing for the Washington Commanders in free agency and leaving someone else to fill his spot.
With that said, the starting duo of Nick Bolton and Drue Tranquill remained. The former is regarded as the on-field coach and leader of the defense — essentially an extension of coordinator Steve Spagnuolo. The latter, meanwhile, was coming off a couple of down years and took a pay cut to return for what could be one last dance in Kansas City.
Four games into the season, the expectations of many haven't aligned with reality. Bolton and his $19.25 million cap hit have been outplayed by Tranquill and his $5M mark , although that isn't necessarily the end of the world. It's less of an indictment on Bolton and more a praise of Tranquill's performance thus far.
Coverage numbers tend to vary by site, so it's better to paint a picture of a player's output by coming up with an average. After sorting through Pro Football Reference , Pro Football Focus and NFL Pro 's data, the stat line matches the eye test.
Both players combined for an average of 12 targets in the passing game in Weeks 1-4. Bolton surrendered 10.3 completions, 7.0 yards per target and a 103.0 passer rating. Tranquill, on the other hand, ceded 5.3 completions, 5.3 yards per yarget and a passer rating of 60.0. Add in that Bolton's facing the lowest average depth of target of his career (3.1 yards) and Tranquill's is his highest since 2022 (4.8), and you get a pretty clear read.
Tranquill is also faring better as a disruptor in all phases despite Bolton having 22 "stops" to his 18. The 31-year-old maintains an 11.8% pressure rate to his peer's 9.1% figure, along with a 3.3% missed tackle clip to Bolton's 9.8%. There wasn't a much better game to sum up Tranquill's efforts than him terrorizing the Las Vegas Raiders in Week 4.
Spagnuolo is using Tranquill in a variety of ways, including lining him up along the defensive line on 36 occasions. The 'backer owns a 27.9% blitz rate, which clears 2025 (24.4%) as his most significant usage in that role as a Chief. Bolton himself admitted back in August that there would "never" be a true replacement for Chenal, but Spagnuolo throwing multiple things at the wall and hoping something sticks seems to be the plan. Tranquill is a part of that attempted solution.
The same can't really be said for Jack Cochrane or Jeffrey Bassa. Neither player is making much of an impact on defense, but Bassa did notch a forced fumble on special teams in Las Vegas. The signing of Cam Jones to the 53-man roster signals that Cooper McDonald isn't ready to return, and Cole Christiansen's game-day elevations from the practice squad are capped. This is a depth chart that's extremely top-heavy entering Week 6.
Bolton enjoyed plenty of plus moments before the bye, but it's Tranquill who's been the plus player at that position to this point. The blend of better-than-expected coverage, relentless attacking in run defense and quality fundamentals as both a tackler and blitzer is tough to argue against. The Chiefs can't ask for much more and should instead simply hope this level of play can be sustained.
If the rest of the linebacker room ascends as well, the Kansas City defense will continue to jell post-bye and down the stretch of the regular season.

title: Why Didn't the Chiefs Trade for Marvin Harrison Jr.?
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs need wide receivers.
After Tyquan Thornton suffered a gruesome ankle injury , the Chiefs made a patchwork move, reuniting with Justin Watson . The Chiefs still need wide receivers, both short-term and long.
Many of my pre-draft opinions revolved around my desire for the Chiefs to use one of their premium picks on a pass catcher. They didn't. Much of this summer's training camp hype cycles belonged to fifth-round rookie Cyrus Allen . So far, he's played fewer offensive snaps than defensive tackle Khyiris Tonga.
Looking to the future, there's just as much uncertainty. The Chiefs' No. 1 receiver, Rashee Rice, is in a contract year. Former first-round pick Xavier Worthy is under contract through 2027, but the Chiefs will need to make a decision regarding his fifth-year option after this season. Thornton is under contract for 2027 with a $7.5 million cap hit.
I would make the argument that the Chiefs' biggest need for the rest of the 2026 season and their biggest need for the next several seasons all revolve around the wide receiver position. Why am I rehashing this opinion in mid-October?
Because even I don't think the Chiefs should have beaten the Houston Texans' bid to trade for Marvin Harrison Jr.
To be clear, I was at least somewhat interested in the Chiefs being the "change of scenery" destination for the embattled former No. 4 overall pick, but those delusions were shattered by the reports of what Houston gave up in the deal.
In exchange for Harrison and a 2027 seventh-round pick, the Texans gave up a 2027 second-rounder and a '27 sixth. Essentially, a second-rounder for Harrison and a largely cosmetic late-round pick-swap. Here's the even wilder part: the Texans are 1-4! Right now, that pick would fall at No. 39 overall according to Tankathon . The Texans certainly hope to make a playoff push, but even if they go 8-4 the rest of the way, ending at 9-8 and just outside of the postseason, they'd ultimately be sending a top-50 pick to Arizona in the deal.
From the Cardinals' perspective, that's a worthwhile return. For the 4-0 Chiefs, the apparent only realistic path to Harrison would have included Kansas City's 2027 first-round pick. Even if KC would've gained a mid-round pick from Arizona in this hypothetical, I wouldn't have blamed general manager Brett Veach for hanging up the phone before Arizona finished their pitch.
Should the Chiefs be willing to offer their most precious pick, the 2027 first-rounder, for some wide receivers? Possibly! Do the Philadelphia Eagles want to move DeVonta Smith to jumpstart their rebuild? I'd listen! But for a player in the midst of as disastrous of a season as Harrison? Not even I am receiver-starved enough to make that call.
WR Separation Score vs TPRR 📊 -- Carnell Tate building chemistry with Ward -- Downs, Doubs, Odunze, Pickens prime targets for positive regression -- MHJ in a league of his own pic.twitter.com/kDtxG8H22T
For further context, Bill Barnwell of ESPN took a longer look at just how bad things have been for Harrison in Arizona.
"He hasn't been getting much separation, hasn't hit high-end speed, and isn't winning on contested catches very often," Barnwell wrote. "He needs to be a different player altogether in Houston."
Brutal, right? ...Well, that was just Barnwell's summary on Twitter ! The deep-dive brings some of the stats that underscore the disappointments that have come with Harrison's career so far.
"During his time with the Cardinals, Harrison ranked last in the NFL among all wide receivers (with 50 targets or more over the past three years) in separation, averaging just 2.1 yards of separation when targeted, per NFL Next Gen Stats," Barnwell continued on ESPN.com . "Great receivers—even ones who get plenty of attention from opposing defenses—are typically able to create more space for themselves. The likes of Ja'Marr Chase and Justin Jefferso n average over 3 yards of separation on their routes. In Arizona, McBride averaged 3.3 yards of separation on his targets during that time, while Wilson was at 2.5 yards."
Barnwell's assessment continues at length, with unflattering statistics couched by a few fair criticisms of the Cardinals' offense throughout the dissection.
There's certainly a chance that Harrison does become "a different player altogether" with the Texans, but looking at the deal from the Chiefs' standpoint, there's no way I would have beaten that price for a receiver who needs to be nearly unrecognizable on his new team.

title: Chiefs Injury Report: Kingsley Suamataia Is Back, Updates on Josh Simmons and Rashee Rice
full_text:
The Chiefs received an extended period of rest with their bye week. It was a much-deserved break for a Kansas City squad that started the year with an impressive 4-0 record.
Now, Andy Reid's team will have to play 13 consecutive games without a break, which should make for a brutal stretch down the road. The head coach spoke to the media for the first time in a week to provide a few updates on his team.
Kansas City has already been hit by the injury bug, but left guard Kingsley Suamataia was benched in Week 4 against the Raiders due to a "coaching decision." It appears that no further disciplinary action will be taken against the third-year offensive lineman, who was replaced by Mike Caliendo in the victory. "Yeah, he'll be back," Reid confirmed with the media this afternoon.
When Reid was asked about Suamataia's benching last Sunday, he stated that he didn't want to disclose any further information about the reasoning and that Suamataia would "be better for it." However, that one-game absence seems to be the extent of his punishment.
In addition to Suamataia's situation, the Chiefs have been without starting left tackle Josh Simmons for the entirety of the regular season because of a bulging disc in his back. Despite all the speculation surrounding his status, Reid provided a more positive update on Simmons today.
"I'll know more soon. They [Josh Simmons and Rashee Rice] were in last week," Reid said. "Josh was here all week doing his rehab and stuff. So, we'll see. They'll be back tomorrow, and I'll have a better idea of what's going on."
Although a return doesn't sound imminent, this is a lot more encouraging than Reid's typically vague answers about Simmons' back. It's an excellent sign that he was rehabbing with the training staff during the bye.
Andy Reid, following the Chiefs' bye, said the team signed Justin Watson to the practice squad. Tyquan Thornton (left ankle) is expected to be placed on IR. Reid on Josh Simmons: "Josh was here all [last] week doing his rehab. They'll be back tomorrow & I'll have a better idea."
Getting Suamataia back already bolsters KC's unit in the trenches, but having Simmons back would be an even bigger development. If he's ready to go in Week 6 versus the Chargers, the Chiefs could move acting left tackle Kahlil Benson to the right side and send Jaylon Moore to a swing tackle role.
In the receiver room, Rashee Rice remains day-to-day with the hamstring injury he suffered in the first quarter last game, while Reid confirmed that Tyquan Thornton will likely be placed on Injured Reserve. The breakout speedster dislocated his ankle late in the fourth quarter during a career day in the victory over Las Vegas. To help offset those losses, Kansas City has signed Justin Watson to its practice squad , who won a pair of championships with the team in 2023 and 2024. The Chiefs could elevate him as early as this weekend given his familiarity with the scheme.

title: Chiefs Adding Justin Watson to Insulate WR Room Amid Flurry of Roster Moves
full_text:
Coming out of their Week 5 bye, the Kansas City Chiefs have the chance to take down yet another divisional foe when they square off against the Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday. As a new week of practice soon begins, though, there will be a new face entering the fold.
New to the 2026 Chiefs, at least, as it's a familiar friend signing with the team. Reported by Ian Rapoport of ESPN and NFL Network , Kansas City is signing wide receiver Justin Watson to the practice squad.
Head coach Andy Reid confirmed the move during his Monday media availability, adding that wideout Tyquan Thornton ( ankle ) will likely be placed on the injured reserve list. Linebacker Cam Jones is expected to take his place on the 53-man roster.
"I will tell you that Tyquan is most likely going on IR here," Reid began. "We'd elevate Cam Jones. We also signed Justin Watson to the practice squad, so those are the immediate updates."
Watson, who turned 30 in April, was originally a member of the Chiefs from 2022-2024. That span saw him appear in 50 regular-season games, starting 20 of them. He won a pair of championships in the club's back-to-back run, finishing his initial tenure with 64 receptions on 119 targets for 1,064 yards and seven touchdowns.
The former fifth-round pick was a trusted vertical passing target for quarterback Patrick Mahomes, evidenced by his 17.2-yard average depth of target in KC. He netted 16.6 yards per reception as a Chief in the first go-round.
When asked about the reunion with Watson, Reid praised his versatility and understanding of what's requested of him within the offense.
"He was a good player for us when he was here," Reid said. "He obviously can run fast, and he's got great size. He's willing to do everything, he knows the offense. He's a smart kid. We felt like he could come back in as needed and contribute, step in and go. With just a slight review, he should be fine and good to go."
On Friday, Chiefs On SI covered Kansas City's reported interest in Watson. Here's some of the conclusion after weighing the pros and cons of a potential signing:
"At the end of the day, Watson might just be a more appropriate Thornton replacement than multiple internal options or free agent avenues. Even if he isn't a clear-cut needle-mover, it may not hurt to bring him in and see what he's got as a part-time player. An emphasis should be placed on the part, though, coming with the understanding that the double champion with the Chiefs wouldn't be saving the receiver room."
As a member of the practice squad, Watson can only be elevated to the game-day roster three times. After No. 3, he'd be required to sit on the practice squad for the rest of the regular season or be signed to the 53 directly. With Thornton expected to miss 12-16 weeks following his gruesome ankle injury , adding depth here makes plenty of sense.
The Jones signing stems from linebacker Cole Christiansen reaching his activation limit for the year. Cooper McDonald remains on IR for the time being, so bringing up Jones was a no-brainer. The 26-year-old has played 161 defensive snaps for the Chiefs in 34 regular-season contests, on top of another 567 reps on special teams.
With just six days remaining until a new challenge versus Los Angeles, the Chiefs' roster shuffle continues.

title: While the Chiefs Enjoy a Bye Week, the Rest of the AFC West Has Plenty to Prove
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs are 4-0 and the only undefeated team still standing in the AFC . That, of course, means the Chiefs are in command of the AFC West while the Las Vegas Raiders try to hold on to their second-place standing and the Denver Broncos look to improve on their .500 start.
Oh, and the Los Angeles Chargers would probably like to win a game sooner rather than later, too.
With the Chiefs enjoying their bye week, let's take a look at Sunday's pair of games containing AFC West squads, plus two primetime matchups with other AFC contenders.
The Raiders acquited themselves admirably against the Chiefs last week, taking their first loss of the season in decidedly un-Raider-y fashion. (Un-Raider-y isn't a word, but you know what it means!) In some ways, I'm more convinced that the Raiders are a legitimate playoff-adjacent team now than I was before their loss to the Chiefs. However, they're not getting a break from their upcoming schedule anytime soon.
Las Vegas gets the New England Patriots in Foxborough this week before hosting the Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Rams in the next two weeks. The Raiders don't need to win all of those games to retain their new semi-contender status, but they can't lose four consecutive games and still be taken seriously in the second half of the year.
New England, on the other hand, is coming off an impressive win over the Bills in Buffalo last weekend, stabilizing the team after a blowout loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars in Week 3.
The Raiders may still be a year of progress away from true contention, but Chiefs fans should obviously be pulling for the Patriots in this one.
these posts came a week apart life comes at you fast and all that pic.twitter.com/pVD2tc26og
Even with impressive home victories over the Jaguars and Rams in Weeks 2 and 3, the vibes around quarterback Bo Nix and the Broncos' offense seem to have taken a considerable shift after last week's loss at the San Francisco 49ers. For what it's worth, I still think the Broncos are the second-best squad in the division and should be expected to return to the playoffs again this season, but that confidence would be severely shaken if the winless Chargers can pull off the upset in LA.
The Chargers have been one of the biggest disappointments in all of football this season, and they're running out of time to do something about it. After hosting the Broncos, the Chargers will head to Kansas City in Week 6 before "visiting" the Rams after their Week 7 bye. If there's any life left in the Chargers at all, they'll need to prove it against Denver.
Not that Chiefs fans need my guidance here, but a Chargers win would be good for both the Chiefs' lead over the Broncos and for a week of NFL comedy.
Beyond the AFC West, two of the Chiefs' top AFC rivals will go up against a pair of 2-2 NFC teams in primetime. The Baltimore Ravens (3-1) will face the Atlanta Falcons on Sunday Night Football, while the Bills (3-1) will travel to Los Angeles to take on the Rams for a Monday night showdown.
It's far too early in the year to be seriously considering playoff seeding, but any extra wiggle room for the Chiefs' hunt for the No. 1 seed would be beneficial, especially with Kansas City's Thanksgiving showdown with the Bills looming large.
Chiefs fans should enjoy the experience of rooting for Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson in their new homes on Monday Night Football while pulling for the Falcons to take a game from Baltimore on Sunday night.
Happy Championship Sunday! pic.twitter.com/Mw7LIStU11

title: Chiefs’ Pass-Rush Unit Could Return a Sneaky Weapon From Injury Soon
full_text:
Much has been made of the Kansas City Chiefs' defensive line failing to record a sack in each of the past three games. However, Steve Spagnuolo's unit could be getting a huge boost in the upcoming weeks.
Following Kansas City's bye, the Chiefs will finally be eligible to get 2025 second-round pick Omarr Norman-Lott back on the field. He's been on the PUP (Physically Unable to Perform) list since training camp and was required to miss the opening four contests of the year, but Week 6 marks the first point at which he can return to game action. The University of Tennessee product tore his ACL in Week 7 of last season and has been rehabbing ever since. There was hope he'd progress to full health and participate in offseason sessions, but the front office elected to place him on the PUP list to allow him extra time to recover.
It's been almost a full year since Norman-Lott suffered the injury. Barring any setbacks, it shouldn't be too long before we see him active again. Of course, every ACL tear is different, and not everyone can make a nine-month return like Patrick Mahomes did.
Head coach Andy Reid alluded to Norman-Lott "potentially" returning after the bye in late September. It was the first positive injury update the Chiefs had received on him in quite some time.
Andy Reid also says Chiefs DT Omarr Norman-Lott is a possibility to return from IR after the bye week. Reid says he’s doing more and getting closer to a return.
The Chiefs certainly won't be in any rush to bring Norman-Lott back from a serious knee injury at 4-0. Once they open his 21-day practice window, KC must either activate him during that span or transfer him to the IR for the remainder of the season.
As a rookie, Norman-Lott played sparingly but was an effective interior lineman. Across five contests, he finished with one sack, four solo tackles, and one tackle for loss, earning a 54.2 Pro Football Focus (PFF) grade. While Norman-Lott plays on the inside, his profile is more as a pass rusher than a run defender. He's extremely explosive for his size and has a relentless motor when getting after the quarterback, boasting an impressive 18.9% pass-rush win rate as a senior in college.
As we've noted in recent days on Chiefs at SI, the pass rush hasn't really been as invisible as it seems. It especially started to come alive in the second half of the victory over the Las Vegas Raiders. However, Norman-Lott's return to the squad could open up a plethora of possibilities for the defensive line rotation.
The Chiefs drafted another defensive tackle early in this year's draft, selecting former Clemson standout Peter Woods with the No. 29 overall pick . He and Khyiris Tonga have split snaps throughout the season, with both playing a little under 50% of the defense's reps. Norman-Lott could slot in during passing downs to rush the quarterback alongside Chris Jones on the inside.
When Coach Reid speaks to the media on Monday, we could get more clarity on Norman-Lott's status. It's been quiet on the injury front for ONR lately, but the Chiefs could have a secret weapon in the pass rush ready to deploy when he's healthy.

title: Mansoor Delane and Nohl Williams Star in a Bright Future for the Chiefs' Cornerback Room
full_text:
It was a bit of a surprise when the Kansas City Chiefs traded up to obtain the No. 6 overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, then even more of a surprise when they used that selection on LSU cornerback Mansoor Delane . Immediately, Delane rightfully had sky-high expectations as the new face of the Chiefs' secondary.
Delane was limited throughout the majority of training camp due to a shoulder injury and then played just three snaps (including an interception of Bo Nix) in Weeks 1 and 2 due to an issue with the same shoulder. Even with just two full games under his belt, Delane looks to be worth that draft selection, and he's not alone as a rising star in Kansas City's overhauled cornerback room.
As any Chiefs or Los Angeles Rams fan knows by now, the Chiefs traded away cornerback Trent McDuffie to the Rams this offseason, and Jaylen Watson reunited with McDuffie after leaving for LA in free agency. That left a significant void for the Chiefs to fill at corner.
To begin 2026, veteran cornerback Kristian Fulton was entering the second year of his two-year deal with the Chiefs after a disappointing 2025, and '25 third-round draft pick Nohl Williams was looking to follow his promising rookie campaign with a more consistent workload in his sophomore season.
Delane, Williams and Fulton all hit the ground running .
Highest graded CBs in man coverage this season Mansoor Delane         93.8 Kristian Fulton             92.8 Nohl Williams               91.8 Trent McDuffie            90.9 Travis Hunter               90.3 pic.twitter.com/4Tv5R4kLLU
Delane has been excellent , even when asked to take on difficult coverage responsibilities, as he was asked to do at times against Las Vegas Raiders tight end Brock Bowers. He's also been a missile in run defense, playing with speed and physicality that fits Steve Spagnuolo's defense perfectly.
Mansoor Delane with one of the GREATEST two-play sequences you’ll see from a rook. Registers a TFL on Ashton Jeanty, and follows it up with CLAMPING Brock Bowers. The Chiefs rookie CB NEUTRALIZING some of the NFL’s top weapons 😳🔒 pic.twitter.com/oHzd3YU6qM
Delane has the fifth-highest overall cornerback grade from Pro Football Focus through the first four weeks of the 2026 season, while Fulton lands at No. 11. Williams appears at No. 41 in overall PFF grading but lands at No. 23 with his coverage grade alone.
good player this Mansoor Delane https://t.co/HNmzmM6Pbj pic.twitter.com/XPGheGgX3M
The one area of concern in the Chiefs' cornerback room comes in the slot, where veteran L'Jarius Sneed has provided some value and some tough snaps in his second act with the team. Sneed has the second-worst PFF grade among qualifying cornerbacks (No. 102 of 103), but he's been a positive force against the run and as a blitzer.
Sneed began the season in excellent fashion against the Denver Broncos in Week 1 before being routinely bested by Indianapolis Colts receiver Josh Downs in Week 2. I'll argue that it's a bit too early (and a bit unnecessary) to rush to end the Sneed-reclaimation experiment, but he's certainly struggled more than the team's trio of outside corners to begin the year.
I'd be interested to see Delane get a bit of work in the slot if that would enable Williams and Fulton to hold the outside corner roles in nickel packages, but I'd also understand some hesitance, as Delane's potential value is probably highest as a shutdown outside corner, and he's still acclimating to the NFL game (though you wouldn't know that if you only watched him play).
What other options could the Chiefs have?
Rookie defensive back Jadon Canady was a healthy scratch in Week 4 as safety Chamarri Conner returned to the lineup, while slot corner Kader Kohou remains on the practice squad, so neither Canady nor Kohou seem particularly close to challenging Sneed for those slot corner reps. Versatile DB Chris Roland-Wallace took a season-high 29 defensive snaps against the Raiders, but Sneed has taken more than 72% of the defensive snaps in every game so far this season.
Ultimately, the Chiefs' slot corner position will require more monitoring (and, ideally, better play) in the weeks to come, but the Delane/Williams outside duo—with room for cameos from Fulton this season—appears to be one of the NFL's most promising young pairings.
