title: Rams Are Running Out of Excuses as Special Teams Disaster Strikes Again in Overtime Loss to Bills
full_text:
It may as well have just been another day that ends in “y” for the Los Angeles Rams in their 37-34 overtime loss to the Buffalo Bills on Monday Night Football. Last season, the Rams lined up for a 44-yard field goal to beat the Philadelphia Eagles. The kick was blocked and the Rams lost. On Monday night, Harrison Mevis lined up for a 48-yard field goal to beat the Bills from the same hash. The kick was blocked and five plays later the Bills kicked a game-winning field goal of their own.
The Rams put up 454 yards of total offense. Matthew Stafford threw for 383 yards and three touchdowns. While the defense didn’t play well, they got a timely turnover in overtime to give the Rams a chance to win. Once again, it was the special teams unit letting them down when it mattered most.
"I’m really proud of our group. I thought offensively and defensively we battled," said head coach Sean McVay after the game. "W did some really good stuff and in the kicking game, especially with our PAT field goal, not even close to good enough. It cost us the game tonight.”
It’s been the common theme for the Rams going back to last season. Three losses can be pinned on special teams in 2025. Every week this year, the Rams have had some sort of special teams mistake. On Monday night, the game ended the same way it started. To open the game, the Rams allowed a 70-yard kickoff return. As it ended, it was the special teams failing to rise to the occasion.
Entering Week 5, the Rams needed a win to keep pace in the NFC West. With the San Francisco 49ers beating the Seattle Seahawks on Sunday, they improved to 5-0. A loss to the Bills now puts the Rams 3.5 games behind the 49ers and below .500 for the third time this season.
Coming off of last week’s win against the Philadelphia Eagles, it felt like the Rams had turned a corner. When they drove 98 yards to start their 10-point comeback, it seemed like the offense had found something.
Some of that carried over into Monday night. While the Rams scored just seven first-half points, the offense was moving the ball. Mevis missed a 50-yard field goal, and a penalty stalled another promising drive. The Rams’ first two possessions combined for 28 plays and lasted 14:58. Stafford and Adams also connected in the red zone, displaying how difficult that duo is to defend in that area of the field.
Defensively, the Rams limited Allen and the Bills’ passing game for much of the night, with most of the big plays coming on screens and in the run game. However, the Bills’ 26th-ranked pass defense also managed to limit Stafford's explosiveness early. Stafford completed 16 of 23 passes for just 99 yards in the first half, with his longest completion going for only 12 yards. He was just 2-for-7 on passes beyond 10 yards as the Rams trailed, 13-7.
The Rams wasted little time getting going in the second half, scoring a touchdown on their opening possession and re-taking the lead. It was the first time all season that the Rams had scored on their opening drive of either half.
What started as a defensive battle ended in an offensive shootout. Despite previous inconsistency , Stafford came to life. To end regulation, the Rams and Bills traded six straight touchdown drives. When the Bills took a 19-14 lead, the Rams answered with a six-play, 83-yard touchdown drive of their own. The Rams’ offense struggled to find explosive plays in the first half, but it was a 28-yard pass to Tyler Higbee and then a Corum catch-and-run for 34 yards to set up a Stafford pass to Nacua in the end zone.
Nacua finished with a career-high 17 catches on 24 targets for 138 yards. Other Rams wide receivers combined for six catches for 55 yards. Nacua was the centerpiece of the offense.
After the Bills went 80 yards in five plays and converted a two-point conversion to take a 27-20 lead, the Rams answered again. On a day when the defense struggled to get a stop, the offense kept stepping up to the plate. Stafford hit Tyler Higbee on a no-look pass for 30 yards and then found Davante Adams in the end zone for his second touchdown of the day.
The Bills responded with another touchdown, scoring with 1:39 left to play and leaving the Rams with just one timeout. As Stafford has throughout his career, he rose to the occasion when the pressure was at its highest in the fourth quarter.
Stafford hit a 14-yard pass to Adams before hitting Nacua for 16. With another 15-yard completion to Adams, the Rams were already in the red zone with 47 seconds still left on the clock. On 3rd-and-7 from the nine-yard line, Stafford lasered a pass to Kyren Williams at the one-yard line before the Rams’ running back finished it on the next play with a run up the middle to tie the game at 34 with four seconds remaining.
While the Rams won the toss in overtime, they opted to kick to the Bills. Earlier in the game, linebacker Nate Landman forced a fumble on running back James Cook, but the Bills came out of the pile with the ball. After a 57-yard catch-and-run by Khalil Shakir, the Bills looked in position to score a seventh consecutive touchdown.
However, on the next play, Landman forced a second fumble, and this time it was the Rams’ defense that came away with the ball. It was Landman’s first forced fumble that resulted in a turnover since Week 11 of last season.
Given how the offense had moved the ball in the fourth quarter, the Rams looked to be in prime position to win. Stafford navigated the pocket to find Davis Allen for 21 yards and then hit Nacua for 21 two plays later.
Had McVay continued to call the offense as he had for the previous quarter, it’s hard to say that the Rams wouldn’t have eventually ended up with the ball in the end zone.However, from the 35-yard line, McVay called an under-center pass that went incomplete. On the next play, McVay called a screen to Nacua that went five yards. Facing 3rd-and-5 from the 30, McVay called a run play that gained zero yards.
"I wish I would have had a better play call and gone forward, got it a lot tighter. I'm sick right now with myself," said McVay.
Despite having a kicker who was 1-for-3 from 48 yards in his career and 4-for-7 beyond 45 yards, McVay got conservative and seemed content with a long field goal. Mevis had missed from 50 yards earlier in the game and from 48 yards last week against the Eagles.
For as aggressive as McVay has been at times over the last year, this was his former self taking over with the game on the line. Earlier in the game, the Rams went for it twice on fourth down, including a 4th-and-6. In large part because of the inconsistent field goal unit, McVay’s fourth-down decision-making has become more aggressive. Yet, while going for the win against the Bills on Monday, McVay’s conservative side took over and it was costly.
Greg Rousseau, who had been quiet most of the game, split through the line and blocked Mevis’ kick. After runs of 19 and 13 yards by Allen, the Bills were in field goal range. While Tyler Bass missed a long extra point earlier in the game, there was no doubt about his game-winner from 45.
With the loss to the Bills, the Rams now fall to 2-3. The Rams can certainly bounce back from this loss and could realistically sit at 7-3 at their bye week. At the same time, the Rams will undoubtedly feel a sense of major disappointment after letting this game slip away.
"We put ourselves out there, put a lot of work into it" said Stafford. "You don't get the results you want, feel like you've played well in areas. Gave yourselves opportunity to win games and you don't do it. It's a tough pill to swallow."
Until this team proves otherwise, it’s hard not to compare them to the 2010 Chargers, who had a top offense and defense but were plagued by special teams. We’re five weeks into the season and talking about special teams every single week. How many more games do the Rams have to lose because of special teams?

title: Rams Get Major Boost on Defense as Quentin Lake Officially Active vs. Bills
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams are set to have safety Quentin Lake available on Monday night against the Buffalo Bills. Lake didn’t practice on Thursday and Friday and was a limited participant on Saturday before officially being listed as questionable for Monday’s game on the final injury report . However, despite questions about his availability, Lake is active for Monday night's game against the Buffalo Bills.
Lake missed Thursday and Friday’s practice with a hip injury. However, Rams head coach Sean McVay described it as a minor injury. When McVay spoke to the media on Saturday, he seemed optimistic about the possibility of Lake playing.
“I feel like he's turning in the right direction and feels good so that's a positive for us.”
Having Lake available will provide a huge boost for the Rams’ defense. Lake activates a lot of what the Rams want to do defensively because of his versatility. He is the only player on the Rams’ defense who has played 100 percent of the defensive snaps.
“We're just being smart with him,” said McVay this week as Lake missed practice. “He's played so many snaps. We just wanted to be smart.”
Through four weeks, Lake ranked second among safeties in impact plays with 12 according to Sumer Sports and led all safeties with seven pass breakups. He’s allowed 4.2 yards per target in coverage, which ranks 10th.
Heading into Week 4, Lake was the highest-graded safety according to Pro Football Focus with an overall defensive grade of 91.1. His 92.7 coverage grade was also the highest among all safeties.
Lake's versatility is what makes him such a valuable piece in the Rams’ defense. Rams defensive coordinator Chris Shula calls a lot of multiple-safety looks and Lake allows them to do that. According to PFF, Lake has 67 snaps in the box, along with 71 snaps at free safety and 41 snaps in the slot. His versatility allows Shula to get Kam Curl, Kam Kinchens, and Lake all on the field at the same time.
The Rams will certainly appreciate having Lake in the secondary as they prepare to face one of the NFL's best quarterbacks in Josh Allen . Also expected back on Monday night is cornerback Jaylen Watson, who missed last week’s game with a dislocated shoulder.
While Lake is active, the Rams have listed CJ Daniels, tight end Max Klare, offensive lineman Bill Murray, and defensive lineman Larrell Murchison as inactive. Additionally, quarterback Ty Simpson is inactive, but will be the emergency third quarterback.
The Rams will need their defense at its best to slow down Allen and the Bills on Monday night. Having Lake available gives Shula more flexibility with his personnel and allows the Rams to deploy the multiple-safety looks that have been an important part of their defensive success this season.

title: Hondo’s Raiders Mailbag: Fans Make Their Demands Clear
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (3-2) have turned the page from their brutal loss this past weekend to the New England Patriots (3-2) and are already fully focused on the Buffalo Bills (4-1), who are coming to town for a tilt this weekend at Allegiant Stadium.
If the Raiders play like they did last weekend (we already detailed that in our report card ), they will get blown out.
But, led by a coach who shone brightly in the Patriots' loss , his worst moment as the Raiders coach last week, Klint Kubiak, if they play as they did versus the Kansas City Chiefs, they could steal a win.
I asked the Raider Nation, as I do each week, to let me know via my X account: besides the obvious answer of a win, what are they looking for?
Once again, one of the elite and smartest fan bases, who see their fandom as their way of life , and not just a game, responded in a big way.
The Raiders have no chance of winning over the next two weeks without some semblance of a running game.  I couldn’t agree more.
The issue isn't whether Ashton Jeanty or Mike Washington Jr. is playing; the issue is that the offensive line, as a unit, looked terrible on Sunday.
Tyler Linderbaum and Delmar “DJ” Glaze, the Mule, didn’t look bad, but guards Spencer Burford and Jackson Powers Johnson did, along with LT Kolton Miller.
I asked Kubiak about the poor guard play mentioned above and whether it opened an opportunity for Bryce Cabeldue and Caleb Rogers to get some reps this week.  Not one to lie or deceive, the Raiders' head coach was blunt as always.
"Yeah, we always want competition. We're looking at how to get better at all positions. So, yes."
The Raiders' mindset is to win this weekend, and QB Kirk Cousins said it best on what that takes in this league.
“I think anytime you're one-dimensional, it probably does make it a little bit easier on a defense. I think also playing from a lead, they can probably afford to be flexible with what they're doing because they've created a bit of a cushion. But you certainly want that run-pass threat at all times if you can have it.”
Competitiveness.. like the KC game
This is one of the many reasons why Matt Millen sold me on this fan base, and why I genuinely love you all.  You get it.  You are not unrealistic or foolish.  You don’t ask for much, and in a rebuilding year, facing a team with legit Super Bowl aspirations, you are fair.
Two weeks ago, the Patriots went to Buffalo, then played the Raiders and beat the incoming Bills. Theoretically, that makes the Bills a worse team.  I emphasize theoretically because, despite the loss at home, I think the Bills are better.
Asking your team to be competitive, considering what they did in that same building versus the Chiefs, who I think are better than the Bills and the Patriots, is not asking too much.
“We have a whole lot to prove to ourselves and our fans this week. Really looking forward to playing in front of our fans this week. And our men, our leadership, our coaches, we're up to the challenge, and we have to bounce back.”
A response. Not a reaction. Go Raiders ☠️
I love this for a million reasons, not least of all because my father used to instill this in his sons regularly.  Most don’t know the difference, so let me quickly explain it to them.
A reaction is an automatic, instant reflex fueled entirely by emotion, often creating mistakes that make us, in our best Homer Simpson voice, slap our forehead and say, “Why did I do that?”
A response is a conscious, deliberate choice made after taking a moment to think. It uses your brain to assess and make the right decision.  It is calculated.  Essentially, a reaction is controlled by the situation, but a response keeps you in control.
The Raiders, for the entirety of the time I have covered them, and long before I got here, have been reactionary as a franchise.
With Tom Brady, John Spytek, and Klint Kubiak, that is no longer the plan of attack.  I don’t think the Raiders will win this Sunday.  I do expect them to look better than last week, and the biggest reason is that they aren’t panicking; they are reactionary.  They are calculated.

title: The Biggest Decision Klint Kubiak, Raiders Got Wrong vs. Patriots
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders' Week 5 loss to the New England Patriots featured a long list of mistakes by Klint Kubiak's Raiders.
This article is not to say that any one decision made by Kubiak, his staff, or players led to the loss. It takes a significant number of bad coaching decisions, poorly executed plays by the players, and solid play from the opposing team for a team to be down by 30 points in the NFL.
Pointing fingers gets us nowhere, but it is fair to acknowledge the blatant negatives of the Raiders' all-around disappointing performance against the Patriots. Las Vegas entered Week 5 without two receivers from an already questionable group. Yet, the Patriots were significantly shorthanded, too.
There was nothing more roster-wise that Kubiak and his staff could have done to put themselves in a better position to win Sunday's game, logistically. Considering how quickly things went south for the Raiders, it is fair to assume there was not much more they could have done play-calling-wise, either.
I understand that resting your starting running back while 3-1, with a shot at going 4-1 against a solid Patriots team, may not make sense to some. It could be argued that sitting Ashton Jeanty entering Week 5 goes against all logic, which is fair. However, the Raiders' 3-0 start went against all logic, too.
It is also fair to note that Jeanty is too critical to an already limited passing attack for the Raiders. Sitting Jeanty while already missing Jack Bech and Jalen Nailor would have hurt Las Vegas' passing game even more.
The biggest mistake the Raiders' coaching staff made was not resting Jeanty and putting Roman Hemby on the field. Hemby is not the answer to the Raiders' struggles on the ground, but he could have helped in the short and long term on Sunday against the Patriots.
Las Vegas is in the middle of a four-game stretch that included games against the Kansas City Chiefs and the Patriots. The Raiders will now face the red-hot Buffalo Bills and the Los Angeles Rams. They cannot rest Jeanty during those two games. Sunday against the Patriots was the time to do so.
New England entered the game with more injuries and critical players out than the Raiders, and it was not close. The Patriots entered the game without four of their cornerbacks and multiple wide receivers. They then lost their starting tackle and starting running back before halftime.
Few teams the Raiders will face moving forward will be as injured as the Patriots were. That was the time to rest Jeanty. Doing so would have given him a light workload during the week leading up to the Patriots game, a game off his clearly sore ankles, and extra time off before two tough games.
After facing the Bills and Rams at home in consecutive weeks, the Raiders are on the road for two consecutive weeks. Again, I understand the reasons for not sitting Jeanty, but a significantly shorthanded Patriots team was the week to rest Jeanty.
Also, Hemby has a similar style of play to Jeanty. He isn't Jeanty, but the Raiders did not need him to be. As is, Hemby would have been serviceable enough to get them through what became nearly a 30-point loss anyway. Instead, the Raiders took a huge loss, and Jeanty added wear and tear to his body.
The Raiders don't have any other upcoming games where sitting Jeanty for an entire game makes sense. Their Bye Week is not until Week 13. The closest they can get is to activate Hemby moving forward and begin using Jeanty, Mike Washington, Dylan Laube, and Hemby on more of a rotation.
Jeanty being the team's workhorse is good in theory, but he is hurt. Theory goes out the window here. Las Vegas' coaching staff must start thinking outside the box, as they are another injury or two away from their depth chart getting to a very uncomfortable spot at multiple positions.
Soon, it will be time to begin rotating playing time throughout the secondary levels of the depth chart, in the name of development, and to keep their best players healthy as long as possible. This will require more attention to the latter part of this season and future seasons.
In other words, giving players further down the depth chart experience and letting their best players rest could soon matter more than wins and losses. Hemby was not going to help the Raiders beat the Patriots, but he could have given Jeanty a valuable Sunday off his ailing legs.

title: Hondo’s Raiders Report Card: Why This Week Was So Ugly
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (3-2) host the team that many feel will be heading to the Super Bowl to represent the AFC on Sunday when the Buffalo Bills (4-1) and their throngs of “Mafia” come to town.
It will be the toughest test of the season so far for the overachieving, rebuilding Raiders.
Led by first-year head coach Klint Kubiak, who shone for other reasons in New England, the Raiders won't just accept a loss and lay down.
This Raiders team will come in swinging and try to shock the NFL world once again.
But before we turn our attention to the Bills on Sunday, today, after having already reviewed the winners and losers, we offer our weekly report card recap.
Not a good grade by any standard, but the issues are deeper than that. Kirk Cousins wasn’t the issue at all; he was under pressure the moment he got off the plane, and rumors are rampant that when he dropped off his duffel bag at team headquarters when they returned Sunday night, four Patriots fell out and hit him.
A QB can’t do his job with zero protection.
The same is true for Ashton Jeanty. No Raiders running back could run the football with an offensive line that played so poorly. Jeanty had dropped passes for the second week in a row, but his pass blocking was exceptional, and his lack of yards carrying the ball was an offensive line issue, and not on him.
I asked Kubiak about Jeanty’s drops, and subsequently, the terrific pass blocking.
"Yes, he's always been an excellent pass protector. We count on him on third down, obviously running routes and protecting. And yeah, those are things that are continuing to show up that we have to get fixed as a coaching staff."
Certainly, LT Kolton Miller had to face situations with multiple defenders, and you can’t expect him to block two or three people, but he also got beat one-on-one on multiple occasions, and the guard play was, to be frank, horrendous.
The reality is that the Raiders' offensive struggles against the Patriots came down to blocking breakdowns and an inability to run the ball.
Rick Dennison is the best OL coach in the NFL, but on Sunday, his OL was not good at all, and I am being nice.
​The Patriots dominated the line of scrimmage; they owned it wherever it was on the field, holding the Silver and Black to an abysmal 38 rushing yards with a 2.1 yards-per-carry average. How bad is that? You should be able to simply fall forward for that.
With the score quickly out of hand, the Raiders had to abandon the run, allowing the Mike Vrabel Patriots' pass rush to attack and swarm Kirk Cousins like a tiger hunting a gazelle, pressuring him on nearly 48% of his passes, sacking him three times, and forcing a crucial turnover.
Yes, the Raiders don’t have a WR1. But would that have mattered in hindsight?
After watching the film, the Raiders didn’t lose because of a lack at WR1.
That didn’t help, but it wasn’t the reason.
When an NFL team is forced to go one-dimensional, you won't be successful. Kubiak admitted it.
"I give a lot of credit to New England. They did an excellent job. I just didn't have a good plan for our guys. We didn't execute well. We got behind early, and we weren't able to get the run game going. There's just a lot of reasons that that game didn't work out, and it starts with me."
Everything on offense starts with the offensive line. Tyler Linderbaum had a good day, and Delmar “DJ” Glaze, the Mule, did too, but that is only 40% of your offensive line. The OL grade would be a D- at best, if not an F, but I had to grade the entire offense, and I gave them a D+ because of Cousins' leadership and Brock Bowers' heroic play.
Kirk Cousins echoed his coaches’ sentiments. “I think anytime you're one-dimensional, it probably does make it a little bit easier on a defense. I think also playing from a lead, they can probably afford to be flexible with what they're doing because they've created a bit of a cushion. But you certainly want that run-pass threat at all times if you can have it.”
The Raiders' defense let the 2026 Patriots play like the Tom Brady-led 2007 Patriots, and despite coming off last year's Super Bowl, they are nothing like that 2007 version.
They gave up 45 points and were run over, around, and through all day.
Some individuals played well, but as a unit, they were bad.
During the 45–17 blowout loss, the Silver and Black defense was frankly embarrassed, mainly by explosive plays and Drake Maye's aerial dominance, which topped his stat line with five total touchdowns.
Maye’s effectiveness showed up in crisp passes and relatively little pressure. When Maxx Crosby wasn’t double-teamed or even triple-teamed, the Patriots simply held him, daring the officials to call a holding penalty on every play.
The Raiders have to be more engaged and move Crosby around pre-snap to force offenses to search for him and find him on every play. I asked Kubiak exactly about that after being told after the game that the Patriots accounted for Crosby on every play.
"Yeah, I think those are definitely things as a coaching staff that we're talking about. We got to get him in positions to be successful to get near the quarterback."
The Raiders can’t develop an NFL playoff-caliber defense without other players being more consequential at DE.
John Spytek and Klint Kubiak have invested a lot of money in Malcolm Koonce and Kwity Paye, both great young men who were non-existent on Sunday.
They weren’t the only ones, but playing across from Crosby opens up amazing opportunities that, to their credit, they have done all year, until Sunday.
This aforementioned pass-rush void left the Raiders' secondary repeatedly exposed over the top, surrendering major chunk plays to receivers. At the same time, New England also racked up 165 rushing yards as they totaled 536 yards.
The Raiders' young defense was exploited, but Darien Porter actually played well. Perfect? No, but he far outplayed Hezekiah Masses and it stood out on tape. I asked Kubiak about the young Porter, who has one of the highest football IQs you have ever seen and is only in his sophomore campaign.
"Yeah, I would say that he's a guy that was starting, lost his job for a week, and is so mentally tough that he came back in and played really good football yesterday, and played very competitive. And that's not a surprise. That's the kind of guy that he is, and he's just going to continue to get better, and him and Zeke [Masses] will compete for that job."
The Raiders' defense had a bad day. Credit the Patriots, but also credit the Raiders. Along with Porter and Crosby, who both performed better than their teammates, Adam Butler was outstanding, and Nakobe Dean was, well, Nakobe Dean.
This is a resilient group of men who will rebound, but on this day, they failed.
It is no secret that I am all in on special teams coordinator Joe DeCamillis. He is the best the Raiders have had in a long time. The two monstrous mistakes on his side of the ball were both by veterans. That isn’t on the coach; it's on the veterans, and both hurt.
Those two critical errors were brutal. But one was worse than the other.
The one that hurt, but was more explainable in the weather, was a missed 49-yard field goal by kicker Matt Gay before halftime, which denied them a chance to cut into New England's lead.
The inexcusable, brutal mistake came when cornerback Darrell Luter Jr. failed to down a punt from AJ Cole near the goal line, giving the defense prime field position.
Cole, as always, was exceptional; Alex Ward was terrific, and overall the teams were fine. But that missed FG that I believe the forthright Gay would tell you he has to make, and an egregious error by Luter, hurt. Badly.
It doesn’t change that Luter was a good addition to this team, and Gay has done a very good job as the kicker. But Luter can’t make that mistake again and expect to keep a roster spot.
With a first-year head coach, defensive coordinator (Robbie Leonard), and offensive coordinator (Andrew Janocko), you expect mistakes, and I prepared…

title: What Raiders' Week 5 Loss Changed About Its Trade Deadline Plans
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders are coming off their worst performance of the year after a Week 5 blowout loss to the New England Patriots. Las Vegas entered the game 3-1 and looked like one of the league's best teams. However, the Patriots quickly confirmed that Las Vegas has a long way to go.
The Raiders' front office was diligent this offseason, making a slew of changes that quickly helped Las Vegas rise above the league's worst teams. However, Klint Kubiak and the Raiders' coaching staff were always honest about where the team stood.
The Raiders' past two games reminded everyone of their roster deficiencies, even after a quality offseason. Las Vegas has improved, but it is still a young team in the early stages of a rebuild and is currently on a two-game losing streak.
After starting the season 3-0 with wins over teams they would have lost to a season ago, the Raiders' offseason progress was undeniable. Yet Sunday's double-digit road loss to the defending AFC Champions was undeniable. Kubiak explained where Las Vegas currently sits.
“Well, in the NFL, there's always people working on your weaknesses at all times. So, the Patriots did a great job of exposing ours, and all I'm asking them to do is their jobs, and it's our jobs as coaches to get them prepared and put them in position to play successfully. So, they're young guys, they'll keep playing, and we count on them to play at a high level," Kubiak said the day after the game.
The season's first three weeks and Las Vegas' past two weeks have been polar opposites. However, so have the teams the Raiders have faced this season. The Raiders faced some of the worst teams to start the season, then some of the league's best.
Kubiak's staff did a solid job of keeping the team grounded when undefeated. Now, he and his coaching staff will have to keep getting the most out of the roster they have.
“I just think that if guys know what to expect from you that you're the same guy, whether you win or you lose, at least that's what I try to be; I'm not saying that I'm successful at that, but that's what I want from others to be consistent,” Kubiak said.
“Some of that you can count on, hold someone to a standard, and if it's not there, tell you the truth. If it is there, tell you, 'Good job'. But however you handle something, win or loss, the goal is to win the game. And we did not win yesterday, and we have a long season ahead of us, and we have big goals."
The sheer number of moves the Raiders made this offseason left little room for more quality moves. The money spent and the talent that was brought in were more than enough for the Raiders to work with this season. They were more than aware of the roster's pitfalls.
Still, Las Vegas' front office did all they realistically could to address as many of those pitfalls as possible. The Raiders are in the beginning stages of rebuilding what has been one of the league's worst overall rosters over the past three seasons. It will take more than one offseason.
Las Vegas' front office must stay the course regardless of what happens during the regular season. The Raiders' roster is all but set. If they add another player, it likely will not be via trade.
Doing so would give up draft capital during a season when the Raiders were not expected to contend for the playoffs. If the Raiders were going to make a trade, Marvin Harrison would have been a logical target. Now that he is gone, few sure-bet players worth giving up resources for.
The 3-2 Raiders are what they are, and the chances of Las Vegas' front office making a sizeable trade, or any trade at all, before the deadline appear slim to none. The Raiders' front office did more this offseason than any other. Kubiak and his staff have to work with the roster they have.

title: 4 Burning Concerns Arising for Raiders After Week 5
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders suffered a 45-17 loss to the New England Patriots on Sunday in an uninspiring performance.
Just a couple of weeks ago, the Raiders were riding high following a 3-0 start, with wins over the Dolphins, Chargers, and Saints. That said, the last two weeks have been a reality check for the Silver and Black. Unfortunately, this could be a sign of things to come. With that in mind, here are four reasons Las Vegas should be concerned and worried moving forward.
Many had written off the 38-year-old quarterback after two disappointing years in Atlanta. However, Cousins has been a pleasant surprise, compiling 1,269 passing yards, 12 touchdowns, and four interceptions, while completing 65.1 percent of his passes.
While those are impressive numbers, Cousins' immobility was a factor in the Raiders' loss on Sunday, as he was sacked three times. Again, Las Vegas is in a playoff spot because of the 15-year veteran's impressive start to the season. Yet when teams take substantial leads and know the Raiders have to throw, opposing pass rushers can pin their ears back and hunt Cousins. If the pressure gets there, Cousins will fold, which could be problematic against formidable teams.
Speaking of formidable teams, Las Vegas will face plenty. In five of the next six weeks, the Raiders will face the Bills, Rams, 49ers, Seahawks, and Broncos. That's why the early portion of the season was so important for Las Vegas if it wanted to challenge for a playoff spot. That's what it did with the 3-0 start, but it was quickly followed up with two straight losses.
With the next two games against Buffalo and Los Angeles - before a buffer with the New York Jets in Week 8 - a four-game losing streak is definitely in the cards. This upcoming stretch could derail the Raiders' 2026 season.
Las Vegas' passing attack has funneled through Brock Bowers and Ashton Jeanty. Despite missing the first two games of the season, the superstar tight end leads the team with 24 receptions for 312 yards and three touchdowns. Jeanty is the third-leading pass catcher, with 22 receptions for 215 yards and two touchdowns.
Against New England, those two players were the leading receivers for Cousins , combining for 16 targets, 11 receptions, 160 yards, and one touchdown. Meanwhile, Cody White and Tre Tucker combined for nine targets, six receptions, and 85 yards.
If the Raiders can navigate this stretch of the schedule, stay afloat, and maintain their spot in the playoff race, the front office needs to consider acquiring a weapon before the trade deadline.
The 22-year-old running back is dealing with injury, and it is noticeable in his performance. Through five games, Jeanty has 88 carries for 291 yards (3.3 yards per carry) and zero touchdowns. He has 22 receptions for 215 yards and two touchdowns. However, his effectiveness as a runner is clearly hampered by his injuries. During his postgame press conference, head coach Klint Kubiak highlighted Jeanty's ailments as factors in his struggles.
"Yes. Ashton [Jeanty] is beat up," Kubiak said. "It's a testament to how tough he is that he's out there playing today [Sunday] for his teammates."
As long as Jeanty continues to play, these ailments will inevitably linger. The only way for these injuries to heal is to rest for an extended period, which would obviously weaken the team.

title: Raiders Rookie, Sophomore Power Rankings: Youth Movement Hits Snag
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders spent the offseason making wholesale changes to their coaching staff and roster. Those changes have paid immediate dividends, with the Raiders sprinting out to a 3-0 start to the season. They are unquestionably a better team than last year's team.
However, the last two weeks have confirmed that a sizeable gap remains between the Raiders and the league's elite. Las Vegas entered the season knowing they're far from a finished product and are in the early stages of a rebuild that will take more than one offseason.
Las Vegas' Week 4 loss to the Kansas City Chiefs and Week 5 loss to the New England Patriots were tough losses for a Raiders team that had reason to be cautiously optimistic heading into both games. Yet as Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak noted, Week 5 was a bad day for everyone in silver and black.
“Obviously, yesterday was not up to our standard. It's not what we want our football to look like. We have a whole lot to prove to ourselves and our fans this week. Really looking forward to playing in front of our fans this week. And our men, our leadership, our coaches, we're up to the challenge, and we have to bounce back,” Kubiak said the day after the game.
In the past two offseasons, the Raiders drafted several players they expect to make an impact this season and beyond. Many of those players were thrust into starting roles and heavy playing time early in their careers.
Below are the power rankings of the Raiders' rookie and sophomore players who had a chance to make a legitimate impact in Sunday's loss to the Patriots. It was a long, forgettable day for the rookies, sophomores, and veterans alike.
The Raiders' rookie finally got some regular-season action. Las Vegas' coaching staff put Mendoza in the game with no chance of a comeback. It took the pressure off Mendoza during his first snaps in a meaningful regular-season game.
Mendoza only played one drive, but completed his first five passes in a row. He finished with six completions on eight pass attempts. The plays did not amount to much, but they showed what was possible with Mendoza. He may already give the team its best chance to beat elite teams.
Mendoza was one of the few bright spots for the Raiders' rookies and sophomores, and for the team overall. Although he gave up a few plays, Porter had a few solid ones. Porter had arguably the least-worst game of any rookie or sophomore in Sunday's ugly loss.
Jeanty played behind one of the league's worst offensive lines in his rookie season, breaking the franchise's rookie record for scrimmage yards. He then suffered an ankle injury shortly before the regular season began.
Between his injury and the offensive deficiencies elsewhere, Jeanty is in a tough spot. Still, the second-year back continues to help keep the Raiders' passing game alive.
Kubiak acknowledged that Jeanty's health is being addressed as best as the team's medical staff can.
“It's just a weekly thing that we're battling with him, with his teammates. I have a ton of confidence in our training staff. They do a great job of getting our guys available for the game and continuing to get them healthy, whether it's Ashton [Jeanty] or anybody on the roster. A lot of guys are beat up, it's that time of the year, and it's up to us at the end of the day to make the decision if they can go or not," Kubiak said.
Masses showed his potential early. However, the past two weeks have been the kind of humbling experience nearly every productive cornerback in the league has had early in their careers. Masses has been thrown to a lot early, but he has the potential to handle it.
It will be interesting to see how he bounces back mentally and physically this week.
Masses and Stukes can be switched on this list, as the defensive backfield struggled overall against the Patriots. More than anything, Stukes' inexperience was on display several times while trying to find certain route concepts—still, there was plenty of blame to go around for Sunday's loss.

title: Why Raiders Blowout Defeat Showed Need for Continued Growth
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders, as it turns out, aren't a playoff contender yet.
Las Vegas walked into Foxborough, Massachusetts, on a day when Adam Vinatieri was being honored for his Pro Football Hall of Fame induction and got pelted by the New England Patriots, 45-17, thanks to quarterback Drake Maye's incredible five-touchdown performance as the third-year signal-caller continues to ascend after a slow start.
For head coach Klint Kubiak, it should be considered a humbling experience in his first year leading a franchise. The loss told me something adamantly clear: the Raiders still have a lot of growing to do and flaws that aren't easy to fix.
The Raiders' growth stems from several factors, including youth, inexperience, new systems, and new faces on both sides of the ball. The first three games of the year were somewhat of a tease because of the opponents they faced; the Raiders started 3-0 against teams with a combined one win, while their last two games were against teams with two combined losses.
Las Vegas won the games they needed to and almost beat one of the lone undefeated teams remaining, the Kansas City Chiefs, two weeks ago. However, their last two games have shown flaws on both sides of the ball that involve the aforementioned growing pains.
Kubiak has taken accountability for not giving players opportunities in Sunday's loss, while Rob Leonard is working with the talent he has, trying to diversify his system outside of a heavy dosage of Cover 3. There is only so much you can do with the personnel at your disposal.
On that note, the biggest needs on the Raiders roster are becoming clear with each game, and so far, I can identify wide receiver, defensive tackle, right guard, and potentially left tackle as offseason needs. I do think there needs to be a conversation around Kolton Miller, who hasn't had the best season and has a 2027 cap number of $20.2 million with $15.2 million in potential savings.
Sunday showed the lack of a trustworthy receiver, and tight end Brock Bowers, as special as he is, cannot be relied on as much as he has been in the passing game. They have needed a difference-maker at the position for a while. Defensive tackle is in a similar boat, but the offseason should provide opportunities to improve these units.
This is all a learning curve for the Raiders. I don't get the indication that general manager John Spytek would be a buyer around the trade deadline, which is the right call in this instance, unless they enter their home matchup in Week 10 against the Seattle Seahawks well over .500 and looking at the postseason.
I think Raiders fans must brace for another blowout loss or two this season, and those could come over the next seven weeks with their stretch of games. Again, this is a learning opportunity for everyone in a year that is supposed to be a rebuild, but the early results, despite Sunday's, should be encouraging.

title: One Raider Shined in Patriots Loss: Find Out Who Stood Out
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (3-2) looked terrible in a 45-17 blowout loss to the New England Patriots (3-2) on Sunday.
To say that nearly nothing went right would be correct. While some players did perform well, and I will discuss that in my weekly report card, to call it anything other than a bludgeoning would be disingenuous to the reader and simply journalistic malfeasance. I detailed that in my winners and losers article.
Early this morning, a Raiders player contacted me. They had seen the video I posted of Klint Kubiak’s postgame press conference, and it moved them.
“Thanks for KK [Klint Kubiak’s] press conference after the game. That guy is the real deal man. We let him down, but he owned it in that, I love playing for him.”
After years of Raiders coaching fanning accountability and quietly throwing shade at everyone but themselves, the overachieving first-year head coach didn’t do so.
I have told you for months that as a reporter I appreciate Kubiak’s honesty.
He has been marvelous as the leader of the Silver and Black; the only shocking thing about Sunday was how long it took this team to perform that badly. The fact that we were even considering that they might have flipped the script to talking about the NFL Playoffs is nothing short of amazing.
Missing players at key positions, thin at others, and young nearly everywhere, the Raiders' head man stepped to the microphone and pulled no punches.
“It's on me to get us ready to go, and we weren't ready to go.”
The NFL was watching, and they paid close attention.
One highly successful NFL executive called me shortly after I got off the plane this morning. I called him on my way to the facility, and he told me, “You could see Klint was livid, embarrassed, and he was mad at himself.”
I told him about the player’s comments. He wasn’t shocked.
“Just like his dad man. That is integrity, those guys [Raiders Players] will run through a wall for him when you do that. High class move by him.”
I asked Kubiak today about the message he sent to his locker room. The steely-jawed leader of the Silver Black answered resolutely to a locker room that hangs on his every word.
"Well, I just think that if guys know what to expect from you that you're the same guy, whether you win or you lose, at least that's what I try to be; I'm not saying that I'm successful at that, but that's what I want from others to be consistent."
"Some of that you can count on, hold someone to a standard, and if it's not there, tell you the truth. If it is there, tell you, 'Good job'. But however you handle something, win or loss, the goal is to win the game. And we did not win yesterday, and we have a long season ahead of us, and we have big goals."
After the butt-kicking the Raiders took on Sunday, many people might be shocked to see Kubiak emerge as a shining example of the Raiders' promising future. But here is what you have to understand.
Every player in that locker room who failed on Sunday, and it was many of them, and every coach who failed, and it was many of them, knew coming into the season that this was a rebuild.
To use the proverbial Vegas term, they were playing with house money for one reason: Kubiak.
Kubiak had willed this team to 3-1. They trust him. They believe in him.
They saw him celebrate some terrific wins, and on Sunday they saw the same reaction to getting humiliated. They saw him step to the microphone, and while technically speaking to millions across the NFL pantheon, he was really talking to his players and coaches.
He took the blame. He should have. But several men here should have, in the past, and didn’t. He took the heat; took the blame, and he led from the front.
Anyone who knows anything about football knew what this season was from the start. If you didn’t know, you either haven’t followed my reporting since last December, or you were caught up in the ether of overachieving. Tom Brady, John Spytek, and Kubiak are cutting no corners. This was and is a rebuild.
Coaching the Raiders isn’t easy. Arguably the biggest name in NFL history, Al Davis, looms over this storied franchise. Icons like John Madden and Tom Flores coached here. To say that Kubiak is one of them would be ludicrous and insulting to both Kubiak and those men.
They are the standard that he has set for himself, but he is off to a great start.
After only eight months, to say he has the same character and mentality as those men is not hyperbole, and it is promising. More promising and realistic than the Raiders have had in a long time.
The Raiders are so much better than last year, but they still have a long way to go before they hoist their next Lombardi Trophy. But they know they have their leader.
No off-the-record finger-pointing, no quiet excuses; like a general, the Raiders' young coach stepped up and led.
The Raiders aren’t winning a Super Bowl in 2026. That should surprise no one. But they have found their leader. They have found the anchor of their foundation.
Klint Kubiak is a lot of things, but as one Raiders player put it, “That guy is 100% for f---ing real. That’s my motherf---ing coach.”
He’s your coach, Raider Nation.
He emerged from a terrible loss, leading the Silver and Black out of the smoke and the haze from the front.
I do not know his father, but I do know what he stood for and did. He raised his son in his image. Kubiak lived up to his father’s stellar reputation as a leader of men.
Make no mistake, he is his own man, a Raider man. He’s your man, Raider Nation.
The loss stunk for Raider Nation, but it gave all of us, fan or not, a glimpse of your future.
There will be more tough losses this year, but the balm is that there will be much bigger wins in the future, and more of those than these.
Future free agents love to play for winners, and Kubiak proved that in his worst loss.
If steel is forged in fire, then count Sunday as an inferno.
But out of that inferno, Kubiak showed something tangible, real, and valuable. He has what it takes to lead this rebuild and to take this franchise where it needs to go.
Players won’t magically appear on the roster tomorrow; they'll arrive as these young players develop and mature, and as free agents and future NFL Draft picks are added.
But you have your coach. Finally, and he is a good one. There will be more fires, but the fire he just led his team through should have burned away the doubts. Now, back to the Raiders rebuild.

title: Grading Every Raiders Position Group After Week 5 Loss
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders had a forgettable Week 5 road performance against the New England Patriots. Essentially, everything that could go wrong did, from the very start. Still, the Raiders are in the early stages of a rebuild, which has been clear and will remain so.
Las Vegas' Week 5 matchup against the Patriots was the second game in a handful of games against some of the best teams in the league. Las Vegas will follow up losses against the Kansas City Chiefs and New England Patriots with games against the Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Rams.
Las Vegas is about where most expected them to be at this point in its first season under Klint Kubiak. If anything, they are still ahead of schedule after two consecutive games against top teams. Few expected Las Vegas to be this far along yet.
Below are the grades for each Raiders position group based on their respective Week 5 performances.
What you see is what you are going to get from Kirk Cousins for the rest of the season. The first three games of the season were the ceiling with Cousins under center, which is more than they have had in the last three seasons.
The Raiders' two most recent games are what they will be against top teams with Cousins under center, and likely if Fernando Mendoza takes over. The roster has issues that need both experience and mobility from their play caller.
Cousins has experience; Mendoza has mobility; neither has both. The veteran will continue to start for at least the foreseeable future. However, Mendoza's lone drive against the Patriots, albeit in a blowout and against a much less aggressive defense than Cousins faced, is a glimpse into the future.
Mendoza had the same supporting cast Cousins did, and the offense looked much smoother during his few plays. With Mendoza in, it seemed that even if the pocket broke down, he had the chance to make a play.
His passes were crisper and got to the receivers sooner. Mendoza also showed a pocket awareness that seemed delayed with Cousins under center. There is no magic bullet. Mendoza will struggle too. Yet his struggles are more productive for the organization long-term.
Mendoza may give them their best chance to win right now with the players they have. A few positive Mendoza scrambles can help get eight players out of the box and help open up the run game. Mendoza could be a part of the answer to the Raiders' struggles through the air and on the ground.
It was another dismal day for the ground game. However, defenses having zero respect for the Raiders' passing game could play a part in the struggles Las Vegas is having running the ball.
Connor Heyward does his job.
The Raiders entered Week 5 without two of their starting receivers. It was bound to be a tough day for the group .
The unit could have performed better, but elite defenses have little to worry about when facing the Raiders' offense. Defenses are not scared of Cousins' arm, his ability to move in the pocket, or the Raiders' group of receivers. Defenses can stack the box and bring consistent pressure.
Eventually, that pressure gets to Cousins, and he has nowhere to go. The offensive line can be better, but they could use some help from Cousins, like when he moved the pocket late against the Kansas City Chiefs. Cousins threw the ball 52 times against the Chiefs and wasn't sacked once because he did a solid job of moving in and around the pocket.
If he cannot do that consistently, the Raiders are in trouble. An offensive line can only block for so long with no receivers getting open on passes and eight players in the box on runs because the Raiders' passing game is pedestrian. Las Vegas' offensive problems are circular.
One of the few bright spots for the Raiders on Sunday and likely their most consistent position group overall.
The unit sustained several injuries but still have room for improvement.
We are seeing what the Raiders' defensive backfield is like without a consistent pass rush. Elite teams are exposing what some may have overlooked during the first three weeks of the season. The Raiders likely need another offseason or two to fully rebuild this group.
The Raiders' linebackers are better than what they showed against the Patriots. However, it does not matter what the linebackers do if receivers run wide open downfield and running backs aren't getting touched until they reach the second level of the defense.
Cole punted the ball four times, and averaged nearly 50 yards per punt.
Matt Gay missed his first field goal of the game. His miss shortly before halftime gave the Patriots the ball in scoring position.
Might have been the best outing for the group this season.
Deven Thompkins deserves more action on special teams and potentially even as a wide receiver. He registered one of the Raiders' best punt returns of the season on Sunday.

title: Raiders Stock Report: 3 Players Rising, Falling After Week 5
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders had a rough day on the road against the New England Patriots. Few things went Las Vegas' way. Las Vegas has followed up its 3-0 start with two consecutive losses to two of the league's best teams.
This was always going to be Las Vegas' toughest stretch of games, facing the Kansas City Chiefs, New England Patriots, Buffalo Bills, and Los Angeles Rams back-to-back. While the season's first three games showed growth, the last two showed where it still needs to improve.
The Raiders suffered an ugly loss on Sunday. It would be easy to say there were no positives from the performance, but that would be inaccurate. Just as there are negatives during wins, there are positives during losses, especially for a team in the early stages of a rebuild.
Las Vegas' loss to New England was their worst game of the season. The Patriots' offense posted one of the best offensive outputs in franchise history, yardage-wise. Las Vegas now has a clear idea of where they stand and how far they are from the league's best.
Below are a few players on the rise and some whose stocks are falling following the Raiders' Week 5 road loss to the Patriots.
Bowers continues to look like the league's best tight end after another impressive performance. Every team in the league knows the Raiders want to get the ball to Bowers, yet he still dominates when they need him. Bowers was again the team's leading receiver.
Bowers registered 110 yards on eight catches and gave the Raiders a puncher's chance on a day when they were clearly outmatched, outcoached, and outplayed. Bowers was one of the few bright spots from an all-around bad outing for the Raiders.
Tucker did not fill the stat sheet like he did in Week 2. However, his chances of doing so on an offense with Cody White as its next-best wide receiver are slim. Tucker caught two passes for 21 yards in the first half, both of which were significant for the struggling unit.
Porter had several big plays, including a fumble recovery. He also played solid coverage on several plays, showing the speed that helped him rise up the depth chart. It was a rough day for the Raiders as a whole, but it was encouraging to see Porter have some success.
The Raiders' defensive line is the deepest position group on the roster. Las Vegas needed that depth, losing multiple interior defensive linemen throughout the game. During that time, Butler, one of the Raiders' most experienced defensive linemen, quietly gave the unit solid play.
Shortly before halftime, Butler forced a fumble that was recovered by Porter. It did not result in points for the Raiders' offense, but it helped keep points off the board for the Patriots.
Las Vegas' questionable defensive backfield needed protection from the Raiders' defensive line. Last Sunday against the Kansas City Chiefs and today against the Patriots showed what will likely happen throughout the season if the unit cannot generate a consistent pass rush.
The Raiders' defense has been aggressive all season. On Sunday, the unit seemed unable to generate a pass rush or stop quarterback Drake Maye, who was playing with several of his backup wide receivers.
Many of the struggles Cousins and the Raiders' offense are having are innate. Looking at the depth chart and the team's training camp and preseason, it was evident that the roster still had things to fix, especially on offense. Some of those things can't be fixed until next offseason.
It was well known that Cousins' health and age could affect things. The Raiders would not be 3-2 without Cousins' experience. However, the deficiencies Las Vegas' offense has do not match well with the deficiencies in Cousins' game at this point in his career. Defenses have figured that out.
The Patriots had backup wide receivers wide open downfield multiple times. It was not a talent issue; it was a schematic and roster issue. Las Vegas' defensive backfield and wide receivers are their Achilles' heel.

title: Dolphins Week 5 Report Card: Running Game Delivers, but Mistakes Keep Miami Winless
full_text:
There’s the cliché that numbers never lie, but don’t put too much stock in the final score of this one.
The Miami Dolphins may have lost against the Cincinnati Bengals 31-24, but an impending mistake always felt around the corner.
Cincinnati led 28-10 entering the fourth quarter before Miami’s late touchdowns made things look more competitive.
As the score shows, the Dolphins found ways to produce while rushing for 217 yards and outgaining Cincinnati 331-307 and finishing with more first downs, but three turnovers and another special teams breakdown helped turn any advantages into a loss at Hard Rock Stadium.
Here’s how each position group graded out as Miami fell to 0-5.
After giving Malik Willis some time to adjust to leading a new, inexperienced team, the past couple of weeks have made it clear that pointing to the problems around him can’t explain away his own glaring flaws.
Willis completed 15 of 27 passes for 137 yards, one touchdown and two interceptions, finishing with a 51.0 passer rating. He also fumbled twice, losing one with the Dolphins trailing by 10 late in the fourth quarter.
His first interception came on a tipped pass, when Boye Mafe batted a pass intended for Kevin Coleman Jr., and Jordan Battle came down with the deflection, but the second was a much more avoidable mistake, with Willis throwing back across his body while scrambling and finding Battle again.
And that’s where the feeling of an impending mistake was proven to be correct. Miami had just recovered a Cincinnati fumble near its own goal line, but three offensive plays later, the Bengals had the ball back and were on their way to a 21-7 lead.
The third-quarter goal-line possession was another costly example. After Gordon was stopped for a loss from the 1, Willis took an 8-yard sack on second-and-goal from the 3, a mistake he took responsibility for after the game. Miami eventually settled for a field goal.
He did throw a touchdown, however, rolling to his right and finding Kevin Coleman Jr. in the back of the end zone for a 3-yard score in the fourth quarter, the rookie’s first NFL touchdown.
His legs are still a weapon, as he rushed for 74 yards and a touchdown, including a 39-yard scamper on third-and-13 that helped launch Miami’s first fourth-quarter touchdown drive.
Losing De’Von Achane would have sounded like one of Miami’s biggest potential crises, but Ollie Gordon II looks right at home in an offense that wants to load up on blockers and run through people.
A week after rushing for 100 yards against Minnesota, Gordon followed it up with 88 yards and a touchdown on 18 carries. The Oklahoma State product ranks sixth in rushing yards across Weeks 4 and 5, with 188, through Sunday night.
His 22-yard run on third-and-10 helped keep Miami’s opening possession alive, and he eventually finished that drive with a 1-yard touchdown. He also put together runs of 7, 10 and 13 yards during the third-quarter drive that reached Cincinnati’s 1-yard line.
After Miami got just 2.8 yards per attempt out of the sixth-round pick during his rookie campaign in 2025, Gordon II has thrived off being able to find a rhythm without the one-dimensional predictability that came with being a 6-foot-2, 225-pound back used only in short-yardage situations.
Jaylen Wright continued to struggle, managing 11 yards on six carries. Three of those attempts came while Gordon II briefly was sidelined with an injury early in the fourth quarter.
Malik Washington continues to be Miami’s most reliable receiving option, catching six of eight targets for 43 yards. He also continued to mix in snaps out of the backfield, adding an 18-yard run.
But he averaged just over 7 yards per reception Sunday, and his skill set is better suited to being a reliable, complementary slot option than carrying a team’s entire aerial attack.
Coleman offered more this week, catching three passes for 30 yards, including a 3-yard touchdown and a 23-yard reception that set up Willis’ late rushing score. That said, with Coleman offering a similar but less developed skill set to Washington’s, Miami is yearning for a true No. 1 outside receiver who can put pressure on defenses at every level.
Jalen Tolbert added a 22-yard catch. Chris Bell didn’t record a reception, but his 26-yard reverse helped get Miami into scoring position in the third quarter. His fourth-quarter false start also helped create the third-and-13 that Willis had to escape.
Greg Dulcich caught four of five targets for 37 yards and added the two-point conversion after Coleman’s touchdown.
His 13-yard reception converted fourth-and-1 near the end of the first half, although Miami ran out of time before turning that possession into points. He also moved the chains on third-and-5 during the final touchdown drive.
Will Kacmarek caught just one pass for 5 yards, but on Bell’s 26-yard run, he led the way up the right side of the field before laying a solid block on Bengals cornerback DJ Turner II to help Bell pick up a first down.
Miami averaged 6.4 yards on 34 rushing attempts, with Gordon, Willis, Washington and Bell all producing runs of at least 18 yards.
Willis’ scrambling helped that average, but Gordon’s 88 yards also showed consistency in the ground game.
Unlike last week, no gain was wiped out by a holding penalty.
The protection still had costly breakdowns, however, as Cincinnati finished with three sacks for 23 yards, including Jonathan Allen’s late strip-sack.
That said, Willis’ 8-yard loss near the goal line shows how a quarterback’s decision to keep a play alive can make the protection look worse.
The unit had to adjust after right guard Jonah Savaiinaea left with an ankle injury in the second quarter, with Jarrett Kingston replacing him.
A week after finally collecting their first four sacks of the season, the Dolphins finished with none while also allowing 117 rushing yards
Chop Robinson hit Joe Burrow twice, but Cincinnati’s star quarterback still threw four touchdown passes without an interception.
The Bengals’ rushing total was more a product of volume than efficiency, as Cincinnati ran the ball 31 times for an average of just 3.8 yards per carry. But the bigger problem was how often the Bengals kept possessions alive while converting nine of 13 third downs.
Robinson seemed to come through on a desperately needed fourth-quarter sack with Miami trailing 28-18, only to erase it himself with an offside penalty. Cincinnati received a first down and kept draining the clock. Zach Sieler later turned third-and-7 into third-and-2 with an encroachment penalty, although the defense eventually forced a punt.
Josh Uche did help preserve Miami’s second-quarter takeaway, recovering the ball after Robinson fumbled during his return.
Rookie linebacker Jacob Rodriguez finished with a team-high 11 tackles, but Mike Gesicki beat him on a double move, selling an inside break just long enough to freeze Rodriguez before catching a red-zone touchdown.
With 11:51 left in the second quarter, he gave up another touchdown after allowing Samaje Perine to cut inside of him on an angle route.
Burrow’s third touchdown pass went to Tanner Hudson with Willie Gay Jr. in coverage.
Cincinnati converted seven of eight third downs in the first half, and its first three touchdowns went to two tight ends and a running back.
The secondary made some of Miami’s most important defensive plays.
Chris Johnson forced Chase Brown’s second-quarter fumble near the goal line, and rookie Michael Taaffe also forced a fumble earlier in that possession, but Miami’s recovery was reversed after the referees determined that Gay Jr. was out of bounds after picking up the ball.
Taaffe left with a chest injury before returning, while JuJu Brents dealt with injuries and eventually was ruled out with a stinger.
Jason Marshall Jr. surrendered the game’s biggest passing play, Chase’s 45-yard touchdown late in the third quarter. The second-year cornerback was close enough to contest the catch, but jumped a step early,…

title: Good NFL News for Johnson As He Continues to Deliver for the Dolphins
full_text:
Things have been moving in the right direction for Miami Dolphins rookie Chris Johnson since a rough start to the season.
His performance keeps getting better every week to the point he's as effective as any rookie on the roster — yes, even on a par with the much more heralded Jacob Rodriguez.
And there's been good news on the field as well for Johnson, who successfully appealed his NFL fine resulting from a tackle against Las Vegas Raiders running back Ashton Jeanty.
In addition to getting back the $17,911 he had been fined for a hip-drop tackle — and remember that there was no flag on the play — Johnson also saw disappear one of his three strikes for that particular violation.
As part of a new rule in 2026, repeat offenders in one of three categories now can be suspended for a game with three violations, and hip-drop tackles is one of them — the other two are blindside blocks and hits on a defenseless player.
So now Johnson has his fine money back and he's again got a clean slate with the league.
On the field, Johnson has come a long way since that opener against the Raiders when he was victimized for a couple of touchdown passes.
His performance in Week 5 against the Cincinnati Bengals might have been his best yet, and it went beyond the forced fumble he produced with a perfectly executed "Peanut punch" in the second half.
While we understand that Pro Football Focus' grades shouldn't be viewed as the ultimate gauge, their game-by-game grades for Johnson have indicated the steady and consistent progress everybody who has watched Dolphins games can plainly see.
PFF gave Johnson an 86.9 overall grade for Week 5, his third consecutive game with at least a 69 mark after he was under 50 for the first two games against the Raiders and San Francisco 49ers.
"I thought Chris had a solid game," Hafley said of Johnson's work against Cincinnati. "There's a couple plays where, just like any of us, I'm sure that he wants back, but I see the confidence overall just growing with him. I mean, you can see it when he's playing out there. Early in the season, when he had some moments where guys caught balls on him, I kind of didn't feel like the response was where we needed it to be. I don't feel that anymore. I thought this was a big test for him with the wide receivers they had as a rookie and overall, I'd say he answered it pretty well and regardless of the outcome of certain plays, I love the confidence and the energy that he's playing with."
What always needs to be mentioned when discussing Johnson  is the fact he continues to split time between the slot and outside, a difficult assignment for any cornerback, let alone a rookie.
Whether inside or outside, what's been consistent about Johnson has been his tackling ability, which would have to be considered high end for a cornerback.
Because he hasn't gotten an interception just yet and because of the bend-but-don't-break style of defense the Dolphins have employed, where they're willing to give up underneath completions to protect against the deep ball, Johnson has flown under the radar a lot more than Rodriguez, who keeps racking up the tackles, but the Dolphins have reason to be as excited right now about Johnson's future potential as that of Rodriguez, with the two making up a good start for a foundation on defense.

title: Breaking Down the Latest Dolphins Practice Squad Moves
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins' latest practice squad moves was most noteworthy for the player they let go than the one they brought back.
The team announced Tuesday morning they had signed quarterback Brady Cook to the practice and released running back Jarquez Hunter to make room.
The move with Cook should have been expected (and was predicted here) because the Dolphins need three quarterbacks, even if one of them is on the practice squad.
Cook was on the 53-man roster for the first four games before he was waived Saturday to make room for defensive tackle Kenneth Grant being activated off injured reserve.
The Dolphins did not a minor gamble in another team claiming Cook off waivers, though it seemed pretty safe that it wouldn't happen.
While it's always a possibility that he will be brought back to the practice squad, this move seems to end the Jarquez Hunter experiment that began when he was acquired in a summer trade from the Los Angeles Rams in exchange for veteran wide receiver.
A fourth-round pick out of Auburn in 2025, Hunter represented the kind of player the Dolphins have been looking to investigate and evaluate as they look for hidden gems to carry along beyond this season.
But Hunter never made enough of an impression to earn playing time in Miami.
While he didn't have a chance for the 53-man roster because he was acquired the day before the preseason finale, Hunter saw training camp running back Carlos Washington Jr. overtake him on the depth chart, with Washington getting the call the last two games with injuries at running back.
And then it really was over for Hunter when the Dolphins claimed rookie running back Kaytron Allen off waivers from the New Orleans Saints late last week.
While the move didn't pan out, acquiring Hunter still was a good move because it was a no-risk deal with the potential for good value, and that's because Atwell wasn't going to make the 53-man roster coming out of training camp. He was going to be released, and the trade actually took the Dolphins off the hook for the small guaranteed salary they had committed to Atwell.
Hunter panning out would have been a great bonus. That it didn't happen was no big deal, but it again proved the idea that we've repeated many times about tempering expectations whenever the Dolphins bring in a player who basically was discarded by another organization.

title: What the Week 5 Film Told Us About the Miami Dolphins
full_text:
In the Miami Dolphins' 31-24 loss against the Cincinnati Bengals, a poor mixture of talent and scheme was the difference, but the youth continued to shine. Let's take a look at some of the film from the Week 5 game, along with some key takeaways.
Joe Burrow picked apart the Dolphins’ defense underneath in Week 5. Pending Monday Night Football, he was sixth in EPA per dropback on dropbacks of less than 2.5 seconds and eighth in the same stat on throws of fewer than 10 air yards.
pic.twitter.com/KXcIrAzve5
Burrow was decisive against a defense that dedicated their second- and third-level defenders to stopping over-the-top throws to Ja’Marr Chase or Tee Higgins. On this play, Miami’s quarters look ends up playing similar to a prevent coverage, with the linebackers dropping too deep, leaving Chase Brown open for a ten-yard gain.
It’s a perfect storm of miscues for Miami right now. Their umbrella coverages put too much stress on the linebackers, who haven’t been up to snuff in coverage. Meanwhile, with Chop Robinson receiving chip help and double teams throughout this game, the Dolphins don’t have someone up front who can force the issue. It’s a marriage of below-average personnel with a scheme that’s sticking with the philosophy of limiting possessions, even when the quarterback is more than willing to take the checkdown.
Much like the defensive struggles, Miami’s passing offense garners blame for just about everyone involved. Bobby Slowik couldn’t consistently scheme targets open, the receivers struggled to create separation, and Malik Willis made several back-breaking errors.
Slowik’s designs clearly draw inspiration from his former boss, Mike McDaniel. The issue is, some of these concepts already had outworn their welcome, and without Tyreek Hill or Jaylen Waddle, they’re simply not an efficient way to use your eligible receivers.
pic.twitter.com/1NRVDNxXdi
On too many occasions, there are only two or three receivers out on routes, and in this case, it’s paired with a long-developing play-fake. On second-and-10, Cincinnati’s backers are able to drop into the intermediate window, and Chris Bell can’t sufficiently break the press.
Regardless of the long-term outlook for Bell or Kevin Coleman Jr., Miami does not have the quality of pass-catchers right now to make these looks a staple. To make things easier on Willis, it may be in their best interest to opt for quantity and attack more of the field with their route designs.
pic.twitter.com/sL0MxXtmgO
This doesn’t absolve Willis, who made multiple abysmal decisions in this game. His process has been slow, he hasn’t been willing to move off of his downfield reads, and his awareness of his immediate surroundings has made already poor situations worse.
One of the few positives from this game was that the rookie class continues to show out. This was easily the best game of Chris Johnson’s young career. On top of a forced fumble, I was particularly impressed by a pass-rush rep where he fought through the blocks of three different players to pressure Joe Burrow.
pic.twitter.com/s2uzbkfF7q
Kadyn Proctor and Will Kacmarek also have continued to showcase their physicality. On a toss play to Malik Washington, Proctor was able to cut off Dexter Lawrence while Kacmarek made a crucial crack block on Boye Mafe.
pic.twitter.com/3arYuNtlT4
This class already has shown considerable promise, and if they keep it up, they’ll set the foundation for this Dolphins team by the time they’re ready to compete.

title: Why Dolphins Coach Is Right in Squashing Idea of Benching Willis
full_text:
The question truly was ridiculous, except it needed to be asked because it's fans are talking about it and would want to ask the question themselves, and journalists are conduits between fans and coaches.
So it was that the first question in Miami Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley's regular day-after-the-game media session Monday was this: "Are you giving any thought to starting Kyle McCord against the Jets after the bye?"
That would be quarterback Kyle McCord and the suggestion was whether Malik Willis' performance and stats through five games and maybe even in the Week 5 loss against the Cincinnati Bengals was enough to considering making a change.
But Hafley quickly, and absolutely correctly, shot down that notion.
And the thinking in saying so?
"We've played five games, and Malik is our quarterback."
During the remainder of his 20-minute session, Hafley was asked other questions about Willis and he made it clear that he expects better from his starting quarterback while also indicating that several factors are involved in the success — or lack thereof — of the passing game, such as pass protection and receivers running the correct routes and getting open.
All of it is off right now, up to and including Willis.
Before the Week 5 Monday night game, Willis was last among 29 qualifying quarterbacks in passer rating and completion percentage with only two touchdown passes against four interceptions.
There is nobody who should be happy with Willis' work so far this season or think it's anywhere near good enough for him to even begin being considered as a long-term answer.
And it's five games with a young and sub-par supporting cast, one that's been without it's best player (De'Von Achane) for almost three games and without its most dynamic wide receiver at the moment (Caleb Douglas) for three-plus games.
Remember when some folks were calling the Dolphins wide receiver corps about as bad a group as there's been in the NFL in a long time? Well, that group always was about long-term potential and that potential has not been reached yet.
And let's also not pretend that Willis has benefited from great pass protection, either, because pressure is getting there in a hurry on a pretty regular basis.
This isn't to excuse everything that Willis has struggled with, but it absolutely does explain some of the poor numbers.
"I think you guys are going to get tired of my answers however the questions are phrased, it's everything," Hafley said. "It's a detail of the route running. It starts with the protection. It's going through the progression. It's everybody being on the same page, and everybody being more efficient in their 1/11."
But, of course, the quarterback is the one who's going to be in the spotlight and Willis also is the one outside free agent the Dolphins signed all year for something beyond the minimum or almost-minimum salary.
Hafley and GM Jon-Eric Sullivan talked about Willis in terms of handing him the keys to the offense and building around him, and so far that construction project is not looking very good.
But would it make any sense whatsoever to give up after five games?
Or even go with this idea of having Willis sit for a bit and give Kyle McCord a shot to see what he can do?
Sure, the idea of McCord might be intriguing for those who liked him at Syracuse, but do we need to remind everyone that after the Philadelphia Eagles selected him in the sixth round of the 2025 draft, they waived him and then let him leave off their practice squad for Green Bay this year, only to have the Packers trade him to the Dolphins for a 2028 sixth-round pick?
Again, let's repeat that: 2028 sixth-round pick. Using the gauge of dropping a pick for every year down the road, that's the equivalent of a 2026 eighth-round pick.
Yes, the Packers don't believe in keeping three QBs on their roster, but if they valued McCord, would they have basically just given him away like that, much the same way the Dolphins gave away Quinn Ewers?
Maybe McCord will become a good NFL quarterback at some point, but the reality is it's probably a long shot.
And maybe the same holds true for Willis.
Except that Willis actually has appeared in an NFL regular season game and he actually looked very good doing it during his time with the Packers, where Hafley and Sullivan also got to watch him first-hand on a daily basis.
What's happened so far in the 2026 season probably isn't what they had in mind or hoped, but suggesting for even a millisecond they would give up on Willis this quickly bordered on ridiculous.
The Dolphins have 12 games remaining in the 2026 regular season and that's plenty of time for things to change, to get better with Willis, the passing game and the entire offense.
None of it is good enough right now. But the Dolphins don't have to make any decisions right now as it applies to 2027 and they owe it to Willis and more importantly to themselves to give him a chance to show what he can do.
