title: Ventola: Patriots Rookie Class Criminally Underrated in Recent Rankings
full_text:
In a recent ranking of all 32 teams' rookie classes by On SI's Justin Melo , the New England Patriots' 2026 draftees were placed 24th, a criminally underrated ranking for a group which has already made substantial contributions just five weeks into their careers.
Here's how New England's rookie class has proven itself to be far better than the subpar ranking it earned.
Lomu has had a limited role early this season for the Patriots, but has impressed in the opportunities he has gotten.
New England drafted the former Utah lineman in the first round as the long-term replacement to veteran right tackle Morgan Moses. Through the Patriots' first four games of the season, Lomu had solely been used on a limited snap count in relief of Moses and as a jumbo tight end.
However, on Sunday against the Las Vegas Raiders, Lomu had his first opportunity for extended playing time. When starting left tackle Will Campbell went down with an injury early in the matchup, Lomu stepped up.
All of Caleb Lomu's snaps at Left Tackle yesterday in his Rookie Debut for the Patriots Thought he was pretty solid in pass pro, lost a few reps to the outside, but overall pretty good showing pic.twitter.com/E9GUBWslr2
The 21-year-old allowed just one pressure on his 25 pass blocking snaps. The 4% pressure rate allowed was second-best among New England linemen, behind just Alijah Vera Tucker (0 pressures on 38 pass blocks).
"I don't think it was too big for him," head coach Mike Vrabel said regarding Lomu's performance. "I think he was able to settle down. You didn't really notice him a lot, so I think that's probably a good thing. He was able to anchor at times on some power and allowed Drake (Maye) to be able transfer up into the pocket. I thought it worked together well with (Alijah Vera-Tucker) when he got in there."
While Lomu hasn't quite contributed on a game-by-game, play-by-play basis, he has thrived in his role as a sixth lineman and emergency fill-in.
The start to Jacas' tenure in New England was filled with its fair share of turmoil. However, since then, the second-round pick has helped revitalize the Patriots' edge rusher room. The 22-year-old's top-tier strength has shown up through the first five weeks of his career.
Elijah Ponder and Gabe Jacas are DUDES pic.twitter.com/Hbj8saXg75
"He cares an extreme amount," Vrabel said on Sept. 20. "He comes in early; he stays late; he's with (outside linebackers coach) Mike Smith; he works with me; he works with all the coaches; he cares about his teammates. He goes hard, makes mistakes. The thing about Gabe is that he can work through mistakes, and I think that's really critical for any young player trying to improve."
Through his first five career games, Jacas has tallied 1.5 sacks, 17 total tackles and an interception.
When Raridon was first drafted, it seemed uncertain he would have an opportunity to carve out a substantial role in the Patriots' offense. However, after veteran Julian Hill suffered a season-ending injury in the summer, Raridon was quickly thrown into the fire as the Patriots' second tight end.
The rookie has taken full advantage of his opportunities thus far. Raridon has shown flashes of being a true multi-tool player for New England's offense. Against the Raiders, the 22-year-old caught all five of his targets for 57 yards.
Rookie TE Eli Raridon's 5 targets against the Raiders this week You can really see the athleticism and speed when they get him on crossers. Also love how he slightly sold his route being in the flat, before getting upfield on the wheel route. He finished with 5 catches for… pic.twitter.com/jQ2HtrC7yk
"I think it was good to see Eli work at the line of scrimmage, block a little bit, but then also be able to get out and do some things in the pass game and things that he'll have to improve on," Vrabel said on Monday about Raridon's performance in Week 5. "If you're targeted five times as a tight end, you want five catches."
While the Patriots' first few draft picks have gotten extended looks early on, New England has also gotten plenty of contributions on the back-end of its roster from a handful of rookies. Five of the team's six picks on the final day of the NFL Draft made the 53-man roster. The team also currently carries a trio of undrafted free agents, with another two currently on injured reserve.
Operating with a roster fresh off a Super Bowl appearance, which has since made signifcant upgrades through trades and free agency, the Patriots still getting valuable play out of late-round and undrafted rookies is a positive sign for what the group can do in the future.
From the significant contributions by early-round pick to the work being done by the rest of the Patriots' rookies, ranking New England's draft class 24th is simply blasphemous.

title: Patriots Don't Have Clear Update on TreVeyon Henderson's Ankle Injury Just Yet
full_text:
FOBXORO — TreVeyon Henderson missed the New England Patriots' first game of the year with an ankle injury he suffered in practice. Another ankle injury forced him out of their Week 5 game as well, and now he might miss some more time.
The Patriots, in the midst of their 45-17 drubbing of the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday , were forced to go the entire second half without Henderson and offensive tackle Will Campbell — who both got banged up on the same drive in the second quarter.
The second-year running back had four carries for 22 yards, and one reception for 16 yards on a lateral play from wide receiver Efton Chism III . He was slow to get up on the sideline, and then after a few snaps, would depart to the sideline. Henderson wouldn't go into the blue medical tent, and would walk to the locker room ahead of halftime.
Henderson would be spotted walking in the locker room after the game once reporters entered.
Speaking on Monday, head coach Mike Vrabel shared an update on Henderson's ankle — and how he's in a similar boat to Campbell this close to the game ending.
"We'll evaluate here and see how it looks," Vrabel said. "Wasn't able to finish the game, and you know, if we see that on Wednesday he's going to be limited, then we'll let you know he'll be limited. And I know that those two players will do everything that they can to get back, but unfortunately, they weren't able to finish the game.
"So I don't know where their availability will be just less than 24 hours after the game."
The Patriots would have to go the rest of the way with just Rhamondre Stevenson and Corey Kiner in the backfield. Vrabel calling the running game "inconsistent" postgame, as Stevenson (13 carries, 64 yards, one touchdown) had some productive runs, but nothing was able to be stretched out for all four quarters.
On Kiner's first carry of the game, he had the ball punched out by former Patriots defensive tackle Adam Butler.
"There was some good ones in there, and then we got too many for, you know, no yardage," Vrabel said Sunday. "We just wanna be able to stay consistent with that. But there was some good ones there at the end, and I thought it was just enough, and Drake made some good decisions with his legs."
Both Henderson and Campbell underwent tests Monday, and NFL Network's Ian Rapoport reported that Campbell is believed to have suffered a knee bruise on the same knee that he tore his MCL in a season ago. That injury could force him to the sidelines for a little bit, putting some more stress on an already-banged up offensive line unit.
"It'll get looked at and (Campbell will) continue to rehab," Vrabel confirmed. "(He) wasn't able to finish the game."
Rookie Caleb Lomu would likely step up at left tackle if Campbell isn't able to go next week.
Edge rusher Dre'Mont Jones and cornerback Charles Woods also left the game with shoulder injuries. Defensive tackle Cory Durden also got rolled up on late.
We'll get another update on Henderson and his status on Wednesday when the Patriots take the field for their first practice of Week 6. If Henderson isn't able to go, the Patriots could potentially elevate second-year back Lan Larison from the practice squad. He made his NFL debut in Week 1 in Seattle .

title: Drake Maye's Confidence Never Wavered — And It Showed in Patriots Win
full_text:
Drake Maye, ladies and gentlemen. Just a few weeks after the sky was falling ( and I said it's time for concern ), the New England Patriots quarterback rebounded back to his normal self.
He was surgical, mistake-free and operated with conviction as the Patriots trounced the Las Vegas Raiders, 45-17, at Gillette Stadium. Maye had five total touchdowns, one of them with his legs, and just took full control of an offense down several starters.
A.J. Brown. Mack Hollins. Mike Onwenu. TreVeyon Henderson. Will Campbell .
It didn't matter for Maye, who returned to his usual confident poise under center. He says his confidence remains sky-high for every game, but he just looked like a totally different player than he did in losses to Seattle and Jacksonville.
"I'm gonna be confident going into every game," Maye said postgame. "I'm confident in the guys around me, confident in myself, and I think it's just really just an example of practice execution showing up in the game."
With no Brown and Hollins recently placed on IR with a calf injury, it was a slim wide receivers room for the Patriots. They entered the game with just four on the active roster, and only two of them had really made dents to this point.
All of them contributed in the win , with DeMario Douglas and Kyle Williams both finding the end zone for the first time this season. Romeo Doubs helped move the chains by drawing two defensive pass interference calls, and Efton Chism III caught five balls.
But their play was elevated by their quarterback, who gave them catchable balls and put them in positions to succeed.
"It's just awesome for me to see guys like Caleb (Lomu) getting in there and playing his butt off and different guys and Pop (Douglas) have been playing and running routes well all year and finally getting rewarded," Maye said. "I just love to see guys that do the right things over and over and finally get rewarded in the game, and I think that's one of the best things about my position is able to spread the wealth and see other guys succeed and it's beautiful to watch."
After a few weeks where a bad turnover (or two, or three) felt like a given, there was no worry about if Maye might throw a costly interception this week . He delivered the ball with speed and accuracy, and had the footwork to move in and out of the pocket with ease. Maye completed 26 passes on 34 attempts and finished with a quarterback rating of 150.9 (the highest it can be is 158.3).
He's now sitting at 3-2 and could end up being back in first place if the Buffalo Bills lose . But more important, the Patriots feel like they can lean on the 24-year-old Maye. His confidence remains even-keeled, and now the results are starting to show.
"I'm gonna come into every game and every week and attack it, and I'm confident in myself and my abilities and the guys around me," Maye said.

title: 5 Winners, 2 Losers in Patriots' Blowout Win Over Raiders
full_text:
The New England Patriots are back to a winning record for the first time this season. The team dominated the Las Vegas Raiders in Gillette Stadium on Sunday, 45-17.
From domination in the trenches to depth pieces stepping up in their increased roles, here are the biggest winners, and losers, from Sunday's victory.
Another week, another step up for Maye. The third-year signal caller tossed just one touchdown and seven interceptions through the Patriots' first three games of the season. A week ago against the Buffalo Bills, he tossed for three scores and combined for a pair of turnovers.
But against the Raiders, Maye was near-perfect. The 24-year-old scored five touchdowns (four passing, one rushing), completed over 76% of his passes and had his first turnover-free game of the year.
"It was beautiful to be a part of today," Maye said after the win. "(Offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels) was clicking on all cylinders, making us look good, and we were executing. I think that's what it's like when we put some things together and, and we still have some. I mean, it's crazy to say we still got some, some left to to squeeze."
The Patriots traded for Kiner prior to roster cuts to be the team's third running back. Prior to Sunday's battle with the Raiders, the former Arizona Cardinal had fit that role perfectly.
However, against Las Vegas, Kiner was responsible for New England's sole turnover of the day. On his first rush attempt of the day, with the Patriots up by just one possession, the 24-year-old had the ball punched away from him to give the Raiders possession in field-goal range.
Heading into Sunday, Douglas had a very tame stat-line on the season: just nine receptions for 82 yards and no touchdowns. Against the Raiders, however, he had one of his best performances of his career.  The 25-year-old caught four passes for 65 yards and a pair of scores, marking his first-ever multi-touchdown day.
"It's just awesome for me to see guys like Caleb getting in there and playing his butt off and different guys and (Douglas) have been playing and running routes well all year and finally getting rewarded," Maye said on Sunday. "I just love to see guys that do the right things over and over and finally get rewarded in the game, and I think that's one of the best things about my position is able to spread the wealth and see other guys succeed and it's beautiful to watch."
When the Patriots drafted Lomu in April, the plan seemed for him to be an "in case of emergency" option at tackle as he developed to be the long-term replacement to Morgan Moses. On Sunday, however, that emergency situation arose. New England's first-round pick played 49 snaps after left-side starter Will Campbell suffered an injury.
In Lomu's action, he allowed just one pressure. Plus, the 21-year-old wasn't called for any penalties.
"Just proud of our offensive line, and I wanna recognize them," Vrabel said after the win. "I thought that they understood what the protection was and how to keep the middle of the pocket clean...And so that's a testament to them for understanding what they have to be able to do, and guys stepped up. You know, Caleb [Lomu] had to go in there, and, you know, everybody, we had all hands on deck."
While Campbell and Lomu held their own at left tackle, Moses had his struggles on the right side. The veteran allowed three pressures and a quarterback hit in his 38 pass block snaps. Even worse, however, were the penalties.
Moses was flagged twice on Sunday, each in detrimental situations. The 35-year-old was called for holding on a third-and-2. Later on that same drive, he was penalized for a false start on first-and-goal from the 1-yard line. While New England fought through both calls, those easily could have wiped points off the board.
Heading into the afternoon, the Patriots were incredibly thin at cornerback. New England was without starters Christian Gonzalez and Carlton Davis III, plus depth pieces Karon Prunty and Channing Canada. One of only three players active at the position on Sunday, Vildor stepped up.
The 28-year-old allowed just two receptions and broke up a pass in the five targets he saw. He also forced a fumble on Raiders star tight end Brock Bowers.
"Just exactly what we would expect," Vrabel said regarding Vildor's performance. "You know, that's why we had him in that position and had ability for him to be elevated or get signed and step in there and compete. And nothing was perfect. Nothing is ever gonna be perfect, but, you know, for him to understand what he has to do and, you know, great opportunistic hammer and turnover and punch out there, it's, you know, the competitive spirit of some of these guys is, is really truly special."
Ponder has been a force to be reckoned with this season for the Patriots. He has already surpassed his sack total from last season with 4.5 (team-high). Two of those came on Sunday, including a forced fumble at the end of the first half which could have led to another score had New England recovered.
The former undrafted free agent also notched a pair of run stops and pressured the quarterback on four of his pass rushes. Although the Patriots' edge rusher group was looked upon as one of the worst in the NFL heading into 2026, Ponder has played a substantial role in bringing the pass rush's production up to par.

title: Patriots Don't Get Positive Initial Update on OT Will Campbell's Knee Injury
full_text:
The New England Patriots lost a pair of offensive linemen earlier in the season, forcing them to make changes at the right guard position. Now they might need to make a change at left tackle.
According to NFL Network's Ian Rapoport , Will Campbell is believed to have suffered a knee sprain in the first half of the Patriots' 45-17 win over the Las Vegas Raiders Sunday. He'll receive an MRI tomorrow to confirm and the injury would "likely cause him to miss some time."
Campbell would leave the game after Rhamondre Stevenson got tackled into his right leg. It was the same leg that Campbell tore his MCL in a season ago, forcing him onto injured reserve. He would remain on the field for a little bit while he got checked out by members of the training staff before heading to the sideline.
He was replaced by first round rookie Caleb Lomu at left tackle . The Patriots also had running back TreVeyon Henderson, edge rusher Dre'Mont Jones and cornerback Charles Woods leave the game with injuries.
After the game, the rookie — who allowed just one pressure since entering the game — spoke about getting thrust into the starting lineup.
"That’s just one of the things that Vrabes and even this league is all about," Lomu said. "Lots of things can happen. Injuries are part of football, which sucks. You know, praying for everyone who has an injury, especially Will, but whatever happens, you got to prepare like a starter is what coach Vrabes tells us. And it’s completely true. Anything can happen. So prepare as a starter throughout the week, even if you’re not going to start, because things like this can happen."
Campbell would head to the locker room during the game, but would briefly return to the sideline to ride a stationary bike. After halftime, he wouldn't return to the sideline and would later be ruled out.
It was a great start to the 2026 season for the LSU alum, who has solidified himself as the cornerstone left tackle for the Patriots . He had only allowed 11 pressures and one sack through the first four-plus games. A year ago, Campbell was also playing well before an MCL tear against the Cincinnati Bengals forced him out for four games. After he would return to the active roster, he wasn't the same player and struggled in the postseason.
"I was ready to go," said Lomu, who played a career-high 47 snaps. "Always just like I said, preparing like a starter no matter what happens, you know, as soon as it happened, I was ready to go, do what I could do to help the team win."
Lomu, the Patriots' first round selection back in April, spent most of the year at right tackle in a backup role. Now, he'll have the opportunity to line back up at left tackle, the position he played at Utah during his collegiate career.
The Patriots already lost guards Mike Onwenu and Greg Van Roten earlier in the season, and may now lose Campbell for a few weeks. They could decide to activate Marcus Bryant off of injured reserve, who was placed on the list ahead of Week 1 and was already designated to return. They've yet to activate his 21-day practice window.
Players will return to the practice field Wednesday as they prepare for their next home game against the New York Jets.

title: Gayle Benson Breaks Silence as Saints' 1-4 Start Puts Leadership Under Fire
full_text:
New Orleans Saints owner Gayle Benson declared the team's 1-4 start to the season was “not acceptable" on Monday, issuing a stern warning to leadership and staff as frustration mounts across the franchise and fan base.
Speaking at the Greater New Orleans Quarterback Club following Sunday's 23-13 loss to the Minnesota Vikings , Benson emphasized that accountability extends across the entire organization.
"That is not acceptable to me, and it falls short of what our fans deserve," Benson said. "I hear the frustration directed toward our team and our organization. It is not lost on me."
Benson emphasized that accountability begins with her but extends throughout the organization, specifically identifying General Manager Mickey Loomis , second-year head coach Kellen Moore , the coaching staff, and the players.
"I will not make excuses, and I will not accept this level of performance as our standard," Benson said. "I am committed to making the decisions necessary to improve this team."
While Benson did not say anything straightforward on whether organizational changes were imminent, her comments came nearly two years after she overruled Loomis and fired former coach Dennis Allen following a seven-game losing streak.
In what should have been a year of continued improvement from last season’s second-half success, along with an emerging quarterback in Tyler Shough , this year should have been full of great vibes. Instead, the Saints have been putrid throughout the first five games of the franchise's 60th anniversary season, which has featured several celebrations overshadowed by disappointing performances.
New Orleans suffered an embarrassing 45-24 loss to the Atlanta Falcons during the 20th anniversary celebration of the historic 2006 "Domecoming" game. Six days later, the Saints lost to Minnesota during a ceremony honoring Drew Brees ' Pro Football Hall of Fame induction and his addition to the team's Ring of Honor.
At the end of both games, supporters of the Falcons and Vikings overtook the lower bowl of the stadium as “ATL” chants were heard throughout last Monday night, and “Skol” chants were also heard, but the latter were more audible because there were many Minnesota fans in attendance.
Benson referenced Brees' legacy while emphasizing the importance of restoring the standards that helped New Orleans win Super Bowl XLIV.
"It also includes a standard of preparation, discipline and accountability," Benson said. "The best way to honor that legacy is to uphold those standards today."
She also outlined the responsibilities of the organization's leadership:
"Kellen Moore and his coaches are responsible for preparing our players to perform. Mickey Loomis and our football staff are responsible for building a roster capable of sustained success. Our players are responsible for their preparation and execution. I am responsible for holding this organization accountable."
Despite her strong remarks, Benson acknowledged that public statements alone would not restore confidence in a franchise that has not reached the playoffs since 2020.
"Words will not restore our fans' confidence," Benson said. "Our performance must do that."
The Saints will attempt to end their losing streak Sunday against the New York Giants before traveling to Paris to face the Pittsburgh Steelers .
Benson concluded by reiterating her commitment to the franchise's supporters.
"We cannot change the results of our first five games. We are responsible for what we do next. I expect better. Our fans deserve better. And I am determined to see that we deliver it."

title: Social Media Rips Saints After Loss to Vikings, Lack of Homefield Advantage
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints' frustrating start to the 2026 season continued Sunday with a 23-13 loss to the undefeated Minnesota Vikings , dropping New Orleans to 1-4 and intensifying criticism surrounding second-year head coach Kellen Moore.
What was supposed to be a memorable afternoon celebrating Drew Brees' induction into the Saints Ring of Honor instead became another disappointing chapter in a season rapidly slipping away.
The Saints managed just 142 yards of total offense, while quarterback Tyler Shough struggled against Minnesota's relentless defensive pressure. Even an 87-yard fumble return touchdown by rookie safety Jonas Sanker wasn't enough to prevent New Orleans from suffering its fourth loss in five games.
The defeat also highlighted the Saints' deteriorating home-field advantage, with Vikings fans making their presence felt inside the Caesars Superdome.
As frustration continues to grow, three major talking points have emerged surrounding Moore's coaching, the defense's performance and the team's inability to protect its home field.
Of everyone facing criticism amid the New Orleans Saints' disappointing start, second-year head coach Kellen Moore has arguably received the most.
While Moore faced scrutiny throughout his first season, many fans remained patient, understanding that the franchise was undergoing a rebuild. However, that patience has steadily worn thin, particularly following the Saints' embarrassing loss to the Atlanta Falcons on the 20th anniversary of Domecoming .
The criticism reached a new level following Sunday's loss to Minnesota, marking New Orleans' third consecutive defeat, all coming inside the Caesars Superdome.
Much of the frustration centered on Moore's offensive play calling and his inability to make adjustments against Minnesota's relentless blitz packages.
Offensive sequences don't get much worse than this: MIN 46 1-10: Kendre Miller run (-1) MIN 47 2-11: Holding, Donaldson (-10) NO 43 2-21: False start (-5) NO 38 2-26: INT, Shough, plus, holding Kamara (-10, declined)
Even Saints legend Drew Brees questioned the predictability of Moore's offense during Fox's broadcast, further fueling criticism of the struggling head coach.
Drew Brees has been disgusted with Kellen Moore's play-calling all game. He's just dropping hints without bashing his franchise too hard.
The only reason Brees doesn’t really cut loose on this organization is because he doesn’t want to hurt Loomis or Gayle. But what he just said about our offense is probably the most blunt he can be without trying to offend them.
With New Orleans managing just 142 total yards, including 96 passing, questions continue to mount about Moore's offensive philosophy, game planning and ability to turn the franchise around.
What began as patience during a rebuilding process has increasingly turned into frustration, with fans questioning whether Moore is the right coach to lead the Saints into the future.
Someone threw out a great stat on my show last week.  Not a positive one but… The @Saints have a lower winning percentage post @drewbrees than before him arriving in New Orleans.  That includes the teams first 20 years of ineptness.  Last 5+ years, some lousy football. Not good
In Kellen Moore's 22 games with the #Saints : - 7-15, 3-8 at home. - Have never scored more than 7 in the 1st quarter. - 1 first-quarter lead. - 4 first-half leads. - Fewest 1st quarter points scored (35) - Most 1st quarter 3-and-outs (29) - Third-worst turnover margin (-10)
While the offense received much of the blame, the defense also drew scrutiny after allowing Minnesota to produce its most productive offensive performance of the season.
The Vikings finished with 364 total yards, including 153 rushing, while quarterback Kyler Murray threw for 229 yards and rushed for another 54.
Aaron Jones rushed for 113 yards and a touchdown, while Justin Jefferson added six receptions for 79 yards and a touchdown. He became the third player to rush for over 100 yards or more after Detroit's Jahmyr Gibbs and Atlanta's Bijan Robinson
This isn't the only bad performance as New Orleans allowed Atlanta to have over 420 yards, including 205 on the ground.
While they haven't allowed as many gaudy passing yards (because their opponents are having success running the ball), the Saints secondary isn't any better.
Cornerback Kool-Aid McKinstry has been a major liability in the Saints' secondary through five games, earning a dismal 55.6 overall Pro Football Focus (PFF) grade and an even worse 51.7 coverage grade. Opposing quarterbacks have completed 60.7% of their passes when targeting him, resulting in 255 yards and a touchdown, while McKinstry has yet to record an interception.
That has earned him the nickame "Sugar Water McKinstry" from ESPN 104.5 radio host Matt Moscona.
LMAO Matt Moscona called Kool-Aid McKinstry “Sugar Water McKinstry” 😭😭 ultimate slander name pic.twitter.com/H2r78MvHk4
Despite forcing two turnovers, including Sanker's fumble return touchdown, the Saints struggled to get Minnesota off the field in critical situations.
That scoop and score was the perfect embodiment of being a Saints fan since Brees has retired. The second you get excited and rejuvenated, they turn right around and kill your vibes.
The performance raised further questions about a defense that has struggled with consistency throughout the early season.
While the Saints’ defense surrendered season-high numbers to a weak Minnesota offense , Sunday's loss highlighted a bigger issue off the field: the Caesars Superdome has lost its elite home-field advantage.
Historically one of the NFL's toughest environments, the venue no longer intimidates visitors. New Orleans has dropped three of four home games this season and sits at 15-21 at home since coach Sean Payton left after 2021, with only one winning home season (5-3 in 2023). The collapse is even sharper recently, with 14 losses in their last 17 home games since 2024.
Compounding the loss, traveling Vikings fans filled the stands with loud "Skol" chants.
Fan frustration continues to grow alongside the home struggles, proving that restoring the Dome's advantage requires winning games, not just past reputation. Until Moore's team delivers, visiting crowds will remain right at home.
It’s bad pic.twitter.com/rrwsCU7nPV
For perspective on how many Vikings fans were in the Superdome today. There was a Saints third down late in the game that you might’ve thought this was a road game. Tough to put into words just how far down the sentiment around this season has fallen in the span of three weeks. pic.twitter.com/Ne8pCQBUDa
In a span of 7 days, you can hear audible ATL chants and SKOL chants. What this franchise has done to our Superdome since Brees retired should be punishable by crime.

title: Drew Brees Questions Kellen Moore's Offense as Saints' Struggles Continue Against Vikings
full_text:
During the second half of the New Orleans Saints' 23-13 loss to the Minnesota Vikings , franchise legend Drew Brees openly criticized head coach Kellen Moore 's offensive approach on a nationwide broadcast.
Working as a Fox analyst shortly after being inducted into the Saints Ring of Honor at halftime, Brees pointed to New Orleans' inability to adjust against Minnesota's relentless blitzing defense .
Specifically, Brees called the Saints' first-down play calling "pretty predictable," questioned the lack of play-action passes, and criticized setup choices that left running back Alvin Kamara in unfavorable matchups.
"You gotta have answers," Brees said, highlighting the team's ongoing struggles in front of a national audience.
Quarterback Tyler Shough suffered through the toughest game of his fledgling career as the Saints (1-4) were held to a paltry 142 total yards—their lowest output since Week 2 of 2021.
Preliminary charting from Pro Football Focus showed Minnesota bringing blitz pressure on 23 of Shough's 27 dropbacks. The second-year passer managed only 16 completions on 25 attempts for 96 yards, throwing two interceptions and posting a career-worst 38.1 passer rating.
Head coach Kellen Moore admitted the team's offensive strategy was ineffective against the Vikings' aggressive scheme.
"I felt like we had a plan (against the blitz)," Moore stated. "Obviously the plan wasn't good enough. They did a better job."
"Obviously, that's on me."
The offensive struggles stemmed from an inability to sustain early momentum and adapt late. New Orleans opened with a promising 15-play, 66-yard scoring drive capped by a 1-yard Kendre Miller touchdown run, but the rushing attack completely stalled afterward. Over their next six drives, the Saints generated a mere 10 yards on the ground as penalties and negative plays continually forced them into obvious passing downs.
A reluctance to adjust the play calling aggravated these issues down the stretch. According to FTN Fantasy, New Orleans entered the contest utilizing play action on just 17.7% of offensive snaps—the fourth-lowest rate in the NFL. Against Minnesota, they called only one play-action pass, which gained 14 yards to Chris Olave .
Special teams miscues and missed chances further doomed the Saints. Jayden Price lost a fumble on the second-half opening kickoff, while Daniel Carlson missed a point-after attempt following an 87-yard fumble return touchdown by Jonas Sanker .
The defense's takeaway went unrewarded, while Minnesota (5-0) anticipated the Saints' aerial concepts, as demonstrated by Byron Murphy intercepting Shough on a late double move intended for Olave.
"They were really prepared for those moments," Shough remarked.
With a 1-4 record through five games, Moore faces mounting criticism during a difficult start to his second year, as New Orleans struggles with preparation, execution, and identity.
"Sometimes, you go through storms," Moore acknowledged. "Inevitably, storms end. But we're going through a little bit of one."

title: Saints vs. Vikings: The Good, Bad and Ugly From New Orleans' 23-13 Loss
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints' struggles continued Sunday as they fell 23-13 to the Minnesota Vikings inside the Caesars Superdome.
The defeat dropped New Orleans to 1-4 for the second consecutive season, further exposing the growing problems facing second-year head coach Kellen Moore and a team that continues to take steps backward .
Here is the Good, Bad and Ugly from the Saints' 23-13 loss to the Vikings.
In one of the few bright spots in the loss to the Vikings, Saints 2nd year safety Jonas Sanker provided a game-changing spark by returning a fumble 88 yards for a touchdown to tie the game at 13-13 late in the second quarter.
Sanker's touchdown demonstrated that New Orleans still has young players capable of making an impact despite a disappointing 1-4 start, though Daniel Carlson subsequently missed the go-ahead extra point.
Fumble 🗣️ Jonas Sanker recovers and takes it to the end zone to tie it up! @MINvsNO on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/W52Ypr6gtT
The second-year defensive back has been tasked with helping rebuild a Saints defense that has undergone significant turnover, delivering an impressive defensive scoring play against Minnesota's undefeated squad.
Ultimately, the Saints' offense failed to capitalize on the momentum, leaving the defense with little margin for error as New Orleans dropped its fourth game of the season.
Shough has been the Saints’ best player throughout the season as he, along with a few others, is the bright spot on what is a bad football team at the moment and if it weren’t for him this season would be a complete disaster.
However, his performance was not good enough for New Orleans to win this game.
Shough had his worst game of the season, completing 16 of his 25 passes for only 96 yards and two interceptions. A lot of his struggles could be placed on the Vikings’ defense and their blitz packages, which present a lot of looks that could deceive a quarterback and his offensive line.
"It was obviously very difficult," Shough said of going up against Minnesota’s defense. "They presented a lot of looks. That's what they're extremely good at. I felt like we were ready for all those looks. We just didn't execute in some of those moments, and now we're second and 20, or third and 15, and — I mean, you're not — those odds are not really in your favor for those situations.
"And we got to be in those third-and-six, third-and-five, third-and-three ranges, where we can convert and dictate tempo. We had a couple good drives and moments, but I don't care who we're playing, we got to be better there. And especially against that team, they're really well coached, really played really well."
While the Saints’ defense allowed a putrid Minnesota offense to put up its best numbers of the season, the most concerning aspect of Sunday's defeat occurred off the field.
The game served as a stark reminder that the Caesars Superdome no longer offers the formidable environment it was once famous for.
Historically, New Orleans boasted one of the premier home-field advantages in the NFL, where deafening crowd noise and an unyielding Saints team made life miserable for visiting opponents.
That distinct edge appears to have vanished.
The Saints have lost all of their four home games this year (including preseason), extending a troubling pattern that began after former head coach Sean Payton left the team following the 2021 campaign.
Since Payton's departure, New Orleans has posted a sub-.500 record of 15-21 at home, managing just a single winning season in the Superdome (5-3 in 2023).
The situation has grown even more dire recently, as the Saints have dropped 14 of their last 17 home contests since the start of 2024.
Yet, the venue's atmosphere on Sunday was perhaps just as unsettling as the loss itself.
A massive contingent of traveling Vikings supporters made their presence felt, filling the Superdome with loud, distinct "Skol" chants.
For perspective on how many Vikings fans were in the Superdome today. There was a Saints third down late in the game that you might’ve thought this was a road game. Tough to put into words just how far down the sentiment around this season has fallen in the span of three weeks. pic.twitter.com/Ne8pCQBUDa
For an organization that built its reputation on creating a hostile environment for opponents, watching opposing fans dominate sections of the stadium underscored the team's ongoing decline.
Understandably, persistent losing eventually takes a toll on crowd enthusiasm and game-day attendance.
With little evidence of progress on the field, fan frustration continues to mount alongside the team's home struggles.
Reestablishing a true home-field advantage will require more than past glory or fan loyalty.
It must be reclaimed by winning football games.
Until Moore and the Saints deliver better results in front of their home crowd, visiting teams and their fans will continue to feel right at home in New Orleans.

title: Saints Must Accomplish 3 Things to End Minnesota's Perfect Start
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints (1-3) enter Sunday's Week 5 matchup against the unbeaten Minnesota Vikings (4-0) looking to bounce back from a humbling 45-24 loss to the Atlanta Falcons on Monday night.
However, getting back on track won't be easy against a Minnesota team that has relied on one of the NFL's most dominant defenses to overcome its offensive struggles.
Sunday's matchup will also be a special occasion for the franchise as legendary quarterback Drew Brees will be inducted into the Saints Ring of Honor, adding even more significance to a game in which New Orleans desperately needs a victory.
For the Saints, the challenge will be giving their former quarterback and the home crowd something to celebrate while avoiding a third consecutive loss at the Caesars Superdome.
Doing so will require significant improvements on both sides of the ball, particularly against a Vikings defense that has consistently overwhelmed opposing offenses.
Here are three keys to victory for the Saints as they look to hand Minnesota its first loss of the season.
The Saints’ matchup against the Vikings will hinge on whether New Orleans can handle Minnesota’s league-leading blitz and pressure package. Minnesota enters Week 5 with arguably the NFL's best defense through four games, allowing a league-low 12.8 points per game while racking up 16 sacks, four interceptions and a plus-five turnover differential, the second-best mark in the league.
That is a major concern for a Saints offense that has struggled with consistency, protection, and turnovers. New Orleans has surrendered 12 sacks through four games, turned the ball over too often and enters Sunday with a minus-five turnover differential. Against a defense that thrives on disguising coverages, generating pressure from different alignments and forcing difficult decisions, the Saints cannot afford to fall behind early or repeatedly find themselves in obvious passing situations.
The biggest individual matchup is quarterback Tyler Shough against Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores ’ blitz-heavy system. Shough has already been sacked a dozen times this, with nine coming against the blitz, and New Orleans will need clear answers built into the game plan to avoid exposing him to the same issues again.
There are reasons for optimism. When Shough has gotten the ball out against blitzing defenses, he has been productive, posting a 105.1 passer rating while completing 71.9% of his passes and throwing for 442 yards, four touchdowns and one interception. But Minnesota has been uniquely effective at creating negative plays, and the Vikings’ No. 2 pressure rate will make life difficult if the Saints cannot keep the pocket clean.
Containing opposing top receivers has plagued the Saints through four games, making Sunday’s matchup against Vikings superstar Justin Jefferson a severe challenge.
Despite Minnesota ranking last in passing and 31st in total offense, Jefferson’s elite route-running, explosiveness, and contested-catch ability threaten New Orleans’ vulnerable secondary.
These defensive struggles were evident in Week 3 when Raiders tight end Brock Bowers posted 10 catches, 119 yards, and a touchdown from Kirk Cousins in Las Vegas' 31-28 win.
They continued Monday against Atlanta, as Drake London caught five passes for 96 yards, including a 37-yarder over Kool-Aid McKinstry , despite the Falcons leaning on the run.
New Orleans' secondary has struggled with missed tackles, blown coverages, penalties, and big plays.
Falcons quarterback Michael Penix Jr. averaged 11.2 yards per attempt, going 15-for-20 for 223 yards and a touchdown.
Cornerbacks Quincy Riley (58 yards, TD allowed; 28.0 PFF grade) and McKinstry (60 yards allowed, two penalties; 29.5 PFF grade) were especially exploited.
These defensive flaws create major concerns facing Jefferson.
Unlike Bowers' versatile tight end mismatches or London's size, Jefferson combines route precision, speed, and versatility across alignments.
Leaving McKinstry or Riley isolated on Jefferson could prove disastrous for defensive coordinator Brandon Staley .
New Orleans must disguise coverages and offer safety help to force Kyler Murray elsewhere.
However, over-committing to Jefferson risks leaving tight end T.J. Hockenson (13 catches, 119 yards last week vs. Miami ) open underneath against an injured Saints linebacker corps.
Ultimately, New Orleans must force Minnesota into long, sustained drives without letting Jefferson dominate.
The four-game difference between these teams centers on protecting the football and capitalizing on errors.
Minnesota's plus-five turnover differential ranks tied for second-best in the NFL, whereas New Orleans ranks among the worst at minus-five. This 10-turnover gap clarifies how undefeated Minnesota overcomes an unproductive offense, while New Orleans loses despite averaging 367 yards and 26.3 points.
The Saints cannot afford to let turnovers, defensive breakdowns, and self-inflicted mistakes ruin offensive output against Minnesota's elite defense. Additionally, the Vikings lead the league in punt return average and rank second in kickoff return average, threatening a Saints squad already struggling with field position.
To succeed, New Orleans must secure the ball, limit penalties, convert in the red zone, force long drives, and avoid slow starts that play into Flores's pressure scheme. Even with Drew Brees honored at halftime and a supportive home crowd, emotional momentum will not offset repeated mistakes.

title: Saints Face a Vikings Team With One Major Strength and a Glaring Weakness
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints will have their hands full Sunday when they welcome one of the NFL's remaining undefeated teams to the Caesars Superdome.
Coming off a 45-24 loss to the Atlanta Falcons on Monday night, New Orleans (1-3) will look to avoid its fourth consecutive defeat against a Minnesota Vikings team that has emerged as one of the NFL's early surprises.
Minnesota enters Week 5 with a 4-0 record following a 15-10 victory over the Miami Dolphins. While the Vikings haven't necessarily overwhelmed opponents offensively, their defense has been among the league's best, and they've consistently found ways to win close games.
Under head coach Kevin O'Connell , Minnesota has relied on a combination of aggressive defense, timely offensive production and an ability to capitalize on opponents' mistakes.
Here are three things Saints fans should know about the Vikings heading into Sunday's matchup.
Sunday’s matchup between the Saints and Vikings will hinge on whether New Orleans can handle Minnesota’s league-leading blitz and pressure package. Minnesota enters Week 5 with arguably the NFL's best defense through four games, allowing a league-low 12.8 points per game while racking up 16 sacks, four interceptions and a plus-five turnover differential, the second-best mark in the league.
That is a major concern for a Saints offense that has struggled with consistency, protection and turnovers. New Orleans has surrendered 12 sacks through four games, turned the ball over too often and enters Sunday with a minus-five turnover differential. Against a defense that thrives on disguising coverages, generating pressure from different alignments and forcing difficult decisions, the Saints cannot afford to fall behind early or repeatedly find themselves in obvious passing situations.
The biggest individual matchup is quarterback Tyler Shough against Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores ’ blitz-heavy system. Shough has already been sacked 12 times this season, with nine coming against the blitz, and New Orleans will need clear answers built into the game plan to avoid exposing him to the same issues again.
There are reasons for optimism. When Shough has gotten the ball out against blitzing defenses, he has been productive, posting a 105.1 passer rating while completing 71.9% of his passes and throwing for 442 yards, four touchdowns and one interception. But Minnesota has been uniquely effective at creating negative plays, and the Vikings’ No. 2 pressure rate will make life difficult if the Saints cannot keep the pocket clean.
New Orleans (1-3) will need to rely on a game plan that can sustain those positive trends under pressure. Without much help from the rushing attack, the Saints must produce through the air to pull out their first home win, and Minnesota is built to complicate exactly that.
A key question for Sunday's game is whether Minnesota All-Pro receiver Justin Jefferson will play.
Jefferson, who has 13 catches for 179 yards and two touchdowns in three games, is recovering from a Week 3 ankle injury. After missing last week's game against Miami, he returned to practice on a limited basis and has been listed as questionable for Sunday’s game.
With a bye following Sunday's game, Minnesota is evaluating whether to rest Jefferson to allow additional recovery time before Oct. 25, according to head coach Kevin O'Connell.
The Vikings face other offensive injury concerns: receiver Jordan Addison (hamstring) and tackle Brian O'Neill are also questionable, while tackle Christian Darrisaw will miss the game.
Jefferson's absence would aid a struggling Saints secondary, though Minnesota still retains offensive threats like tight end T.J. Hockenson .
Despite being undefeated, the Vikings have averaged just 21.5 points (18th in the NFL) and 263 yards per game.
Quarterback Kyler Murray has 433 passing yards, one touchdown and two interceptions. Running back Aaron Jones leads Minnesota with 297 rushing yards, while tight end T.J. Hockenson leads the team with 22 catches for 195 yards and one score.
In their 15-10 win over Miami, the Vikings did not score a single touchdown, highlighting their reliance on defense.
If New Orleans can contain Jones, limit Murray and force long third downs, it will have a chance to keep the game competitive. However, the Saints must still score against a formidable Minnesota defense to avoid another loss.

title: Giants Hold Their Position in Week 6 MMQB Power Rankings
full_text:
For most New York Giants players and fans, it was tough to say how they should have felt after the franchise’s 27-27 overtime tie with the Washington Commanders in Week 5.
Head coach John Harbaugh summed it up best, saying he was “happy it wasn’t a loss and sad it wasn’t a win.” It was a performance that showed two very different sides of his locker room on either side of halftime.
Even SI’s Conor Orr seemed stuck in the middle about how to analyze Big Blue’s surprising final result, which is why he held firm on their spot in his weekly MMQB NFL power rankings , leaving the Giants at No. 21 ahead of Week 6.
“I think my favorite part of the disastrous end-of-game Commanders-Giants footage is when Deonte Banks flies across the line of scrimmage after the clock strikes zero. Followed closely by the fact that the most game situation-aware player on the field during that moment was rookie Arvell Reese,” Orr said.
Sunday’s draw might go down as one of the craziest finishes of the season, but for Harbaugh’s Giants, it was a Week 5 testament to the never-say-die culture the Super Bowl-winning coach has instilled in every player and coach under his wing.
Aside from another week of less-than-favorable weather, the Giants fell behind the Commanders early as their offense struggled to move the ball. Even when they did, the kicking game didn't help, as Dominic Zvada missed three field goals.
The Commanders came out swinging in the second half. They scored back-to-back touchdowns off the speedy legs of quarterback Jayden Daniels to extend their lead to 27-13 entering the final frame of regulation.
Given the organization’s recent history, that used to be the kind of situation that would make the Giants keel over and accept defeat.
Instead, they made the right adjustments, including letting Jameis Winston go a little off-script and testing the Commanders’ secondary with his arm and a duo of active pass-catchers in Malik Nabers and Isaiah Likely.
The result was Winston regaining his confidence as he completed 74.6% of his passes in the second half, including three touchdown connections to Nabers and Likely that leveled the score and gave the Giants a chance to win in overtime.
New York never found the one scoring play it needed to escape Washington with the coveted win, but the tie helped it hold its first-place lead in the division.
More importantly, Winston found a way to silence the outside critics who were about two more ugly quarters away from shouting from the rooftops for the recently acquired backup J.J. McCarthy to supplant him as the starter.
The only question that lingers is whether he and the Giants offense can learn from the few mistakes that nearly cost them the game against the Commanders and get back into the win column next Sunday, when they host the New Orleans Saints at MetLife Stadium.
Any result on the NFL gridiron can offer some takeaways for a growing team, and this past week’s game showed that the Giants have the heart and talent to compete with whoever is in front of them and overcome adversity.
Even against tougher opponents in the second half of the year, that fight should remind everyone that an early lead on the scoreboard won’t be enough to feel comfortable that they’ve buried this Giants team.

title: NFL Insider Explains Why Giants Really Traded for J.J. McCarthy
full_text:
New York Giants quarterback Jameis Winston, one of the league’s best veteran backups , is playing well enough to keep the Giants at 2-0-1 since taking over as the starter for the injured Jaxson Dart.
But some skeptics still believe it’s only a matter of time before Winston is benched in favor of J.J. McCarthy, whom the Giants acquired in a trade with the Minnesota Vikings a couple of weeks ago.
Speculation has intensified after Giants head coach John Harbaugh not only acknowledged that a package of plays was ready for McCarthy just one week into the quarterback’s tenure with the team, but also said McCarthy saw the field for a handful of snaps Sunday.
Does that mean Winston is officially on notice that he will be pulled from the lineup the moment he has a bad game?
“I don’t see a scenario anytime soon in which J.J. is playing,” NFL insider Jordan Schultz told the Locked On Giants podcast .
“I think as long as Jameis continues to play well, it’ll be a minute before J.J.’s on the field.”
Winston, a team captain and member of the eight-player leadership council, is highly respected in the locker room. He has also drawn praise from Harbaugh and offensive coordinator Matt Nagy, both of whom, at least for now, are willing to take the good with the bad.
So why trade for McCarthy, the No. 10 overall pick in the 2024 draft? What’s the plan for him going forward? And is there a world in which McCarthy might actually challenge Dart for the starting job?
“Dart’s the guy, and they want him to be the guy for the next decade,” Schultz said. “There was a misconception, I think, nationally about the McCarthy trade. They did not trade for J.J. McCarthy to supplant Jameis Winston. They traded for him because the price had dropped significantly.
“Jim and John Harbaugh had multiple conversations about the type of person and player he can be. As he explained to me, John Harbaugh loved [McCarthy’s] hockey background, his toughness, and much of the winning he did at Michigan. But he’s not going to be the starter.”
Jim Harbaugh, John’s brother, coached McCarthy at Michigan.
McCarthy, according to Schultz, is additional insurance in case the injury bug hits the Giants’ quarterback room again. However, the league insider acknowledged that if the wheels fall off on the Giants offense with Winston under center, things could change.
For now, the Giants are simply evaluating what they have in McCarthy, who has a positive relationship with Nagy.
“They do wanna see whether or not someone drafted that high and that young is capable of being a backup or even a starter at some point,” Schultz said, adding that there could be more sightings of McCarthy on the field “in certain situations.”
But not as a starter, at least not for the immediate future.
“That would really surprise me,” Schultz said. “If Jameis were to play really badly in a couple of weeks in a row and they lost two in a row, I think it’s a different conversation. I don’t really expect that to happen.
“Not only did they sign Jameis, but they extended him, and they gave him real money in a two-year extension. And that was, I think, a manifestation of how they feel about him, knowing that if he did need to start and play, he could win them football games.”
“There is a lot more unknown about McCarthy than Jameis,” he continued. “I think McCarthy will play at some point, but I’m thinking more of a supplemental role.”

title: Giants Rookie Report after Week 5 Tie Vs. Commanders
full_text:
The New York Giants had to place a lot of trust in their rookies from the jump, and after five games, they should be pretty satisfied with the results.
There have been rough patches, and there will be more before the season's end, but the newcomers have made a noticeable difference overall.
Justin Melo of NFL Draft On SI agrees, as he ranked Big Blue's 2026 draft class No. 2 in the league (the Cleveland Browns got the top spot). The Giants’ group is teeming with upside, with a few players already contributing meaningful snaps to winning football. Others require more development, however.
Here’s a close-up look at the Giants Class of 2026, including key undrafted rookie free agents, following their 27-27 tie with the Washington Commanders in Week 5 . (Note: Offensive lineman J.C. Davis and defensive lineman Bobby Jamison-Travis were inactive in Week 5, as has been the case for both all season.)
Reese, the 21-year-old linebacker, did not dominate the Washington Commanders on the stat sheet as he did the Arizona Cardinals in Week 4.
Per PFF, he missed a tackle and allowed three receptions for 36 yards in coverage. Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels also beat him with his speed.
That said, Reese still made his presence felt at various points of the game. The No. 5 overall pick posted his first career sack and also recorded nine total tackles.
Also, the stat sheet doesn't necessarily capture the hidden contributions that the rookie first-rounder has made by setting his teammates up for success on a given play.
Despite whatever hiccups he had against Daniels, Reese continues to show stellar athleticism, a high motor, and unyielding power that will keep drawing attention from opponents.
Analysts appear split on tackle-turned-guard Francis "Sisi" Mauigoa’s development so far, but he did not allow a single sack against Washington. He also displayed his eye-catching strength multiple times, bowling over guys while protecting Jameis Winston.
There are still some flaws, though. Mauigoa is learning the intricacies of the interior, which shows in his spotty run-blocking. The offensive line as a unit needs to improve there, and with time, the 6-foot-6, 335-pounder should get more comfortable.
It is, however, fair to say he’s trending in the right direction.
Expectations are reasonably high for a top-40 draft selection, and cornerback Colton Hood could still meet them. Still, the solid play of starters Greg Newsome II and Deonte Banks has given Hood time to acclimate to the speed of the game, where he has done so by contributing on special teams.
In Week 5 against Washington, Hood led the Giants with three special teams tackles before a head injury forced him out of the game. He was particularly sharp on kickoff coverage, taking smart angles to force the returner into the coverage.
Defensively, Hood was pressed into action when Banks missed two games with a calf injury. Per PFF, he’s allowed six catches for only 49 yards , and yes, he’s been a magnet for opposing quarterbacks.
But Hood has shown the intensity and skill set that will ultimately pay off for him in this aggressive defensive system.
Although he has only 17 targets, Fields, the big-bodied pass-catcher, is showing impressive skills and instincts.
He totaled two receptions for 20 yards this past Sunday, but might have racked up bigger numbers if he had been thrown to more often. Right now, the coaches seem to be asking him to put his strong downfield blocking skills on more of a display.
But as a pass target, Fields gained notable separation at times, making him a valuable deep threat in the long term. The 6-foot-4 wideout has also yet to drop a pass this season, displaying the kind of sure hands the Giants have lacked in the past.
It might just be a matter of time before Fields gets more involved in the deep passing game, especially if the Giants move away from a struggling, run-heavy offense and let quarterback Jameis Winston do what he does best: sling the ball downfield.
Kelly, the sixth-rounder out of BYU, has not logged a snap at linebacker but has, as expected, stepped into a big role on special teams.  This past week, he nearly blocked a punt late in the first half. He also has one special teams tackle on the year.
New York has made significant progress in the third phase of the game, and this Day 3 pick is one reason why.
It was unrealistic to expect rookie kicker Dominic Zvada never to miss a field goal attempt. So after converting the first nine attempts of his NFL career, his bad day at the office came against Washington in clearly unfavorable weather conditions.
Rain is often unkind to this position, and this outing was no exception. Nevertheless, three misfires warrant fair criticism if you believe a kicker should be able to function regardless of the weather.
Zvada was unsuccessful on attempts from 50, 57, and 46 yards. He did connect from 51 and 56 yards, though, so perhaps there is little reason to worry moving forward. The 22-year-old has earned the benefit of the doubt.

title: Giants Defense and Special Teams Report Card: Dru Phillips Shines, Run Defense Struggles Against Commanders
full_text:
The New York Giants’ defense rode an emotional roller coaster Sunday in a 27-27 tie with the Washington Commanders.
It started badly, with Washington driving 69 yards for a touchdown in four plays on its opening possession, and it continued to be gashed by Washington quarterback Jayden Daniels’ legs all afternoon. The Commanders finished with 202 rushing yards, and Daniels alone had 103 of those plus two touchdowns.
Eventually, though, Giants defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson changed things up a bit and began to blitz more. Per Next Gen Stats, the Giants blitzed 62% of the time (24 times)  against the Commanders, with four of the sacks against quarterback Jayden Daniels coming via the blitz.
Fourteen of the 24 blitzes Wilson dialed up came in the fourth quarter and overtime, and in 10 dropbacks by Daniels, the Giants ran Cover 0 (no deep safeties), resulting in three sacks.
Here is how each defensive player and special teams contributor graded out against the Commanders.
The Giants continued to get solid run defense from this veteran, with Reader finishing with five total tackles from the nose tackle spot and getting into the backfield on a couple of other snaps to disrupt things.
Reader is impossible to move off his mark, even against double teams. The Giants are really getting a bang for the buck, as Reader has had as much of an influence on this year’s improved run defense as anybody.
This huge backup nose tackle worked his way into a tackle on the edge, but he was completely invisible on Washington’s opening 33-yard touchdown run.
What Okoye was doing on the field four snaps into the game is a mystery, but he’s got to do something more than be walked out of his gap.
This defense has had two terrible starts these last two games, and it needs fixing.
With three more tackles and another pass knocked down at the line of scrimmage, Harris is a consistent presence along the line.
The coaches would like to get some pass rush out of him, but his pass breakups and solid run defense are contributions enough.
He’s got a nice combination of physicality and mobility, sprinkling in his experience to get to places he probably shouldn’t be able to go.
We’re starting to see flashes of competitiveness from this second-year player. Alexander doesn’t seem as overwhelmed by double teams as he has in the past, and even when pushed back, he fought his way back into the scrum.
This ability to fight and compete needs to show up every week.
Alexander has gotten a healthy snap count these past two weeks, as the coaches are giving him more responsibility.
He contributed two tackles and a solid push upfield on passing downs, including a smart contain on a broken pocket that forced a throwaway.
Alexander finished the game on the field and seems to be gaining that coaching trust.
Getting his first snaps as a member of the Giants’ 2026 team, the veteran interior player lined up exclusively in a three-point stance and managed a solo tackle in very limited action, taking some of the playing time that Chauncey Golston received.
Ward has a way to go before he approaches the weekly impact Golston has been providing.
Recording his second sack of the young season with an electric weakside pass rush, Carter did well to run down the ever-elusive Washington quarterback from behind.
Carter created more havoc late in the game with his pass rush, as the coaching decision to blitz from every angle freed him to avoid double teams and get into attack mode, where he’s at his best.
Carter finished with five total tackles, his best hit coming in overtime when he blasted a back in the flat, forcing a fumble that Washington was fortunate to recover. Had the Giants recovered, it would have been one of the game’s biggest plays.
Overall, Carter was a bit too complacent in accepting a contain edge role and let a tight end block him. He’s got to become more physical defending his edge.
Playing his best game of the season, Thibodeaux created decent pressure off the weak side, something he hasn’t done at all through the first four games.
Though his rush never got home, it was nevertheless enough to force the ball out of the quarterback’s hands on several occasions.
His run containment was consistently solid and physical. The result of all this positive play? One assist on the sheet.
Through five games, Thibodeaux has been quiet (six tackles), despite being blocked almost exclusively one-on-one. Something has to improve.
Elevated from the practice squad for the second time this season, Ford handled himself well on the edges with a consistently physical presence.
He did well to maintain edge containment but never pushed past the pocket; he stayed in his lane and used his hands well.
Ford was also solid against the run, contributing with one solo tackle in his limited snaps. We expect a signing to the roster in the near future.
Reese tied for the team lead with nine tackles (alongside Tremaine Edmunds), including his first NFL sack.
Though last week didn’t have any splash plays that caught the league’s attention, this week brought a handful of big hits that caught Washington’s attention.
Despite the positives, there were also negatives, including a close-up look at the speed of Jayden Daniels, who outran Reese from the pocket on several occasions.
Better positioning will help Reese in the future, as you can’t rely on athletic ability alone; he’s got to play smarter, including proper angling. Daniels really hurt the defense Sunday with 103 scramble yards and two touchdowns.
Reese was the victim on the majority of those scrambles, getting beaten even while spying him. It was too easy.
Among this veteran’s nine tackles was the sack on the last play of the game when the Commanders allowed the clock to run out.
Give Edmunds credit for his smart positioning on this play with the clock ticking down, and for holding onto the quarterback’s legs after taking him to the ground.
Edmunds played another solid, disciplined game that may have lacked the flash plays and perhaps allowed some too-easy midfield completions to the tight ends, but between the tackles he was consistently sharp and alert. It’s rare to see this veteran caught out of position.
It was unusual to see McFadden on the field lining up to blitz on one edge. After a timeout, he then lined up on the opposite edge when a penalty was called.
McFadden then left the field and never got a defensive snap.
Rarely targeted in coverage, Newsome was his typically aggressive self, attacking ball carriers and registering four solo tackles.
The Commanders stayed away from Newsome as much as they could.
Finishing the day with six tackles, Banks also had a pass defensed.
He allowed several key catches to Terry McLaurin in front of him; his tackling was soft, and his reactions to the ball entering his sphere were also extremely cautious.
For instance, on at least one of Daniels’ scrambles, Banks was very slow to get involved.
On Washington’s opening drive, on a 33-yard touchdown run, Banks backed away to avoid contact. It’s who he is: a non-physical football player, the polar opposite of Dru Phillips.
That said, Banks’ coverage ability will make him some money this offseason. His press coverage continues to shine, but his zone coverage doesn’t.
Two weeks ago against Tennessee, we were ready to enshrine Phillips into the Giants’ Hall of Fame, had he only held onto that interception near the goal line. We say that because of how physically (if not viciously) Phillips had played throughout (11 total tackles).
This week, Phillips was nearly as good. Only five tackles, you say? How about the two sacks, both hits that Jayden Daniels did not want to take.
After those sacks—plus two more hits from Phillips’ blitzes—Daniels was getting rid of the ball as fast as he could.
The defense once again went into blitz overload mode, as it did last week, and that changed the complexion of Sunday’s game. Phillips’ blitzing was the difference.
When he hits you, it hurts. He’s got that…

title: Giants Notebook: Harbaugh on Run Defense, Injuries, Purple Hearts and Bryan Hudson
full_text:
The silver lining amid the dark clouds of the New York Giants ’ Week 5 tie with the Washington Commanders is that Big Blue increased its lead over the rest of the division by a half game.
Still, a win would have been nicer.
“I told the guys, ‘Was it a win?’ No. ‘Was it a loss?’ No. It was a tie,” head coach John Harbaugh said after the game on Sunday. “‘How does that make you feel?’ I’m happy it wasn’t a loss, and I’m sad it wasn’t a win. So that’s how I feel. It’s a tie. It’s a heck of a lot better than a loss, but it’s not as good as a win.”
But as with any game, the coaches and players gained additional insight into what they did well and what they didn’t.
For example, the Giants appear to have found the right formula to bring out the best in quarterback Jameis Winston when New York switched to more of a drop-back passing attack.
“It was good, no question. We’ve been talking about some of the tempo stuff,” Harbaugh said. “We’ve been working on that. It’s been part of our system from day one, really. It’s something we built in from the beginning. And it was good to get to it. We’ve been talking about getting to it. We got to it maybe because we had to.
“So yeah, it opened up the offense. It was good to see, and it probably needs to be part of what we’re doing going forward.”
And then there was the “feast or famine” nature of the run defense, which was gouged for 202 yards by the Commanders, the fourth-highest rushing total of Week 5.
“I think we’ve had too many chunk plays overall,” he said. “We’ve had a lot of really good plays, a lot of really good plays in that game where we stuffed the run, which we’re very capable of doing. And then there are a couple of line of scrimmage runs that get out on us that we’re not happy about that can be played so much better.”
Harbaugh said that pre-snap motion is part of the problem.
“Whether we don’t adjust to a motion the right way, we don’t get over in our gaps, we don’t quite come in through the angles,” he said.
“I think sometimes our tackling in the back end is really good. And sometimes it’s not good, especially if it’s spacey. It’s always tough to tackle a really fast ball carrier, especially a scrambling quarterback who can run in man coverage. And that’s what they caught us in.”
Here are three other things we learned from Harbaugh’s Monday video call with the media.
The Giants came out of the game with injuries to three key players: right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor (calf), safety Tyler Nubin (neck), and cornerback Colton Hood (concussion).
“Yeah, the three main guys are going to be day-to-day this week,” Harbaugh said. “They’ll have a chance for the game. We’ll have to see how it goes throughout the course of the week.”
Cornerback Greg Newsome II was also banged up in the game, though the nature of his injury isn’t known. But Harbaugh didn’t see Newsome’s ailment as one that might keep him out of practice this week, saying that the cornerback “was fine.”
Harbaugh did not offer any updates on safety Jason Pinnock, who missed Sunday’s game with a concussion suffered in the win over Arizona. Pinnock is thought to have traveled with the team to Washington, which would suggest he may be further along in the protocol.
Harbaugh also didn’t want to say whether cornerback Paulson Adebo, who now eligible to have his 21-day practice window opened, would be back at practice this week.
Harbaugh has implemented a merit-based patch system in which players are recognized for superlative efforts with a patch that’s stitched to their practice jerseys. Previously reported patches have rewarded players for meeting a percentage of offseason program attendance and for having played in the postseason as Giants.
He has added a “Purple Heart” patch to the collection. “It’s one of our awards for guys that are working through injury-type things, that they play, or they come back from,” he said.
He revealed that receiver Malik Nabers received a Purple Heart in Week 1, and offensive lineman Andrew Thomas, who has been battling a groin issue over the last several weeks, was a recent recipient.
“I think he’s doing a really good job of just playing through whatever he’s got,” Harbaugh said.
“Guys have things this time of year. He’s doing a great job. He’s so tough. Got the Purple Heart last week. He’s playing at a high level. I mean, it may be laboring for him, but still the result is better than almost every player in the league at that position.”
Harbaugh confirmed that Bryan Hudson will remain the team’s starting center for the upcoming game against the New Orleans Saints.
Harbaugh, who generally doesn’t like to reveal personnel plans, praised Hudson, who has now started two games in place of John Michael Schmitz.
Hudson has allowed just one pressure in 102 pass-blocking snaps , and is PFF’s second-highest-graded Giants offensive lineman in pass blocking, behind Eluemunor.
Hudson has really stood out in run-blocking, where his 72.3 run-blocking grade is the best among Giants offensive linemen this season.
“He played well in the game the week before, and he played well in this past game,” Harbaugh said. “Things he can do better, but things he did really well, and that’s what we based it on.”
The Giants head coach added that Schmitz is still in the plans. However, Harbaugh didn’t specify whether he meant the offense or special teams, where Schmitz contributed in Week 5 against the Commanders. Schmitz did not play in Week 4 against the Cardinals despite being active.

title: Giants Add Dawuane Smoot to Practice Squad Amid Run Defense Concerns
full_text:
The New York Giants continued their search for defensive line help on Monday by signing defensive lineman Dawuane Smoot to their practice squad.
Per the league’s transaction wire, Smoot had been in for a visit, while fellow defensive linemen Julian Okwara and Yannick Ngakoue were both in for tryouts.
Smoot is a 10-year NFL veteran who entered the league as a third-round pick in 2017. The 31-year-old has played in 127 games with 21 career starts and has 27 sacks.
Smoot, 6-foot-3 and 275 pounds, spent the 2024 season with Buffalo before returning to the Jaguars in 2025.
The Giants have been on a nonstop hunt for defensive line help, focusing on depth behind starters Shelby Harris and D.J. Reader. The Giants’ run defense, in particular, has been inconsistent all season, with the unit running hot and cold.
This past weekend, it ran cold, allowing 202 rushing yards on 30 carries (6.7 avg.) to the Washington Commanders in its Week 5 27-27 overtime tie.
That performance means the Giants’ run defense has allowed 638 total rushing yards, tied for sixth most in the league with Green Bay. And the Giants, who have allowed 5.2 yards per carry to opponents, are tied with the Raiders for second in that category.
“I think we’ve had too many chunk plays overall,” head coach John Harbaugh said of the run defense during his Monday video call.
“We’ve played a kind of feast or famine run defense. We’ve had a lot of really good plays, a lot of really good plays in that game where we stuffed the run, which we’re very capable of doing.
“And then there are a couple of line of scrimmage runs that get out on us that we’re not happy about that can be played so much better. Whether we don’t adjust to a motion the right way, we don’t get over in our gaps, we don’t quite come in through the angles.”
To Harbaugh’s point, the Giants are tied for the seventh-most big-play runs allowed (17) with Arizona and Detroit. The Giants are also tied for the fourth-most rushing plays allowed of 20 or more yards with six.
Reader (53%) and Harris (49%) have handled most of the run defense’s snaps up front, but the dropoff has been most evident behind them.
So the Giants have been trying to find the right blend of backup depth to help fortify their first line of run defense, a process that’s been ongoing even before the Giants traded Dexter Lawrence II earlier this year.
